For example, a berry in a pot; or the eye [sense-faculty], etc. That is 'near.' But 'in an invisible location' is the opposite of that — 'distant.' It is not said 'distant [means] invisible.' For something near too may not be seen because of extreme subtlety. But that is not considered 'distant' because its location is visible. For what purpose does the <s>Bhadanta</s> explain it thus? Because the past, etc. are already designated by their own terms. Otherwise, there would be the fault of redundancy. But their distance and nearness, based on the support

body.text: iti. teṣāṃ vedanādīnām amūrtatvenādeśasthatvāt tasmād evaṃ vaktavyaṃ. dūre adṛśyamānāśrayā vedanādayaḥ. antike dṛśyamānāśrayā iti. audārikasūkṣmatvaṃ pūrvavad iti. audārikaṃ paṃcendriyāśrayaṃ. sūkṣmaṃ mānasam iti.
body.translated_text: — because feeling and the rest, being immaterial, are not located in any place, therefore it should be stated thus: 'Feeling, etc. whose support is not visible are distant. Those whose support is visible are near.' 'Grossness and subtlety as before' — gross is that which has the five sense-faculties as its support. Subtle is that which has the mental [faculty as its support].

body.text: cittacaittānām āyam utpattiṃ tanvantīty āyatanāni. dvayaṃ pratītya vijñānasyotpattir iti sarveṣām āyatanatvasiddhiḥ.
body.translated_text: 'They extend (tanvanti) the scope (āyam), i.e., the arising of mind and mental factors — hence they are <s>āyatanas</s> (sense-bases).' 'Consciousness arises depending on two [factors]' — by this, the status of all as <s>āyatanas</s> is established.

body.text: ekasminn āśraye saṃtāne veti. āśraye samudāyalakṣaṇe śarīre. saṃtāne vā cittādīnāṃ pravāhalakṣaṇe. svasyā jāteḥ. kiṃ. ākarā iti prakṛtaṃ. sabhāgahetutvāt. pūrvotpannaṃ cakṣuḥ paścimasya sabhāgabetur ity ākaro dhātuḥ. yato hi suvarṇādyutpattiḥ. te teṣām ākarāḥ. asaṃskṛtaṃ na dhātuḥ syāt. na hy asaṃskṛtam asaṃskṛtasyānyasya vā sabhāgahetuḥ. [Tib. 40b] cittacaittānāṃ tarhīti. kiṃ. ākarā iti prakṛtaṃ. dvayaṃ pratītya vijñānasyotpattir iti sarvadhātavo vijñānasya sasaṃprayogasya pratyayo 'vaśyam ālambanam adhipatiś cety ākarāḥ.
body.translated_text: 'In one support, or in [one] continuum' — 'support' means the body, characterized as an assemblage. Or 'continuum' — the stream-like character of mind, etc. 'Of one's own type' — what? 'Sources' (ākara) — this is the topic. Because of being a homogeneous cause (<s>sabhāgahetu</s>). The previously arisen eye [is] the homogeneous cause of the subsequent [eye] — hence a source (ākara), a <s>dhātu</s> (element). For the sources of gold, etc. are those from which they arise. 'The unconditioned would not be a <s>dhātu</s>' — for the unconditioned is not a homogeneous cause of the unconditioned or of anything else. [Tib. 40b] 'Then, of mind and mental factors' — what? 'Sources' — this is the topic. 'Consciousness arises depending on two [factors]' — therefore, all <s>dhātus</s> are necessarily objects and dominant conditions for consciousness together with its associated [mental factors] — hence they are sources.

body.text: rāśipudgalavad iti. prajñaptisantaḥ skandhāḥ. rāśiśabdavācyatvāt. dhānyarāśivat. pudgalavad vā. sa hi prajñaptisan pudgalaḥ rūpādiprajñaptikāraṇanirapekṣāgṛhyamāṇasvabhāvatvāt dhānyarāśivat. kāryabhārodvahanārtha iti. kāryam eva bhāraḥ. kāryabhāraḥ. tad uhyate teneti udvahanaṃ. kāryabhārasyodvahanaṃ kāryabhārodvaḥanaṃ. śarīrapradeśaḥ sa loke skandha ity ucyate. anenāpi kāryabhāra uhyate nāmarūpapratyayaṃ ṣaḍāyatanam ityādivacanāt. tasmāt skandha iva skandha ity aupacārikaśabdaḥ. pracchedārtho vā. avadhyartho vety arthaḥ. rūpapracchedo yāvad vijñānapraccheda iti. tad etad utsūtram iti. tad etad ubhayaṃ kāryabhārodvahanārthaḥ pracchedārthaś ceti. utkrāntaṃ sūtrād utsūtraṃ. sūtraṃ hīti vistareṇa tat pratipādayati. pratyekam iti vistaraḥ. katham ity āha. sarvam etad atītādirūpam ekaśaḥ ekaikaṃ rūpaskandha iti. samudāyena samudāyidravyam uktaṃ. teṣāṃ hy atītādīnāṃ rūpāṇāṃ sa rāśir ity abhiprāyaḥ. sūtre 'py evam evoktaṃ. pṛthivīdhātuḥ [Tib. 41a] katamaḥ. keśā romāṇīti vistaraḥ. ekaikaṃ keśādidravyaṃ pṛthivīdhātur iti vijñāyate. ayaṃ ca parihāraḥ kāryabhārodvahanārthapracchedārthapakṣayor spi śakyate vaktuṃ. na śakyaṃ evam iti vistaraḥ. aikadhyam adhisaṃkṣipyeti vacanātirekāt. ekaikaṃ rūpaskandha iti na śakyate vijñātuṃ. yadi hy evam artho 'bhaviṣyat. tat sarvaṃ rūpaskandha ity evāvakṣyat. nārtham aikadhyam abhisaṃkṣipyeti vacanena. tasmād rāśivad eva skandhāḥ prajñaptisanta iti sthāpanāpakṣa ācāryasya. dravyasadrūpapratipattis tu skandhanirdeśe tatsamudāyitvād ity avagantavyaṃ. rūpīṇy apīti vistaraḥ. rūpigrahaṇam arūpiviśeṣaṇārthaṃ. arūpi hi manaāyatanaṃ asaṃhatam api kāraṇabhāvaṃ bibharti. rūpīṇy api
body.translated_text: 'Like a heap or a person' — the aggregates (<s>skandhas</s>) exist as designations (<s>prajñaptisantaḥ</s>), because they are expressible by the word 'heap' (<s>rāśi</s>), like a heap of grain. Or like a 'person' (<s>pudgala</s>) — for that person exists as a designation, because its intrinsic nature cannot be grasped independently of the bases of designation such as form, etc. — like a heap of grain. 'For the purpose of bearing the burden of action' — the action itself is the burden; the bearing of the burden of action. A bodily part that is called 'shoulder' (<s>skandha</s>) in the world — by this too, the burden of action is borne, because of the statement 'the six sense-bases are conditioned by name-and-form,' etc. Therefore, '[skandha]' is like 'shoulder' — a figurative term (<s>aupacārikaśabda</s>). Or in the sense of 'portion' (<s>praccheda</s>) — meaning 'in the sense of a division.' A portion of form, up to a portion of consciousness. 'This is contrary to the sūtra' — this means: both [interpretations] — 'for the purpose of bearing the burden of action' and 'in the sense of portion' — go beyond the <s>sūtra</s>. 'For the sūtra says' — and he establishes this at length. 'Individually' — in detail. How? He says: 'All this form — past, etc. — each one individually goes under the designation form-aggregate.' By 'assemblage,' the substance constituting the assemblage has been stated — for those past etc. forms, that heap is meant — this is the intention. In the <s>sūtra</s> too it is stated thus: 'What is the earth-element? [Tib. 41a] Hair [of the head], hair [of the body]' — in detail. It is understood that each individual substance like hair, etc. is the earth-element. And this resolution can be stated for both alternatives — the 'burden-bearing' and the 'portion' interpretations. 'It cannot be so' — in detail. Because of the additional words 'having subsumed into one' (<s>aikadhyam abhisaṃkṣipya</s>) — it cannot be understood that each individual [entity] is the form-aggregate. For if that were the meaning, [the sūtra] would have said simply 'all that is the form-aggregate.' It would not need the words 'having subsumed into one.' Therefore, the <s>Ācārya</s>'s position is that the aggregates exist merely as designations, like a heap. But the apprehension of substance-like [entities] in the exposition of aggregates should be understood as being due to their being constituents of that assemblage. 'Even material [ones]' — in detail. The term 'material' (rūpin) is for the purpose of qualifying the immaterial. For the immaterial mind-base (<s>manāyatana</s>), even without being assembled, bears the status of being a cause. Material [entities] too

body.text: cakṣurādīni āyatanāni samuditāny eva cittacaittāyadvāratāṃ gacchanti nāsamuditānīti. samudāyalakṣaṇatvāt skandhavat prajñāptisanti syuḥ. saṃcitāśrayālambanā hi paṃcavijñānakāyā iti. na. ekaśaḥ samagrāṇāṃ kāraṇabhāvād iti. naitad evaṃ. kasmāt. ekaśaḥ pratyekaṃ samagrāṇāṃ samuditānāṃ kāraṇatvāt. yasmād bahūnām eṣām cakurādiparamāṇūnāṃ parasparam apekṣyamāṇānām ekaikaśaḥ kāraṇabhāvaḥ. na tv asaṃhatānāṃ. tadyathā dārvākarṣaṇe bahūnām ākraṣṭṝṇāṃ [Tib. 41b] pratyekam asāmarthyaṃ. samuditānāṃ tu parasparam apekṣyamāṇānāṃ sāmarthyaṃ. yathā vā keśāḥ pṛthakpṛthag avasthitā na samarthās taimirikacakṣurvijñānakaraṇe. samuditās tv asaṃyuktā api samarthāḥ. tadvac cakṣurādīndriyaparamāṇavo rūpādiviṣayaparamāṇavaś ca cakṣurādivijñānotpādane pratyekam asamarthāḥ. samuditās tu samarthāḥ. śaktiṛ hi bhāvānāṃ tādṛśy avagantavyā. viṣayasahakāritvād veti. yadi bahūnām āyadvārabhāva iti samudāyāyatanatvaṃ syān na dravyāyatanatvaṃ. indriyaviṣayaparamāṇūnāṃ samuditānām āyadvārabhāva iti tat samudāyāyatanatvaṃ syāt. na pṛthagāyatanatvaṃ syāt. iṣyate ca pṛthagāyatanatvaṃ dvādaśāyatanānīti sūtrāt. sādhanaṃ cātropatiṣṭhate. ye sahakāriṇaḥ. na taiḥ saha samudāyātmakāyatanabhūtāś cakṣurāyatanasamudāyadravyaparamāṇavaḥ. cakṣurvijñānakāraṇatvāt. cakṣurāyatanarūpāyatanasamudāyadravyaparamāṇuvat. yathā cakṣurāyatanasamudāyadravyaparamāṇavaḥ. evaṃ yāvat kāyāyatanasamudāyadravyaparamāṇavo yojyāḥ. vibhāṣāyāṃ tūcyata iti. anenāpi prajñaptisantaḥ skandhā iti vyācaṣṭe. ayaṃ tu viśeṣaḥ. adravyasanto 'pi te tatropacāreṇa pradarśyanta iti. viśeṣārthas tuśabdaḥ. skandhaprajñaptim apekṣate iti. skandha iti prajñaptim apekṣate. rāśir iti prajñaptim [Tib. 42a] apekṣata ity arthaḥ. paramāṇur ekasya dhātor iti. daśānāṃ cakṣurādīnāṃ rūpiṇāṃ dhātūnāṃ anyatamasya pradeśaḥ. evam āyatanānām eṣām evānyatamasya rūpaskandhasya ca pradeśaḥ. kasamāt. na hi prajñaptāv apekṣitāyāṃ pradeśini pravṛttaḥ śabdaḥ pradeśe vyavasthāpyate. atha nāpekṣate. kiṃ. skandhaprajñaptim ity adhikṛtaṃ. sa āha. paramāṇur eko dhātur iti vistaraḥ. sa ekaikas teṣām āyatanadhātūnāṃ yo 'nyatama ukto rūpaskandhaś ca. bhavati hi pradeśe 'pi pradeśivad upacāra iti. pradeśe 'pi paramāṇau anyatamarūpāyatanadhātuvad rūpaskandhavac copacāraḥ. tatra tasyeveti vatiḥ. yathā paṭaikadeśe dagdhe paṭo dagdha iti. yathā paṭaśabdaḥ samudāye pravṛttaḥ. pradeśe 'py upacaryate paṭaikadeśe. tadvat skandhaśabdo
body.translated_text: — the sense-bases beginning with the eye only when assembled become the door for mind and mental factors, not when unassembled. [Objection:] Because of having the character of an assemblage, they would exist as designations, like the aggregates. For the five consciousness-groups have assembled [supports and objects]. [Reply:] No — because [each one] individually when complete is a cause. [Counter-reply:] That is not so. Why? Because individually — that is, each one of the many atoms of the eye, etc. — when complete, [i.e.,] when assembled, [each] is a cause in dependence on the others. But not when unassembled. Just as in dragging timber, [Tib. 41b] many individual draggers are unable [to do it individually], but when assembled, in dependence on one another, they are able. Or, just as individual hairs standing separately are not able to cause the visual consciousness of one with <s>timira</s> (cataract), but when assembled, even though not conjoined, they are able. Likewise, the atoms of the sense-faculties like the eye and the atoms of the sense-objects like form — each individually is unable to produce eye-consciousness, etc. But when assembled, they are able. For the power of entities should be understood to be of this nature. 'Because the sense-object is a co-operating [factor]' — if [you say] 'because many [atoms] function as doors, the sense-base status belongs to the assemblage, not to the substance' — [we reply:] the many atoms of sense-faculty and sense-object, when assembled, function as doors — so that would be assemblage-sense-base status, not individual sense-base status. But individual sense-base status is accepted, from the sūtra 'there are twelve sense-bases.' And a proof is established here: those which are co-operating [factors] — together with them, the atoms that are substances constituting the assemblage of the eye-sense-base are not [themselves] sense-bases — because they are causes of eye-consciousness, like the substance-atoms constituting the assemblage of the eye-sense-base and form-sense-base. As with the substance-atoms of the eye-sense-base assemblage, so up to those of the body-sense-base assemblage should be applied. 'But in the <s>Vibhāṣā</s> it is said' — by this too, he explains that the aggregates exist as designations. But this is the distinction: even though they do not exist as substances, they are shown there figuratively. The word 'but' (tu) is for the purpose of showing the distinction. 'It depends on the designation of aggregate' — it depends on the designation 'aggregate'; [Tib. 42a] it depends on the designation 'heap' — this is the meaning. 'An atom is [an instance] of one dhātu' — a portion of one of the ten material dhātus beginning with the eye. Likewise, a portion of one of these same āyatanas, and of the form-aggregate. Why? For when a designation is in question, the word applied to what possesses parts is not established for a part [alone]. But if it does not depend [on designation] — what? 'The designation of aggregate' — this is the topic. He says: 'An atom is one dhātu' — in detail. Each single one of those āyatanas and dhātus that has been mentioned, and the form-aggregate too. For figurative usage applies to the part just as to what possesses parts. Figurative usage applies to the part — the atom — just as to one of the form-āyatanas and dhātus, and just as to the form-aggregate. 'There, just as' — the word 'just as.' 'Just as when a portion of cloth is burned, one says the cloth is burned.' Just as the word 'cloth' applies to the assemblage, and is figuratively used even for a portion of cloth — likewise the word 'aggregate'

body.text: 'tītādirūpasamudāye pravṛttaḥ. pradeśe 'pi paramāṇāv upacaryata iti. skandhā eva prajñaptisanto nāyatanadhātava iti. rūpādīnāṃ skandhā iti kṛtvā. yadā tu rūpāṇy eva skandhā iti samāsaḥ. tadā dravyasantaḥ skandhā ity abhiprāyaḥ.
body.translated_text: applies to the assemblage of past and other forms, and is figuratively used even for the part — the atom. 'The aggregates alone exist as designations, not the sense-bases and elements.' This is because forms, etc. are 'aggregates' [in the sense described]. But when the compound means 'forms themselves are aggregates,' then the intention is that the aggregates exist as substances.

body.text: idam iha vicāryate. kim atra kāraṇaṃ yad indriyaparamāṇūnāṃ viṣayaparamāṇūnāṃ ca vijñānotpattaye tulye 'py anyonyasāpekṣatve na dvayānām eṣāṃ kevalendriyaparamāṇuvad ekāyatanatvaṃ vyavasthāpyate. yasmāc [Tib. 42b] cakṣurindriyādiparamāṇavaḥ sarve svavijñānotpattau sādhāraṇāni kāraṇāni bhavanti. na tu tathā viṣayaparamāṇavaḥ. tathā hi cakṣurindriyaparamāṇavo nīlaviṣayavijñānotpattāv api kāraṇaṃ bhavanti. pītādivijñānotpattāv api. nīlaviṣayaparamāṇavas tu svavijñānotpattāv eva kāraṇaṃ bhavanti. na pītādivijñānotpattau. ity ataś cakṣurindriyaparamāṇubhis tadviṣayaparamāṇūnām atulyavartitvāt. pṛthaksthānāvasthitatvāt. na cakṣūrūpaparamaṇūnām ekāyatanatvavyavasthānatvaṃ yujyate. evaṃ yāvat kāyendriyaspraṣṭavyaparamāṇūnāṃ ekāyatanatvavyavasthānaṃ na yujyata iti vaktavyaṃ.
body.translated_text: This is being investigated here: What is the reason that, although sense-faculty atoms and object atoms are equally mutually dependent for the arising of consciousness, these two are not established as a single <s>āyatana</s> (sense-base), unlike the sense-faculty atoms alone? Because [Tib. 42b] all the atoms of the eye-faculty, etc. are common causes for the arising of their respective consciousnesses, but the object atoms are not so. For the atoms of the eye-faculty serve as a cause for the arising of consciousness of a blue object, and also for the arising of consciousness of yellow, etc. But the atoms of a blue object serve as a cause only for the arising of their own [blue-]consciousness, not for the arising of consciousness of yellow, etc. Therefore, because the object atoms do not function in the same way as the eye-faculty atoms — because they occupy separate locations — it is not justified to establish the eye and form atoms as belonging to a single <s>āyatana</s>. And so on, up to: it is not justified to establish the body-faculty and tangible atoms as belonging to a single <s>āyatana</s>.

children.translated_text: 'Because of the threefold [division] of delusion, faculties, and inclination' —

body.text: iti. saṃmohaprajñādhimokṣatraidhād ity arthaḥ. trayaḥ prakārās traidham iti. tridhaiva traidham iti svarthe 'ṇpratyaya ity eke. tridhābhāvas traidham iti bhāve 'ṇpratyaya ity apare. mohendriyarucīnāṃ traidhaṃ. tasmād iti. piṇḍātmagrahaṇata iti. kecic caittān piṇḍato gṛhītvā tān evātmato gṛhṇanti. piṇḍagrāhe saty ātmagrāhapravṛtteḥ. teṣāṃ skandhadeśanā. tasyāṃ hi vedanāsaṃjñāsaṃskārabhedena tridhā caittā deśitāḥ. nāyam ekaḥ pinḍaś caittaviśeṣā ihety ātmagrāhaḥ pratipakṣito bhavati. atha vā piṇḍarūpo 'yam ātmabhāvaḥ. sa cātmā vedayitā saṃjñātā cetayiteti kecit saṃmūḍhāḥ. teṣāṃ skandhadeśanā. nāyam ātmarūpaḥ piṇḍaś caittā iheme vedanāsaṃjñāsaṃskārāḥ [Tib. 43a] pravartante ity ātmagrāhaḥ pratipakṣito bhavati. kecid rūpa eveti. piṇḍātmagrahaṇataḥ saṃmūḍhā ity adhikṛtaṃ. teṣām āyatanadeśanā. tasyāṃ hi rūpaṃ cakṣurādibhedena bahudhā vibhaktaṃ. caittās tv aikadhyam eva dharmāyatanatvena cittaṃ ca manaāyatanatveneti. kecid rūpacittayor iti. saṃmūḍhāḥ piṇḍātmagrahaṇata ity adhikṛtam eva. teṣāṃ dhātudeśanā. tasyāṃ hi rūpaṃ cakṣurādibhedena bahudhā vibhaktaṃ. cittaṃ cakṣurvijñānādidhātubhedena. na tu caittā dharmadhātutvenaiva deśitatvād iti. tayā rūpacittapiṇḍagrāhasaṃmohaḥ pratipakṣito bhavati.
body.translated_text: The meaning is: because of the threefold [division] of confusion, insight, and conviction. Three kinds [constitute] 'the threefold.' Some say the <s>aṇ</s>-suffix is in its own sense (<s>svarthe</s>): '<s>tridha</s> itself is <s>traidham</s>.' Others say the <s>aṇ</s>-suffix is in the <s>bhāva</s> sense: 'the state of being threefold is <s>traidham</s>.' The threefold [division] of delusion, faculties, and inclinations. 'Therefore' — 'from grasping the aggregate as self' (<s>piṇḍātmagrahaṇataḥ</s>): some grasp the mental factors (<s>caittas</s>) as an aggregate and then grasp them as self. Because the grasping of self occurs when there is grasping [of them] as an aggregate. For those, the teaching in terms of aggregates (<s>skandhas</s>) [is given]. For in that [teaching], the mental factors are taught as threefold — divided into feeling (<s>vedanā</s>), perception (<s>saṃjñā</s>), and formations (<s>saṃskāra</s>) — and thus the self-grasping [that thinks] 'this single aggregate is the mental factors here' is counteracted. Alternatively, 'this body-form is the self (<s>ātman</s>), and that self is the experiencer, the perceiver, the intender' — some are deluded [in this way]. For those, the teaching of aggregates [is given], and the self-grasping [that thinks] 'this body-like aggregate is the self' is counteracted [by showing]: 'here these are feeling, perception, and formations' [Tib. 43a]. Some are deluded regarding form only — this relates to 'from grasping the aggregate as self.' For those, the teaching of sense-bases (<s>āyatanas</s>) [is given]. For in that [teaching], form is divided in many ways according to the eye-faculty, etc., while the mental factors are grouped together simply as the <s>dharma-āyatana</s>, and mind as the <s>mana-āyatana</s>. Some are deluded regarding both form and mind — this again relates to 'from grasping the aggregate as self.' For those, the teaching of elements (<s>dhātus</s>) [is given]. For in that [teaching], form is divided in many ways according to the eye-faculty, etc., and mind according to the eye-consciousness element, etc. But the mental factors, being taught merely as the <s>dharma-dhātu</s>, are not [further divided]. By that [teaching], the confusion of grasping form and mind as an aggregate is counteracted.

body.text: indriyāṇy apīti vistaraḥ. trividhaḥ pudgalaḥ tīkṣṇamadhyamṛdvindriyatvāt. atha vā trividhaḥ pudgalaḥ udghaṭitajño vipaṃcitajñaḥ padaparama iti.
body.translated_text: 'Faculties too' — and so on in detail. Persons are threefold because of having sharp, medium, and dull faculties. Alternatively, persons are threefold: one who understands at a hint (<s>udghaṭitajña</s>), one who understands through exposition (<s>vipaṃcitajña</s>), and one for whom the words are the maximum (<s>padaparama</s>).

body.text: tatra tīkṣṇendriyāṇāṃ skandhadeśanā. te hi tīkṣṇendriyatvāt skandhabhedenaiva āyatanadhātubhedaṃ pratipattuṃ śaknuvanti. yathoktaṃ yad bhikṣo na tvaṃ sa te dharmaḥ prahātavya iti. ājñātaṃ bhagavann ity āha. yathā katham asya bhikṣo saṃkṣiptenoktasyārtham ājānāsi. rūpaṃ bhadanta nāhaṃ. sa me dharmaḥ prahātavya iti vistaraḥ. madhyendriyāṇām āyatanadeśanā. te hi madhyendriyatvān [Tib. 43b] madhyenaiva nātivistīrṇenāyatanaprabhedena dhātuprabhedaṃ pratipattuṃ śaknuvanti. na tu saṃkṣiptena skandhaprabhedena. mṛdvindriyāṇāṃ dhātudeśanā. te hi mṛdvindriyatvāt nāvibhaktaṃ svabuddhisāmarthyena pratipattuṃ śaknuvanti.
body.translated_text: Of these, for those with sharp faculties, the teaching of aggregates [is given]. For they, being of sharp faculties, are able to understand the division into sense-bases and elements from the division into aggregates alone. As it is said: 'O monk, what is not you, that <s>dharma</s> should be abandoned.' 'Understood, Blessed One,' he said. 'How, O monk, do you understand the meaning of what was briefly stated?' 'Form, Venerable Sir, is not me; that <s>dharma</s> should be abandoned' — and so on in detail. For those with medium faculties, the teaching of sense-bases [is given]. For they, being of medium faculties, [Tib. 43b] can understand the division into elements through the medium-sized — not overly extensive — division into sense-bases, but not through the condensed division into aggregates. For those with dull faculties, the teaching of elements [is given]. For they, being of dull faculties, are unable to understand what has not been analyzed, through the power of their own intelligence.

body.text: rucir api trividheti. pūrvābhyāsayogād ruces traividhyaṃ. atha vā śamathacaritānāṃ saṃkṣiptā ruciḥ. śamathavipaśyanācaritānāṃ madhyā ruciḥ. vipaśyanācaritānāṃ vistīrṇā rucir iti.
body.translated_text: 'Inclination too is threefold' — The threefold [nature] of inclination is due to the connection with previous practice (<s>pūrvābhyāsa</s>). Alternatively, those of <s>śamatha</s>-temperament have a condensed inclination; those of combined <s>śamatha-vipaśyanā</s> temperament have a medium inclination; those of <s>vipaśyanā</s>-temperament have an extensive inclination.

body.text: (I.21) kiṃ punaḥ kāraṇam iti vistaraḥ. nanu ca kāraṇam uktaṃ piṇḍātmagrahaṇataś caittasaṃmūḍhānāṃ skandhadeśaneti. satyam uktaṃ. caittās teṣāṃ vibhaktā iti. vedanāsaṃjñe eva tu saṃskāraskandhāt pṛthak skandhīkṛtaḥ. na punar anya iti kim atra kāraṇaṃ. kāmādhyavasānam iti vistaraḥ. kāmeṣu ca dṛṣṭiṣu cābhiṣvaṃgaḥ. tayor vivādamūlayor adhyavasānayor vedanāsaṃjñe yathākramaṃ pradhānahetur iti. pradhānagrahaṇād avidyādayo 'pradhānahetava ity arthata uktaṃ bhavati. vedanāsvādavaśād dhi kāmān abhiṣvajante gṛhiṇaḥ. viparītasaṃjñāvaśāc ca dṛṣṭīḥ. kim. abhiṣvajanta ity adhikṛtaṃ. adharme dharmasaṃjñino dharme cādharmasaṃjñino 'nātmādiṣu cātmasaṃjñinas tās tādṛśīḥ śīlavrataparāmarśādīr abhiṣvajante. ke te. prāyeṇa pravrajitāḥ. vedanāgṛddho hīti [Tib. 44a] vistaraḥ. vedanāsaktaś caturbhir viparyāsair viparyastaḥ saṃsāre janmaparaṃparāṃ karoti kramakāraṇād iti. catvāri kāraṇāni skandhānukrame vakṣyaṃte.
body.translated_text: (I.21) 'What then is the reason' — and so on in detail. [Objection:] Has not the reason already been stated — 'For those deluded about mental factors, from grasping the aggregate as self, the teaching of aggregates [is given]'? True, it was stated that 'the mental factors have been differentiated for them.' But feeling (<s>vedanā</s>) and perception (<s>saṃjñā</s>) alone have been made into separate aggregates from the formation-aggregate — and not others. What is the reason for this? 'Fixation on desires' — and so on in detail. Attachment to desires and to [wrong] views — these are the two roots of dispute. Feeling and perception are, respectively, the chief cause of those two fixations. By the word 'chief,' it is implied that ignorance, etc. are non-chief causes. For householders, through the influence of savoring feeling, become attached to desires. And through the influence of perverted perception, [they become attached] to views. Which [views]? Those such as grasping at rituals and observances, etc. — perceiving <s>dharma</s> in what is not <s>dharma</s>, non-<s>dharma</s> in what is <s>dharma</s>, and self in what is non-self, etc. — they become attached to such [views]. Who are they? Predominantly, the renunciants. 'One who is greedy for feeling' [Tib. 44a] — and so on in detail. One who is attached to feeling, perverted by the four perversions, generates a succession of births in <s>saṃsāra</s>, because of the sequential causation. Four reasons for the order of the aggregates will be stated.

children.translated_text: 'According to grossness, defilement, vessel[-and-contents], and element' —

body.text: iti. rūpaṃ hi sapratighatvāt sarvaudārikaṃ. arūpiṇāṃ vedanā pracāraudārikatayā. tathā hi vyapadiśanti. haste me vedanā pāde me vedaneti. dvābhyām audārikatarā saṃjñā. vijñānāt saṃskārā ity ato yathaudārikaṃ tat pūrvam uktam ity prathamaṃ kāraṇaṃ. atha vānādimati saṃsāre strīpuruṣā anyonyaṃ rūpābhirāmāḥ. te ca vedanāsvādagardhāt. tadgardhaḥ saṃjñāviparyāsāt. tadviparyāsaḥ kleśaiḥ. cittaṃ ca tatsaṃkliṣṭam iti yathāsaṃkleśaṃ krama iti dvitīyaṃ. bhājanādyarthena vā bhājanabhojanavyaṃjanapaktṛbhoktṛbhūtā hi
body.translated_text: Form, being resistant (<s>sapratigha</s>), is the grossest of all. Among formless [aggregates], feeling is the grossest by way of its range of activity (<s>pracāra</s>). For they designate: 'I have a feeling in my hand, I have a feeling in my foot.' Grosser than both [feeling and formations] is perception. 'Formations are [next] from consciousness' — thus the order follows grossness, and the grosser is stated first. This is the first reason. Alternatively, in beginningless <s>saṃsāra</s>, men and women are delighted by each other's form; and that [delight] is from greed for the savoring of feeling; that greed is from the perversion of perception; that perversion is from the afflictions (<s>kleśas</s>); and the mind is defiled by those — thus the order follows defilement. This is the second [reason]. Or, by the analogy of vessel, etc.: for the aggregates of form, etc. are like the vessel, the food, the condiment, the cook, and the eater —

body.text: rūpādayaḥ skandhā iti tṛtīyaṃ. dhātuto vā kāmarūpaprabhāvito hi kāmadhātuḥ. vedanāprabhāvitāni dhyānāni. saṃjñāprabhāvitās traya ārūpyāḥ. saṃskāramātraprabhāvitaṃ bhavāgram. etā vijñānasthitayas tāsu ca pratiṣṭhitaṃ vijñānam iti kṣetrabījasaṃdarśānārthaḥ skandhānukrama iti caturthaṃ kāraṇam. atha eva ca kramakāraṇāt vedanāsaṃjñe [Tib. 44b] pṛthak skandhīkṛte. yata ete audārikatare saṃkleśānukramahetū bhojanavyaṃjanabhūte tatprabhāvitaṃ ca dhātudvayam iti.
body.translated_text: this is the third [reason]. Or, from the perspective of realms (<s>dhātu</s>): the desire-realm is dominated by desire for form; the <s>dhyānas</s> (meditative absorptions) are dominated by feeling; the three formless [attainments] are dominated by perception; the peak of existence (<s>bhavāgra</s>) is dominated by formations alone. These are the stations of consciousness, and consciousness is established in them — the order of aggregates is for the purpose of showing the field-and-seed [metaphor]. This is the fourth reason. [Tib. 44b] And for just this reason of sequential causation, feeling and perception have been made into separate aggregates — because these are grosser, are the causes in the sequence of defilement, serve as food and condiment, and the pair of realms [<s>dhyāna</s> and formless] is dominated by them.

body.text: (I.22ab) na tāvad eṣv evāntarnetuṃ śakyate arthāyogād iti. rūpaṇāder arthasyāyogād asaṃbhavāt. rūpasvabhāvaṃ yāvad vijñānasvabhāvam iti vā na śakyam eṣv eva paṃcaskandheṣv antarnetum. atatsvābhāvyāt. na cāpi ṣaṣṭhaḥ skandho vaktuṃ śakyate. kutaḥ. arthāyogāt. atītādyarthayogād ity arthaḥ. nanu ca bahutvād asaṃskṛtānāṃ asaṃskṛtaskandho 'nyo yokṣyate. kim atītādyartheneti. etac cāyuktam asaṃskṛtānāṃ deśasaṃnikarṣābhāvenābhisaṃkṣepāyogāt. saṃkleśavastujñāpanārtham iti vistaraḥ. na saṃkleśavastv anāsravatvāt. na vyavadānavastv asaṃskṛtatvāt. vyavadānahetur hi vyavadānavastv ity abhiprāyaḥ. atha vā rūpaskandha ity ukte yāvad vijñānaskandha ity ukte saṃkleśavastu vyavadānavastu ca rūpaskandho yāvad vijñānaskandha iti vijñāyate. na tv asaṃskṛtaskandha ity ukte saṃkleśavyavadānavastu vijñāyata iti na saṃbhavati asaṃskṛtaskandha iti. teṣāṃ dhātvāyataneṣv apy eṣa prasaṃga iti. teṣām evaṃvādināṃ yathā ghaṭoparamo na ghaṭaḥ. evaṃ dhātūparamo na dhātuḥ. āyatanoparamo nāyatanam iti dharmadhātvāyatanayor apy asaṃskṛtaṃ na vyavasthāpitaṃ syāt. sarvadharmasaṃgrahaś ca dhātvāyataneṣv abhipreta ity ayuktam etat.
body.translated_text: (I.22ab) 'First, these [unconditioned dharmas] cannot be included in these [five aggregates], because the purpose does not apply' — because the purpose of alteration (<s>rūpaṇa</s>), etc. does not apply, is not possible. [That is,] what has the nature of form, up to what has the nature of consciousness — [the unconditioned] cannot be included in just these five aggregates alone, because they do not have that nature. 'Nor can a sixth aggregate be posited. Why? Because the purpose does not apply.' The meaning is: because the purpose of 'past, etc.' does not apply [to the unconditioned]. [Objection:] But because the unconditioned are numerous, a separate 'unconditioned aggregate' could be posited — what [need is there] for the purpose of 'past, etc.'? [Reply:] This is improper, because the unconditioned, lacking proximity in space, cannot be grouped together. 'For the purpose of making known the basis of defilement' — and so on in detail. [The unconditioned] is not a basis of defilement, because of being undefiled (<s>anāsrava</s>). Nor is it a basis of purification, because of being unconditioned. The intended meaning is: the cause of purification is [called] the basis of purification. Alternatively, when 'form-aggregate' through 'consciousness-aggregate' is stated, the basis of defilement and the basis of purification — namely, the form-aggregate through the consciousness-aggregate — are understood. But if 'unconditioned aggregate' were stated, neither the basis of defilement nor of purification would be understood — so 'unconditioned aggregate' is not possible. 'This unwanted consequence would apply to elements and sense-bases too' — for those who argue thus: just as the cessation of a pot is not a pot, so the cessation of an element is not an element, and the cessation of a sense-base is not a sense-base — then the unconditioned would not be established even in the <s>dharma-dhātu</s> and <s>dharma-āyatana</s>. And since comprehensiveness of all <s>dharmas</s> is intended for elements and sense-bases — this [objection] is improper.

children.text:
uktaḥ skandhānām [Tib. 45a] anyaḥ prakāraḥ.
kramaḥ punar
children.translated_text:
[Tib. 45a] 'Another mode of the aggregates has been stated.
Now, the order' —

body.text: ity anyaprakāravacanāpekṣāḥ punaḥśabdopanyāsa iti darśayati. sarvaudārikam iti. sarvebhyo vedanādibhya audārikaṃ rūpaṃ. sanidarśanasapratighatvādiyogāt. arūpiṇāṃ vedanādīnāṃ. nirdhāraṇe ṣaṣṭhī. vedanā audārikī pracāraudārikatayā samudācāraudārikatayety arthaḥ. dvābhyāṃ saṃskāravijñānābhyāṃ. audārikī saṃjñā. nimittaparicchedena sujñātatvāt. vijñānāt saṃskāra audārikaḥ sukhī syāṃ na duḥkhī syām ity abhisaṃskāralakṣaṇatvāt. vijñānaṃ tu sarvasūkṣmam upalabdhimātralakṣaṇatvāt. yathaudārikaṃ ca vineyānām arthapratipādanaṃ nyāyyam iti evaṃ skandhānukramaḥ. te ca vedanāsvādagardhāt. te ca strīpuruṣā vedanāsvādasakter anyonyaṃ rūpābhirāmā bhavanti. tadgardha iti. vedanāgardhaḥ. saṃjñāviparyāsād iti. nityādikān nimittodgrahaṇāt.
body.translated_text: He shows that the word 'now' (<s>punaḥ</s>) is introduced in expectation of the statement of another mode. 'The grossest of all' — form is grosser than all [other aggregates] — feeling, etc. — because of its connection with being visible, resistant, etc. 'Among the formless' — feeling, etc. — the sixth case is in the sense of determination (<s>nirdhāraṇa</s>). 'Feeling is gross because of the grossness of its range of activity' — meaning because of the grossness of its occurrence. 'Than both' — than formations and consciousness. 'Perception is gross' — because it is easily known through the apprehension of marks. 'Formations are grosser than consciousness' — because they have the characteristic of volition (<s>abhisaṃskāra</s>), [as in the thought] 'May I be happy, may I not suffer.' 'Consciousness is the most subtle of all' — because its characteristic is mere apprehension. And the presentation of meaning to the trainable should follow grossness — thus is the order of aggregates. 'And they, from greed for the savoring of feeling' — those men and women, through attachment to the savoring of feeling, become delighted by each other's form. 'That greed' — the greed for feeling. 'From the perversion of perception' — from the grasping of signs as permanent, etc.

body.text: sukhāpi hi vedanā saṃskāravipariṇāmaduḥkhatayā duḥkhā. bhājanabhojanam iti vistaraḥ. rūpaṃ bhājanabhūtaṃ vedanāśrayatvāt. vedanā bhojanabhūtā āsvādyatvāt. saṃjñā vyaṃjanabhūtā vedanāṃ tannimittodgrahaṇena vyaṃjayatīti kṛtvā. saṃjñāvaśena vā vedanā rocata iti kṛtvā vyaṃjanabhūtā samjñā. cetanā paktṛbhūtā vipākavedanām abhisaṃskṛtya upanayanāt. [Tib. 45b] vijñānaṃ bhoktṛbhūtaṃ tadanugrahād iti. bhājanādyarthena vānukramaḥ. dhātuto veti vistaraḥ. kāmaguṇā eva rūpāṇi. taiḥ prabhāvitaḥ prakarṣitaḥ kāmadhātuḥ. vedanāprabhāvitāni dhyānāni. saumanasyasukhendriyaprabhāvitaṃ prathamaṃ dhyānaṃ. saumanasyendriyaprabhāvitaṃ dvitīyaṃ. sukhendriyaprabhāvitaṃ tṛtīyaṃ. upekṣendriyapariśuddhiprabhāvitaṃ caturthaṃ dhyānaṃ. saṃjñāprabhāvitās traya ārūpyāḥ. ākāśasaṃjñāprabhāvitam ākāśānaṃtyāyatanaṃ. vijñānasaṃjñāprabhāvitaṃ vijñānānaṃtyāyatanaṃ. ākiṃcanyasaṃjñāprabhāvitaṃ ākiṃcanyāyatanaṃ. saṃskāramātraprabhāvitaṃ bhavāgraṃ. tatra hi cetanā aśītiṃ kalpasahasrāṇy āyur ākṣipati. vijñānaṃ kasmāt sarveṣāṃ paścād uktam ity ata āha etā vijñānasthitaya iti vistaraḥ. catasro vijñānasthitayaḥ. rūpopagā vijñānasthitiḥ kāmadhātuḥ. vedanopagā catvāri dhyānāni. saṃjñopagā traya ārūpyāḥ. saṃskāropagā bhavāgraṃ. tāsu catasṛṣu vijñānasthitiṣu pratiṣṭhitaṃ vijñānaṃ tadāśritatvāt sarvapaścād uktaṃ. ity evaṃ kṣetrabījasaṃdarśanārthaḥ skandhānukrama ukto bhavati. ata eva ca paṃca skandhā nālpīyāṃso na bhūyāṃsa iti. yathaudārikādibhiḥ kāraṇair nālpīyāṃso na bhūyāṃsa ity arthaḥ.
body.translated_text: For even pleasant feeling is suffering through the suffering of transformation of <s>saṃskāras</s> (formations). 'Vessel and food' — this is the elaboration. Form is like a vessel, because it is the basis of feeling. Feeling is like food, because it is savored. Perception (<s>saṃjñā</s>) is like a condiment, because it manifests feeling through grasping its distinguishing marks. Or, because feeling is relished on account of perception, perception is like a condiment. Volition (<s>cetanā</s>) is like a cook, because it prepares and brings forth the feeling [that is] the maturation-result (<s>vipāka</s>). [Tib. 45b] Consciousness (<s>vijñāna</s>) is like the eater, because of its being sustained by that [food]. Or, the [sequential] order [follows] the analogy of vessel and the rest. 'Or by [the order of] elements' — this is the elaboration. The <s>kāmaguṇas</s> (qualities of sensual desire) are precisely forms (<s>rūpa</s>). The <s>Kāmadhātu</s> (desire-realm) is dominated, i.e., characterized, by them. The <s>dhyānas</s> (meditative absorptions) are dominated by feeling. The first <s>dhyāna</s> is dominated by the faculties of mental pleasure (<s>saumanasya</s>) and physical pleasure (<s>sukha</s>). The second <s>dhyāna</s> is dominated by the faculty of mental pleasure. The third <s>dhyāna</s> is dominated by the faculty of physical pleasure. The fourth <s>dhyāna</s> is dominated by the purity of the faculty of equanimity (<s>upekṣā</s>). The three formless [attainments] are dominated by perception (<s>saṃjñā</s>). The sphere of infinite space (<s>ākāśānantyāyatana</s>) is dominated by the perception of space. The sphere of infinite consciousness (<s>vijñānānantyāyatana</s>) is dominated by the perception of consciousness. The sphere of nothingness (<s>ākiṃcanyāyatana</s>) is dominated by the perception of nothingness. The peak of existence (<s>bhavāgra</s>) is dominated by formations (<s>saṃskāra</s>) alone. For therein, volition (<s>cetanā</s>) projects a lifespan of eighty thousand <s>kalpas</s>. 'Why is consciousness stated last among all [the aggregates]?' — to this he says: 'These are the stations of consciousness' — and so on in detail. [There are] four stations of consciousness (<s>vijñānasthiti</s>): the form-based station of consciousness is the <s>Kāmadhātu</s>; the feeling-based [station is] the four <s>dhyānas</s>; the perception-based [station is] the three formless [realms]; the formations-based [station is] the peak of existence. Consciousness, being established in those four stations of consciousness, because it depends on them, is stated last among all [aggregates]. Thus, the sequential order of the aggregates has been stated for the purpose of showing the field and the seed. For this very reason, the five aggregates are neither fewer nor more — meaning they are neither fewer nor more by [such] reasons as grossness and the rest.

body.text: (I.23) paṃca vartamānaviṣayatvāt pūrvaṃ uktānīti. yāni [Tib. 46a] vartamānaviṣayāni. tāni parisphuṭaviṣayāṇi. parisphuṭaviṣayāṇi ca sugamānīti pūrvam uktāni. vartamānaviṣayāṇi ca pūrvavṛttīni bhavanty evaṃ ca pūrvam uktāni. manas tv aniyataviṣayam ity ākulaviṣayitvāt asugamaṃ. paścādvṛtti ca prāyeṇa. katham ity āha. kiṃcid vartamānaviṣayaṃ kiṃcid yāvat tryadhvānadhvaviṣayam iti. yāvacchabdena kiṃcid atītaviṣayaṃ kiṃcid anāgataviṣayaṃ kiṃcit tryadhvaviṣayaṃ. sarvadharmā anātmāna iti yathā. kiṃcid anadhvaviṣayam asaṃskṛtaviṣayam ity arthaḥ. evam aniyataviṣayaṃ manaḥ. tathā ca na tat sugamam iti paścād uktaṃ. sugamaṃ hi loke pūrvam upadiśyamānaṃ dṛśyate.
body.translated_text: (I.23) 'Five [sense-bases] are stated first because they have present objects.' Those [Tib. 46a] that have present objects — those have clear objects. And those with clear objects are easy to understand — hence they are stated first. And those with present objects function first — thus too they are stated first. But <s>manas</s> (mind) has indeterminate objects — hence, because its objects are confused, it is not easy [to understand]. And it mostly functions afterwards. How? He says: 'Some [mental consciousness] has a present object; some,' up to, 'has an object in three time-periods or timeless.' By the word 'up to': some has a past object, some a future object, some has an object in all three time-periods. As in [the statement] 'All <s>dharmas</s> are non-self.' 'Some has a timeless object' — meaning an unconditioned object. Thus mind has indeterminate objects. And therefore it is not easy [to understand] — hence it is stated last. For in the world, what is easy to understand is seen to be taught first.

children.translated_text: 'The four [starting from] the eye, because of having material objects' —

body.text: iti cakṣurādicatuṣṭayaṃ rūpādyupādāyarūpaviṣayaṃ. tasmāt. tat kāyāt pūrvam uktaṃ. kāyasya tv aniyato viṣayaḥ. kadācid bhūtāni kadācid bhautikaṃ
body.translated_text: the four [beginning with] the eye, etc. have derived form (<s>upādāyarūpa</s>) such as visible form and so forth as their objects. Therefore they are stated before the body [sense-base]. But the body has an indeterminate object — sometimes [it grasps] primary elements (<s>bhūtas</s>), sometimes derived [form]

body.text: yadi vyavacchedagrahaṇaṃ. kadācid ubhayaṃ yady avyavacchedagrahaṇaṃ. śeṣaṃ punar itarasmād yathāyogaṃ dūrāśutaravṛttyā pūrvam uktam iti. śeṣaṃ cakṣurādi. tad itarasmāt saṃbhavato dūrāśutaravṛttyā dūravṛttyā dūrataravṛttyā āśutaravṛttyeti vibhajya dvayaṃ dvayāt. ekaṃ caikasmāt punar ekaṃ caikasmād iti yojyam ity arthaḥ. katham ity āha. cakṣuḥśrotraṃ hi dūraviṣayaṃ tat pūrvam uktaṃ dvayāt ghrāṇajihvātaḥ. tayor api cakṣuḥśrotrayoḥ [Tib. 46b] cakṣuṣo dūratare vṛttiḥ. paśyato 'pi dūrān nadīṃ tacchabdāśravaṇāt. atas tat pūrvam uktam iti vartate. cakṣuḥ śrotrāt pūrvam uktaṃ. tayor āśutaravṛttitvād iti. tayor ghrāṇajihvayor ghrāṇaṃ pūrvam uktaṃ jihvāyāḥ. katham ity āha. aprāptasyaiva jihvāṃ bhojyasya gandhagrahaṇād iti.
body.translated_text: if the apprehension is discriminating. Sometimes both, if the apprehension is non-discriminating. 'The remaining, however, in relation to the other, are stated first according to their far-ranging or swift functioning.' The remaining [means] the eye and the rest. They are [ordered] in relation to the other [i.e., each other], by far-ranging or swifter functioning — by far-ranging functioning, by farther-ranging functioning, by swifter functioning — [this should be] analyzed as: a pair [is ordered] relative to [another] pair, and one relative to one, and again one relative to one — this is the meaning. How? He says: For the eye and ear have far-ranging objects — they are stated before the pair of nose and tongue. And of those two — the eye and ear — [Tib. 46b] the eye has a farther range of functioning, because even when one sees a river from far away, one does not hear its sound. Therefore it is stated first — the eye is stated before the ear. Of those [remaining] two, the nose is stated before the tongue because of its swifter functioning. How? He says: because the smell of food [still] not reaching the tongue is grasped [by the nose].

body.text: idam iha vicāryate. ghrāṇajihve prāptaviṣayagrāhiṇyau. kathaṃ. bhojyastho gandhaḥ tena ghrāṇena gṛhate. na tv abhojyastho gṛhyate. vāyos tu gandhāntaram udbhavati bhojyāvayavena vā sūkṣmeṇa sahāgato gandho gṛhyate. niruchvāsasya gandhāgrahaṇāt. na tarhīdaṃ vaktavyaṃ. aprāptasyaiva jihvāṃ bhojyasya gandhagrahaṇād iti. yat tat piṇḍarūpaṃ bhojyaṃ. taj jihvām aprāptam ity abhisaṃdhāyavacaṇād adoṣaḥ. evaṃ hy āśutaravṛtti ghrāṇaṃ yad bhojyāvayavasahāgatam api gandhaṃ jighrati. jihvā tu bhojyāvayavasahāgataṃ rasaṃ nāsvādayati. piṇḍabhojyasahāgatam eva tu rasam āsvādayatīti na sāśutaravṛttir ity avagantavyaṃ.
body.translated_text: This is examined here. The nose and tongue are both graspers of proximate objects. How? The smell residing in food — that is grasped by the nose. But smell not residing in food is not grasped. Rather, a different smell arises from the wind, or smell is grasped together with a subtle particle of the food. [This is known] because one who does not breathe in does not grasp smells. Then this should not be stated: 'because the smell of food not yet reaching the tongue is grasped [by the nose].' [Reply:] Because the statement is made with the intention that the food in its lump-form (<s>piṇḍarūpa</s>) has not reached the tongue, there is no fault. For it is to be understood that the nose functions more swiftly because it smells even the smell that is associated with a food-particle. But the tongue does not taste the taste associated with a food-particle — it tastes only the taste associated with the lump-food — therefore it does not function as swiftly.

body.text: (I.24) kathaṃ viśeṣaṇārtham iti pratipādayann āha. yathā gamyeta pratyekam iti vistaraḥ. yathā vijñāyeta ekaikaśa eṣāṃ daśānāṃ āyatanatvaṃ cakṣurādīnāṃ paṃcānāṃ viṣayitvena. rūpādīnāṃ ca paṃcānāṃ viṣayatvena vyavasthānāt. na samastānām āyatanatvaṃ rūpāyatanam ity ekam eveti. tathā ca parasparato viśeṣaṇaṃ na syāt. yadi viśeṣaṇārthaṃ nāmantarāṇy ucyante navānāṃ cakṣurāyatanasya yāvat kāyāyatanasya śabdāyatanasya yāvat spraṣṭavyāyatanasyeti. rūpāyatanasyāpi kasmān nāmantaraṃ nocyate. [Tib. 47a] ata āha. cakṣurādibhiś ca viśeṣitair yan na cakṣursaṃjñakaṃ rūpaṃ ca. tad rūpāyatanaṃ jñāsyata ity asya nāmāntaraṃ nocyate. tadyathā sarvāsu goṣv aṃkitāsu yā gaur nāṃkitā. tasyā anaṃkanam evāṃkanaṃ bhavati. tadvat. prādhānyād iti tribhiḥ kāraṇai rūpāyatanasya prādhānyaṃ. pānyādisaṃsparśair bādhanālakṣaṇād rūpaṇāt. idam ihāmutreti deśanidarśanarūpaṇāt. idam eva rūpam iti lokapratītatvāc ca. viśeṣaṇārtham evaikaṃ dharmāyatanam uktam iti. kathaṃ viśeṣaṇārthaṃ. yathā gamyeta pratyekam eṣāṃ dvādaśānām āyatanatvaṃ viṣayiviṣayatvena vyavasthānāt
body.translated_text: (I.24) Explaining how [the designation serves] the purpose of qualification, he says: 'So that each may be understood' — and so on in detail. So that the <s>āyatana</s>-hood of each of these ten — of the five [beginning with] the eye as subject [faculties], and of the five [beginning with] form as objects — may be known individually, since they are established by being subjects and objects respectively. Not that [all of them] collectively [constitute] a single <s>āyatana</s>-hood as 'the form sense-base.' And thus mutual qualification would not be possible. If alternative names are stated for the purpose of qualification, [then what about] the alternative names of the nine — from the eye sense-base up to the body sense-base, and the sound sense-base up to the tangible sense-base? [But] why is no alternative name stated for the form sense-base? [Tib. 47a] To this he says: When the eye and the rest are qualified [by their own names], whatever form is not designated as 'eye[-form]' and so forth, and [is also] form — that will be known as the form sense-base. Hence no alternative name is stated for it. Just as, when all the cows have been branded, whichever cow is unbranded — for her, the very lack of branding serves as branding. Similarly. 'Because of predominance' — the form sense-base has predominance for three reasons: because of the alteration (<s>rūpaṇa</s>) characterized by obstruction through contact with water and the like; because of the alteration that is the demonstration of location — 'this is here, that is there'; and because of being popularly recognized as 'this alone is form.' 'For the purpose of qualification alone, the single <s>dharma</s>-sense-base is stated.' How is it for the purpose of qualification? So that the <s>āyatana</s>-hood of each of these twelve may be known, since they are established by being subjects and objects respectively

body.text: na samastānām iti. cakṣurādibhiś ca viśeṣitair yan na cakṣurādisaṃjñakaṃ dharmaś ca. tad dharmāyatanaṃ jñāsyata iti tasya nāmāntaraṃ nocyate. vedanādīnām ity ādiśabdena saṃjñāsaṃskārāvijñaptyasaṃskṛtānāṃ grahaṇaṃ. viṃśatiprakāratveneti.
body.translated_text: — not of all collectively. And when the eye and the rest are qualified, whatever is not designated as 'eye' and so forth, and [is also] a <s>dharma</s> — that will be known as the <s>dharma</s>-sense-base. Hence no alternative name is stated for it. 'Of feeling, etc.' — by the word 'etc.', perception, formations, non-manifest [form], and the unconditioned are included. 'In twenty types' —

body.text: vacanāt. cakṣustrayagocaratvāc ca. māṃsacakṣur asmadādīnāṃ. divyaṃ cakṣur devānāṃ. āryaṃ prajñācakṣur āryāṇām anāsravaṃ jñānaṃ satyacatuṣṭayālambanaṃ. ato rūpam eva cakṣustrayagocaraṃ. na cakṣurādayaḥ. tasmāt. tad eva rūpāyatanam uktaṃ nānyāni.
body.translated_text: so it is said. And because it is the domain of the threefold eye. The fleshly eye [is] of us [ordinary beings] and the like. The divine eye [is] of the <s>devas</s>. The noble wisdom-eye (<s>prajñācakṣus</s>) [is] of the Noble Ones — non-outflow knowledge having the four truths as its object. Therefore, form alone is the domain of the threefold eye — not the eye and the rest. Therefore, that alone is designated as the form sense-base, not the others.

body.text: (I.25) yeṣām vāksvabhāvaṃ buddhavacanam iti. yeṣāṃ sautrāntikānāṃ [Tib. 47b] vāgvijñaptisvabhāvaṃ. teṣāṃ tāni rūpaskandhasaṃgṛhītāni. śabdāyatanasya rūpaskandhasaṃgṛhītatvāt. yeṣāṃ nāmasvabhāvam iti. yeṣāṃ nikāyāntarīyāṇāṃ cittaviprayuktaṃ nāmāsti. teṣāṃ saṃskāraskandhena saṃgṛhītāni. saṃskāraskandhasaṃgṛhītatvān nāmnaḥ. ābhidhārmikāṇāṃ tūbhayasvabhāvaṃ buddhavacanam iṣṭaṃ. tathā hi jñānaprasthāna uktaṃ. katamad buddhavacanaṃ. tathāgatasya yā vāg vacanaṃ vyāhāro gīr niruktir vākpatho vāgghośo vākkarma vāgvijñaptiḥ. buddhavacanaṃ kuśalaṃ vaktavyaṃ. avyākṛtaṃ vaktavyaṃ. syāt kuśalaṃ. syād avyākṛtaṃ. katarat kuśalaṃ. kuśalacittasya tathāgatasya vācaṃ bhāṣamāṇasya yā vāg yāvad vāgvijñaptiḥ. katarad avyākṛtaṃ. avyākṛtacittasya tathāgatasyeti pūrvavat. punas tatraivānantaram uktaṃ buddhavacanaṃ nāma ka eṣa dharmaḥ. nāmakāyapadakāyavyaṃjanakāyānāṃ yā anupūrvaracanā anupūrvasthāpanā anupūrvasamāyoga iti. teṣām ābhidhārmikāṇāṃ rūpaskandhena saṃskāraskandhena ca tāny aśītidharmaskandhasahasrāṇi saṃgṛhītāni. sātirekāṇi me aśītidharmaskandhasahasrāṇi bhagavato 'ntikāt saṃmukham udgṛhītānīti sūtravacanaṃ. caturaśītidharmaskandhasahasrāṇīti nikāyāntare sūtrapāṭhaḥ.
body.translated_text: (I.25) 'Those for whom the <s>Buddha</s>-word has speech as its nature' — for those <s>Sautrāntikas</s>, [Tib. 47b] [the <s>Buddha</s>-word] has the nature of vocal expression (<s>vāgvijñapti</s>). For them, those [eighty thousand <s>dharma</s>-aggregates] are included in the form aggregate, because the sound sense-base is included in the form aggregate. 'Those for whom [it] has name as its nature' — for those belonging to other schools (<s>nikāyāntarīya</s>), there exists 'name' (<s>nāman</s>) as a [dharma] dissociated from mind (<s>cittaviprayukta</s>). For them, [the dharma-aggregates are] included in the formations aggregate, because 'name' is included in the formations aggregate. But for the <s>Ābhidharmikas</s> (Abhidharma specialists), the <s>Buddha</s>-word is accepted as having the nature of both. For it is said in the <s>Jñānaprasthāna</s>: 'What is the <s>Buddha</s>-word? Whatever speech, utterance, vocalization, song, enunciation, path of speech, sound of speech, act of speech, vocal expression of the <s>Tathāgata</s>. The <s>Buddha</s>-word should be called wholesome (<s>kuśala</s>). It should be called indeterminate (<s>avyākṛta</s>). It may be wholesome; it may be indeterminate. What is wholesome? When the <s>Tathāgata</s> with a wholesome mind speaks — whatever speech, up to vocal expression. What is indeterminate? When the <s>Tathāgata</s> with an indeterminate mind' — and so on as before. Again, immediately thereafter in the same [text] it is said: 'The <s>Buddha</s>-word is \"name\" — what <s>dharma</s> is this? It is the sequential composition, sequential establishment, sequential conjunction of name-groups, phrase-groups, and syllable-groups.' For those <s>Ābhidharmikas</s>, those eighty thousand <s>dharma</s>-aggregates are included in the form aggregate and the formations aggregate. 'I have received, face to face from the Blessed One, more than eighty thousand <s>dharma</s>-aggregates' — this is the <s>sūtra</s> statement. 'Eighty-four thousand <s>dharma</s>-aggregates' — this is the <s>sūtra</s> reading in the other schools.

children.translated_text: 'The measure of the treatise — some [say] a single [dharma-aggregate]' —

body.text: iti. śāstrasya pramāṇaṃ śāstrapramāṇaṃ. śāstrapramāṇaṃ [Tib. 48a] pramāṇam asya. so 'yaṃ dharmaskandhaḥ.
body.translated_text: 'The measure (<s>pramāṇa</s>) of the treatise' means [having] the treatise as its measure. [Tib. 48a] 'Having the measure of the treatise as its standard' — that is this <s>dharmaskandha</s> (dharma-aggregate).

children.translated_text: 'The measure of the treatise, some say' —

body.text: tāvad āhuḥ. tac ca ṣaṭsahasrāṇīti. tac ca śāstraṃ harmaskandhasaṃjñakaṃ granthaprāmāṇyena ṣaṭsahasrāṇīti. tāni tv aśītidharmaskandhasahasrāṇy antarhitāni. ekaṃ tv etad avaśiṣyata iti kathayanti.
body.translated_text: thus they say. 'And that is six thousand.' And that treatise bearing the designation '<s>Dharmaskandha</s>' has a textual measure of six thousand [verses]. Those eighty thousand <s>dharma</s>-aggregates, however, have been lost. But this one remains — so they relate.

children.translated_text: 'The discourse on the aggregates and the rest, individually [constitutes a dharmaskandha].'

body.text: apara āhur iti vākyādhyāhāraḥ. skandhādīnām ekaikā kathā dharmaskandhaḥ. te ca dharmaskandhā aśītisahasrasaṃkhyā vyākhyāyaṃte. pratītyasamutpādādīni ceha vyākhyāsyante. praṇidhijñānāraṇādīnām ity ādigrahaṇena saṃgrahavastukarmapathāśubhānapānasmṛtyādīni gṛhyante.
body.translated_text: 'Others say' — this is to be supplied to complete the sentence. Each individual discourse on the aggregates and the rest is a <s>dharmaskandha</s>. And those <s>dharmaskandhas</s>, numbering eighty thousand, are explained [as follows]. '<s>Pratītyasamutpāda</s> (dependent origination) and the rest are explained here.' 'Of resolution-knowledge (<s>praṇidhijñāna</s>), unobstructed [knowledge] (<s>araṇa</s>), and so forth' — by the word 'and so forth': inclusion (<s>saṃgraha</s>), topics (<s>vastu</s>), courses of action (<s>karmapathas</s>), [contemplation of] the impure (<s>aśubhā</s>), mindfulness of breathing (<s>ānāpānasmṛti</s>), and the like are included.

children.translated_text: 'But the <s>dharmaskandha</s> has been described as the antidote to a [particular] disposition (<s>carita</s>)' —

body.text: iti tuśabdaḥ pūrvoktapakṣanirākaraṇartho 'vadhāraṇārtho vā. rāgadveṣamohamānādicaritabhedeneti. ādiśabdena dṛṣṭivicikitsādīnāṃ grahaṇaṃ. kecit sattvā rāgacaritāḥ. kecid dveṣacaritāḥ. kecin mohacaritāḥ. kecin mānacaritāḥ. kecid dṛṣṭicaritāḥ. kecid vicikitsācaritāḥ. kecid rāgadveṣacaritāḥ. kecid rāgadveṣamohacaritāḥ. kecid rāgāśayā dveṣaprayogāḥ. kecid dveśāśayā rāgaprayogāḥ. kecit kṛtrimarāgā nigṛhyadveṣāḥ. kecit kṛtrimadveṣā nigṛhyarāgā iti. teṣāṃ pratipakṣeṇa bhagavatā tāny uktānīti.
body.translated_text: The word 'but' (<s>tu</s>) is for the purpose of refuting the previously stated positions, or for emphasis. 'By the distinction of dispositions such as attachment (<s>rāga</s>), aversion (<s>dveṣa</s>), delusion (<s>moha</s>), pride (<s>māna</s>), and so forth' — by the word 'and so forth,' views (<s>dṛṣṭi</s>), doubt (<s>vicikitsā</s>), and the like are included. Some beings have an attachment-disposition; some have an aversion-disposition; some have a delusion-disposition; some have a pride-disposition; some have a view-disposition; some have a doubt-disposition; some have a mixed attachment-aversion disposition; some have an attachment-aversion-delusion disposition; some have an attachment-inclination but an aversion-mode-of-action; some have an aversion-inclination but an attachment-mode-of-action; some have artificial attachment but suppressed aversion; some have artificial aversion but suppressed attachment. As an antidote to those [dispositions], those [dharma-aggregates] were spoken by the Blessed One.

body.text: (I.27) ye 'py anye skandhāyatanadhātava iti vistaraḥ. [Tib. 48b] ye 'pi skandhāyatanadhātavaḥ. te 'py eṣv eva skandhāyatanadhātuṣu pratipādyāḥ praveśayitavyāḥ. svaṃsvaṃ svabhāvaṃ eṣāṃ yathā vyavasthāpitam asmin śāstre vimṛṣya skandhāḥ skandheṣu pratipādayitavyā āyatanāny āyataneṣu dhātavo dhātuṣu. śīlaskandho rūpaskandhasaṃgṛhīta iti. kāyavāgviratirūpasvabhāvatvāt śīlaskandhasya. śeṣāḥ saṃskāraskandheneti. samādhyādīnāṃ caitasikatvāt. vimuktir ihādhimokṣo 'bhipretaḥ. vimuktijñānadarśanaṃ ca prajñāviśeṣa eveti. aṣṭāv alobhasvabhāvatvāt dharmāyataneneti. katamāny aṣṭau. pṛthivyaptejovāyunīlapītalohitāvadātakṛtsnāyatanāni. tāni ca alobhasvabhāvāni apadekṣyante
body.translated_text: (I.27) 'Whatever other aggregates, sense-bases, and elements there are' — and so forth in detail. Whatever [other] aggregates, sense-bases, and elements there are — those too should be demonstrated, that is, subsumed, under these very aggregates, sense-bases, and elements. Having examined, in this treatise, each of their own intrinsic natures as established — aggregates should be demonstrated within aggregates, sense-bases within sense-bases, elements within elements. 'The morality-aggregate is included in the form-aggregate' — because the morality-aggregate has the nature of bodily and verbal restraint-form. 'The rest [are included] in the formations-aggregate' — because concentration and the others are mental factors. 'Liberation' here refers to <s>adhimokṣa</s> (resolution/determination). 'And the knowledge-and-vision of liberation' is simply a specific [type of] wisdom. 'The eight, being of the nature of non-attachment (<s>alobha</s>), [are included] in the <s>dharma</s> sense-base' — which eight? The earth-totality, water-totality, fire-totality, wind-totality, blue-totality, yellow-totality, red-totality, and white-totality sense-bases. That they have the nature of non-attachment will be explained [later]:

body.text: iti. alobhaś ca dharmāyatane 'ntarbhavati. tena tatsaṃgrahaḥ. saparivārāṇi tu paṃcaskandhasvabhāvatvān manodharmāyatanābhyāṃ. kiṃ. saṃgṛhītāni. tasyālobhasya parivāro 'nuparivartirūpaṃ rūpaskandho vedanāsaṃjñe vedanāsaṃjñāskandhau cetanādayaḥ saṃprayuktā jātyādayaś ca viprayuktāḥ saṃskāraskandhaḥ. vijñānaṃ cātra kalāpe vijñānaskandha iti paṃcaskandhasvabhāvāni tāni bhavanti. navamadaśame tv ākāśānaṃtyāyatanavijñānānantyāyatanakṛtsne paścād vakṣyete. [Tib. 49a] tathābhibhvāyatanānīti tāny alobhasvabhāvatvāt dharmāyatanena. saparivārāṇi tu paṃcasvabhāvatvān manodharmāyatanena pūrvavat vyākhyātavyāni. ākāśavijñānānantyāyatanakṛtsne catvāri cākāśānantyāyatanādīni. ākāśavijñānākiṃcanyanaivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatanāni catuḥskandhasvabhāvatvān manodharmāyatanābhyāṃ saṃgṛhītāni. na hi tatra rūpaskandho 'sti. paṃca vimuktyāyatanānīti vistaraḥ.
body.translated_text: And non-attachment is included in the <s>dharma</s> sense-base; hence their inclusion in that. 'But with their retinue, [they are included] in the mind and <s>dharma</s> sense-bases, because they have the nature of five aggregates.' What? They are included. The retinue of that non-attachment: accompanying form is the form-aggregate; feeling and perception [are] the feeling and perception aggregates; volition and the other associated [mental factors] and birth and the other dissociated [formations] are the formations-aggregate; and consciousness in this complex is the consciousness-aggregate — thus they have the nature of five aggregates. The ninth and tenth — the totalities of infinite space and infinite consciousness — will be explained later. Likewise the <s>abhibhvāyatanas</s> (bases of mastery) — because they have the nature of non-attachment, [they are included] in the <s>dharma</s> sense-base. But with their retinue, because they have five natures, they should be explained by the mind and <s>dharma</s> sense-bases, as before. 'The totalities of infinite space and infinite consciousness, and the four [formless attainments] beginning with infinite space' — the [four formless] sense-bases of infinite space, infinite consciousness, nothingness, and neither-perception-nor-non-perception — 'are included in the mind and <s>dharma</s> sense-bases, because they have the nature of four aggregates.' For there is no form-aggregate there. 'The five bases of liberation (<s>vimuktyāyatana</s>)' — and so forth in detail.

body.text: sūtra uktaṃ. paṃcemāni vimuktyāyatanāni. katamāni iha bhikṣo śāstā dharmaṃ deśayati. anyatarānyataro vā vijño gurusthānīyaḥ sabrahmacārī. yathāyathāsya śāstā anyatarānyataro vā vijño gurusthānīyaḥ sabrahmacārī dharmaṃ deśayati. tathātathā teṣu dharmeṣv arthapratisaṃvedī bhavati dharmapratisaṃvedī ca. tasyārthapratisaṃvedino dharmapratisaṃvedinaś cotpadyate prāmodyaṃ. pramuditasya prītir jāyate. prītamanasaḥ kāyaḥ praśrabhyate. praśrabdhakāyaḥ sukhaṃ vedayate. sukhitasya cittaṃ samādhīyate. samāhitacitto yathābhūtaṃ prajānāti yathābhūtaṃ paśyati. yathābhūtaṃ prajānan yathābhūtaṃ paśyan nirvidyate. nirviṇṇo virajyate. virakto vimucyate. [Tib. 49b] idaṃ prathamaṃ vimuktyāyatanaṃ. yatra sthitasya bhikṣor vā bhikṣuṇyā vā anupasthitā smṛtir upatiṣṭhate. asamāhitaṃ cittaṃ samādhīyate. aparikṣīṇāś cāsravāḥ parikṣīyante. ananuprāptaṃ cānuttaraṃ yogakṣemaṃ nirvāṇam anuprāpnoti. punar aparaṃ na haiva bhikṣo śāstā dharmaṃ deśayaty anyatarānyataro vā vijño gurusthānīyaḥ sabrahmacārī. api tu yathāśrutān dharmān yathopadiṣṭān yathāparyavāptān vistareṇa svareṇa svādhyāyaṃ karoti. yathāyathā tān yathāśrutān yathopadiṣṭān yathāparyavāptāṃ vistareṇa svareṇa svādhyāyaṃ karoti. tathātathā teṣu arthapratisaṃvedī bhavati pūrvavat. idaṃ dvitīyaṃ vimuktyāyatanaṃ. yatra sthitasyeti pūrvavat. punar aparaṃ na haiva bhikṣo śāstā dharmaṃ deśayati anyatarānyataro vā vijño gurusthānīyaḥ sabrahmacārī. nāpi yathāśrutān dharmān yathopadiṣṭān yathāparyavāptān vistareṇa svādhyāyaṃ karoti. api tu yathāśrutān dharmān yathopadiṣṭān yathāparyavāptān vistareṇa parebhyaḥ saṃprakāśayati. yathāyathā yathāśrutān dharmān yathopadiṣṭān yathāparyavāptān vistareṇa parebhyaḥ saṃprakāśayati. tathātathā teṣu dharmeṣv arthapratisaṃvedī bhavatīti pūrvavat. idaṃ tṛtīyaṃ vimuktyāyatanaṃ. yatra sthitasyeti pūrvavat. punar aparaṃ na haiva bhikṣo śāstā pūrvavat. nāpi svādhyāyaṃ nāpi parebhyaḥ saṃprakāśayati. api tu yathāśrutān yāvad yathāparyavāptān cintayati tulayati upaparīkṣate. [Tib. 50a] yathāyathā yathāśrutān yāvad yathāparyavāptān cintayati yāvad upaparīkṣate. tathātathā teṣu dharmeṣv arthapratisaṃvedī pūrvavat. idaṃ caturthaṃ vimuktyāyatanaṃ. yatra sthitasyeti pūrvavat. punar aparaṃ na haiva bhikṣo śāsteti pūrvavat. nāpi svādhyāyaṃ nāpi parebhyaḥ saṃprakāśayati nāpi cintayati. api tv anenānyatamaṃ bhadrakaṃ samādhinimittaṃ sādhu ca suṣṭhu ca sūdgṛhītaṃ bhavati sumanasikṛtaṃ subhāvitaṃ sujuṣṭaṃ supratividdhaṃ. tadyathā vinīlakaṃ
body.translated_text: It is stated in the <s>Sūtra</s>: 'There are these five bases of liberation. What are the five? Here, O monk, the Teacher teaches the <s>Dharma</s>, or some other learned fellow-practitioner worthy of being a teacher [does so]. In whatever way the Teacher or some other learned fellow-practitioner worthy of being a teacher teaches the <s>Dharma</s>, in that way he becomes one who experiences the meaning and one who experiences the <s>Dharma</s> regarding those teachings. For one who experiences the meaning and the <s>Dharma</s>, delight (<s>prāmodya</s>) arises. For one who is delighted, rapture (<s>prīti</s>) is born. For one whose mind is enraptured, the body becomes tranquil. One whose body is tranquil feels pleasure (<s>sukha</s>). For one who is pleased, the mind becomes concentrated. For one whose mind is concentrated, he knows as it really is, he sees as it really is. Knowing as it really is, seeing as it really is, he becomes disenchanted (<s>nirvidyate</s>). Being disenchanted, he becomes dispassionate. Being dispassionate, he is liberated. This is the first base of liberation — where, for a monk or nun who dwells [in it], mindfulness that has not arisen arises, the unconcentrated mind becomes concentrated, outflows (<s>āsrava</s>) that have not been exhausted are exhausted, and the unsurpassed security from bondage — <s>Nirvāṇa</s> — not [yet] attained, is attained. Furthermore, O monk, it is not the case that the Teacher teaches the <s>Dharma</s> or that some other learned fellow-practitioner worthy of being a teacher [does so]. Rather, he recites aloud (<s>svādhyāya</s>) the <s>dharmas</s> as heard, as instructed, as mastered, extensively, in full voice. In whatever way he recites those [<s>dharmas</s>] as heard, as instructed, as mastered, extensively, in full voice, in that way he becomes one who experiences the meaning regarding those [teachings] — as before. This is the second base of liberation — where he dwells, as before. Furthermore, O monk, it is not the case that the Teacher teaches the <s>Dharma</s> or that some other learned fellow-practitioner worthy of being a teacher [does so], nor does he recite aloud. Rather, he illuminates for others the <s>dharmas</s> as heard, as instructed, as mastered, extensively. In whatever way he illuminates for others the <s>dharmas</s> as heard, as instructed, as mastered, extensively, in that way he becomes one who experiences the meaning regarding those teachings — as before. This is the third base of liberation — where he dwells, as before. Furthermore, O monk, it is not the case that the Teacher [teaches] — as before — nor does he recite aloud, nor does he illuminate for others. Rather, he reflects on, examines, and investigates the <s>dharmas</s> as heard, up to as mastered. In whatever way he reflects on, up to investigates, the <s>dharmas</s> as heard, up to as mastered, in that way he becomes one who experiences the meaning regarding those teachings — as before. This is the fourth base of liberation — where he dwells, as before. Furthermore, O monk, it is not the case that the Teacher [teaches] — as before — nor does he recite aloud, nor does he illuminate for others, nor does he reflect. Rather, he has well and properly grasped a certain wholesome <s>samādhi</s>-sign (<s>samādhinimitta</s>), well attended to, well cultivated, well practiced, well penetrated — such as the blue[-swollen corpse]

body.text:
vā vipūyakaṃ vā vyādhmātakaṃ vā vipaṭumakaṃ vā vilohitakaṃ vā vikhāditakaṃ vā vikṣiptakaṃ vā asthi vā asthisaṃkalikā vā. yathāyathā khalv anenānyatamānyatamaṃ bhadrakaṃ samādhinimittaṃ pūrvavat yāvat supratividdham. tathātathā teṣu dharmeṣv arthaprativedī bhavati pūrvavat. idaṃ paṃcamaṃ vimuktyāyatanaṃ. yatra sthitasyeti pūrvavat. vimukter āyadvāraṃ prajñāviśeṣaḥ. prajñā ca dharmāyatanena saṃgṛhītā. saparivārāṇi śabdamanodharmāyatanaiḥ. deśanāsvādhyāyaparasaṃprakāśaneṣu śabdagrahaṇāc chabdāyatanam asti. manodharmāyatane tu prajñāparivārabhūte sarvatrasthe iti tribhiḥ saṃgrahaḥ. dvayor āyatanayor iti. sūtra uktaṃ. rūpiṇaḥ santi sattvā [Tib. 50b] asaṃjñinaḥ apratisaṃjñinaḥ. tadyathā devā asaṃjñisattvāḥ. idaṃ prathamam āyatanaṃ. arūpiṇaḥ santi sattvāḥ sarvaśa ākiṃcanyāyatanaṃ samatikramya naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatanam upasaṃpadya viharanti. tadyathā devā naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatanopagāḥ. idaṃ dvitīyam āyatanam iti. anayor dvayor āyatanayor asaṃjñisattvā daśabhir āyatanaiḥ saṃgṛhītāḥ. gandharasāyatanayor eva tatrābhāvāt. bhavati hi cyutyupapattikālayos teṣāṃ manaāyatanam iti. naivasaṃjñānasaṃjñāyatanopagā manodharmāyatanābhyāṃ saṃgṛhītā ity adhikṛtaṃ. teṣām arūpitvāt. bahudhātuke 'pi dvāṣaṣṭir dhātava iti. sūtra uktaṃ. āyuṣmān ānando bhagavantam etad avocat. kiyatā bhadanta paṇḍito dhātukuśalo bhavati. bhagavān āha. paṇḍita ānanda aṣṭādaśa dhātūñ jānāti
paśyati yathābhūtaṃ. cakṣurdhātuṃ rūpadhātuṃ cakṣurvijñānadhātuṃ. evaṃ yāvan manodhātuṃ dharmadhātuṃ manovijñānadhātum iti. itīmān ānandāṣṭādaśa dhātūñ jānāti paśyati yathābhūtaṃ. ṣaḍ api dhātūṃ jānāti paśyati yathābhūtaṃ. pṛthivīdhātum abdhātuṃ tejodhātuṃ vāyudhātum ākāśadhātuṃ vijñānadhātum iti. aparān api ṣaḍ dhātūṃ jānāti paśyati yathābhūtaṃ. kāmadhātuṃ vyāpādadhātuṃ [Tib. 51a] vihiṃsādhātuṃ naiṣkramyadhātum avyāpādadhātum avihiṃsādhātum iti. aparān api ṣaḍ dhātūñ jānāti paśyati yathābhūtaṃ. sukhadhātuṃ duḥkhadhātuṃ saumanasyadhātuṃ daurmanasyadhātum upekṣādhātum avidyādhātum iti. caturo 'pi dhātūñ jānāti paśyati yathābhūtaṃ. vedanādhātuṃ saṃjñādhātuṃ saṃskāradhātuṃ vijñānadhātum iti. trīṇy api dhātūṃ jānāti paśyati yathābhūtaṃ. kāmadhātuṃ rūpadhātum ārūpyadhātum iti. aparān api trīn dhātūṃ jānāti paśyati yathābhūtaṃ. rūpadhātuṃ ārūpyadhātuṃ nirodhadhātum iti. aparān api trīn dhātūṃ jānāti paśyati yathābhūtaṃ. atītaṃ
body.translated_text: or the festering or the bloated or the fissured or the blood-smeared or the gnawed or the scattered [corpse], or a skeleton or a chain of bones. In whatever way he has well [grasped], up to well penetrated, one or another wholesome <s>samādhi</s>-sign — as before — in that way he becomes one who experiences the meaning regarding those teachings — as before. This is the fifth base of liberation — where he dwells, as before.' The gateway to liberation is a specific [type of] wisdom. And wisdom is included in the <s>dharma</s> sense-base. With their retinue, [they are included] in the sound, mind, and <s>dharma</s> sense-bases — because in teaching, recitation, and illumination for others, the sound sense-base is present due to the grasping of sound. The mind and <s>dharma</s> sense-bases, being the retinue of wisdom, are present everywhere — hence the inclusion in three [sense-bases]. 'Of the two sense-bases' — it is stated in the <s>Sūtra</s>: 'There are beings with form, without perception and without experience of perception — such as the gods [born as] beings without perception. This is the first sense-base. There are beings without form who, having completely transcended the base of nothingness, attain and dwell in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception — such as the gods born in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. This is the second sense-base.' Of these two sense-bases: beings without perception are included in ten sense-bases — because only the smell and taste sense-bases are absent there. For at the time of death and rebirth, they do have the mind sense-base. [Beings in] the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception are included in the mind and <s>dharma</s> sense-bases — this has been discussed — because they are formless. 'In the <s>bahudhātuka</s> [sūtra] too, sixty-two elements' — it is stated in the <s>Sūtra</s>: 'The Venerable <s>Ānanda</s> said this to the Blessed One: "By how much, Venerable Sir, is a wise person skilled in elements?" The Blessed One said: "A wise person, <s>Ānanda</s>, knows and sees the eighteen elements as they really are — the eye-element, the form-element, the visual-consciousness element, and so on up to the mind-element, the <s>dharma</s>-element, the mental-consciousness element." "Such a one, <s>Ānanda</s>, knows and sees the eighteen elements as they really are. He also knows and sees six elements as they really are — the earth-element, the water-element, the fire-element, the wind-element, the space-element, and the consciousness-element. He also knows and sees another six elements as they really are — the element of sensual desire, the element of ill-will, the element of harmfulness, the element of renunciation, the element of non-ill-will, and the element of non-harmfulness. He also knows and sees another six elements as they really are — the element of pleasure, the element of pain, the element of mental pleasure, the element of mental displeasure, the element of equanimity, and the element of ignorance. He also knows and sees four elements as they really are — the feeling-element, the perception-element, the formations-element, and the consciousness-element. He also knows and sees three elements as they really are — the desire-realm element, the form-realm element, and the formless-realm element. He also knows and sees another three elements as they really are — the form element, the formless element, and the cessation element. He also knows and sees another three elements as they really are — the past

body.text: dhātum anāgataṃ dhātuṃ pratyutpannaṃ dhātuṃ. aparān api trīn dhātūṃ jānāti paśyati yathābhūtaṃ. hīnaṃ dhātuṃ madhyamaṃ dhātuṃ praṇītaṃ dhātum iti. aparān api trīn dhātūṃ jānāti paśyati yathābhūtaṃ. kuśalaṃ dhātum akuśalaṃ avyākṛtaṃ dhātum iti. aparān api trīn dhātūṃ jānāti paśyati yathābhūtaṃ. śaikṣaṃ dhātum aśaikṣaṃ dhātuṃ naivaśaikṣaṃnāśaikṣaṃ dhātum iti. dvāv api dhātū jānāti paśyati yathābhūtaṃ. sāsravaṃ [Tib. 51b] dhātum anāsravaṃ dhātum iti. aparāv api dvau dhātū jānāti paśyati yathābhūtaṃ saṃskṛtaṃ dhātum asaṃskṛtaṃ dhātum iti. imau dvau dhātū jānāti paśyati yathābhūtaṃ. iyatā cānanda paṇḍito dhātukuśalo bhavatīti. itīmāny atrābhisaṃbandhīni vākyāni pratyekaṃ madhye 'pi paṭhitavyāni. vistarabhayāt tu mayā na likhitānīti bodhavyaṃ. yathāyogaṃ saṃgraho veditavya iti. aṣṭādaśa tāvad dhātavas ta eva ta iti. ebhis te saṃgṛhītā evāṣṭādaśasu dhātuṣu. yatra pṛthivīdhātvādayaḥ ṣaṭ. teṣām ādyānāṃ caturṇāṃ spraṣṭavyadhātau saṃgrahaḥ. ākāśadhāto rūpadhātāv ālokatamassvabhāvatvāt. vijñānadhātoḥ saptasu cittadhātuṣu saṃgrahaḥ. kāmadhātvādīnāṃ tu ṣaṇṇāṃ kāmadhātuḥ kāmarāga ihābhipretaḥ. sa ca caitasikaḥ. vyāpādadhātvādayo 'pi caitasikā eveti. teṣāṃ dharmadhātusaṃgrahaḥ. sukhadhātvādīnām api ṣaṇṇāṃ tasminn eva saṃgrahaḥ. vedanādhātvādīnāṃ caturṇāṃ trayāṇāṃ dharmadhātau. vijñānadhātoḥ saptasu vijñānadhātuṣu. kāmadhātvādīnāṃ trayāṇāṃ kāmadhātoḥ aṣṭādaśasu dhātuṣu. rūpadhātoś caturdaśasu vinā gandharasaghrāṇajihvāvijñānadhātubhiḥ. ārūpyadhātor manodharmamanovijñānadhātuṣu. rūpadhātvādīnāṃ tu trayāṇāṃ dvayor uktaḥ saṃgrahaḥ. nirodhadhātor dharmadhātau [Tib. 52a]. atītadhātvādīnāṃ trayāṇāṃ pratyekam aṣṭādaśasu dhātuṣu saṃgrahaḥ. hīnādayas trayo dhātavaḥ kāmadhātvādaya eveti eṣām uktaḥ saṃgrahaḥ. kuśalādīnāṃ trayāṇāṃ kuśalākuśaladhātvo rūpaśabdadharmadhātuṣu saptasu ca cittadhātuṣu. avyākṛtadhātor aṣṭādaśasu dhātuṣu. śaikṣāśaikṣadhātvādīnāṃ trayāṇāṃ dvayor manodharmamanovijñānadhātuṣu. tṛtīyasyāṣṭādaśadhātuṣu. sāsravānāsravadhātvoḥ ādyasyāṣṭādaśasu dhātuṣu. dvitīyasya manodharmamanovijñānadhātuṣu. saṃskṛtāsaṃskṛtadhātvor ādyasyāṣṭādaśasu dhātuṣu. dvitīyasya dharmadhātau saṃgrahaḥ. ta ete dvāṣaṣṭir dhātavaḥ.
body.translated_text: the future element, and the present element. He also knows and sees three further elements as they truly are: the inferior element, the middling element, and the excellent element. He also knows and sees three further elements as they truly are: the wholesome element, the unwholesome element, and the morally indeterminate element. He also knows and sees three further elements as they truly are: the element of a learner, the element of one beyond training, and the element of neither-learner-nor-beyond-training. He also knows and sees two elements as they truly are: the defiled element and the undefiled element. He also knows and sees two further elements as they truly are: the conditioned element and the unconditioned element. He knows and sees these two elements as they truly are. And to this extent, <s>Ānanda</s>, a wise person is skilled in elements.' These connecting sentences should be read individually in the middle [of each exposition] as well. But one should understand that they were not written out by me, out of fear of prolixity. 'The inclusion should be understood as appropriate' — the eighteen <s>dhātus</s> first — they are those very [same ones]. These [elements mentioned in the sūtra] are included by them — within the eighteen <s>dhātus</s>. Therein, the six beginning with the earth element: of the first four, the inclusion is in the tangible-object <s>dhātu</s>. The space element [is included] in the form <s>dhātu</s>, because its nature is light and darkness. The consciousness element [is included] in the seven consciousness <s>dhātus</s>. Of the six beginning with the desire-realm element: the desire-realm [element] here is intended as desire-passion, which is a mental factor. The ill-will element and others are also mental factors — hence their inclusion is in the <s>dharma-dhātu</s>. Of the six beginning with the happiness element, the inclusion is also in that same [<s>dharma-dhātu</s>]. Of the four beginning with the feeling element: three [are included] in the <s>dharma-dhātu</s>; the consciousness element, in the seven consciousness <s>dhātus</s>. Of the three beginning with the desire-realm element: the desire-realm, in all eighteen <s>dhātus</s>; the form-realm, in fourteen — excluding the scent, taste, nose-consciousness, and tongue-consciousness <s>dhātus</s>; the formless realm, in the mind, <s>dharma</s>, and mind-consciousness <s>dhātus</s>. Of the three beginning with the form-realm element: the inclusion of two has been stated. The cessation element, in the <s>dharma-dhātu</s>. Of the three beginning with the past element: each [is included] in all eighteen <s>dhātus</s>. The three elements beginning with inferior are just the desire-realm elements and the rest — their inclusion has been stated. Of the three beginning with the wholesome: the wholesome and unwholesome elements, in the form, sound, and <s>dharma</s> <s>dhātus</s> and the seven consciousness <s>dhātus</s>. The indeterminate element, in all eighteen <s>dhātus</s>. The learner and beyond-training [elements] —

body.text: (I.28) ya ime tatreti bahudhātuke. eteṣāṃ dvayor lakṣaṇam anuktam iti.
body.translated_text: (I.28) 'Those here' refers to [the elements mentioned] in the <s>Bahudhātuka</s> [sūtra]. The characteristics of two of these have not been stated. Thus:

body.text: pṛthivīdhātvādīnām uktaṃ lakṣaṇam amī
body.translated_text: The characteristics of the earth element and the rest have been stated:

children.translated_text: 'Established through functions such as holding — hardness, cohesion, heat, and movement' —

body.text: iti. nanu ca vijñānadhātor apy uktaṃ lakṣaṇaṃ.
body.translated_text: thus. But [one might object:] the characteristic of the consciousness element has also been stated:

body.text: iti vacanāt. satyam uktaṃ sarveṣāṃ vijñānānāṃ lakṣaṇaṃ. vijñānadhātus tu kim iha kiṃcid eva vijñānam ity abhipretaṃ. utāho sarvam iti na vivecitam. asaṃskṛtaṃ cākāśam uktalakṣaṇaṃ. na tv ākāśadhātuḥ. avaśyaṃ hy ayam [Tib. 52b] anya ākāśāt. tathā hi ṣaḍdhātur ayaṃ bhikṣo puruṣa iti sūtrāntaram uktam. ity anayā buddhyābhihitaṃ dvayor lakṣaṇam anuktam iti. ata evāha. tat kim ākāśam evākāśadhātur veditavyaḥ. sarvaṃ ca vijñānaṃ vijñānadhātur iti. mukhanāsikādiṣv ity ādiśabdena śrotrādīnāṃ grahaṇaṃ.
body.translated_text: because of this statement. True — the characteristic of all types of consciousness has been stated. But the consciousness element here — is it intended as some [particular] consciousness?

body.text: kilaśabdaḥ paramatadyotanārthaḥ. svamataṃ tu sapratighadravyābhāvamātram ākāśam iti abhiprāyo lakṣyate. rātriṃdivasvabhāva iti. rātrivartinas tamaso bhāskarātapalakṣyasya cālokasyābhipretatvāt. bāhuliko vāyaṃ nirdeśaḥ. aghaṃ kila citasthaṃ rūpam iti. citasthaṃ saṃghātasthaṃ. atyarthaṃ hanti hanyate ceti aghaṃ nairuktena vidhinā. atyarthaśabdasya akārādeśaḥ kṛto hanteś ca ghādeśaḥ. tasya taṭ sāmantakam iti. tasyāghasya kuḍyādikasya sāmantakaṃ samīpasthaṃ. tad apekṣya vyavasthāpitam ity arthaḥ. atrāpi vyākhyāne kilaśabdo vaibhāṣikavyākhyānapradarśānārthaḥ. svamataṃ tu yat tat paścād ucyate. tad āha. aghaṃ ca tat. anyasya rūpasya tatrāpratighātān na pratihanyate 'nyad rūpam asminn iti kṛtvā. sāmantakaṃ cānyasya rūpasyeti citasthasya. asmin pakṣe karmadhārayaḥ samāsaḥ. aghaṃ ca tat sāmantakaṃ ca tad iti aghasāmantakaṃ.
body.translated_text: the word 'supposedly' (<s>kila</s>) is for indicating the other [school's] position. But his own view is apparently that space is merely the absence of resistant substance — the intent is discernible. 'The nature of night and day' —

body.text: Tib. 53a
body.translated_text: thus. Because the consciousness intended [here]

body.text: iti. janmano hetor vijñānasyābhipretatvāt. kuta iti cet. ata āha. yasmād ime ṣaḍdhātava iṣṭā.
body.translated_text: is the cause of birth. From what [is this known]? Hence he says: 'Since these six elements are desired as'

body.text: ṣaḍdhātur ayaṃ bhikṣo puruṣa iti. ṣaṭ khalu dhātūn pratītya mātuḥ kukṣau garbhasyāvakrāntir iti vacanāt. ete hi janmana iti vistaraḥ. ete hi janmano janakapoṣakasaṃvardhakatvād ādhārabhūtāḥ. janako hy atra vijñānadhātuḥ pratisaṃdhibījatvāt. poṣakāni bhūtāni tatsaṃniśrayabhāvāt. saṃvardhaka
body.translated_text: 'This person, O monk, consists of six elements' — because of the statement 'depending on six elements, the descent of the embryo into the mother's womb [occurs].' For these are [the conditions for] birth,

body.text: ākāśadhātur avakāśadānāt. ata evaiṣāṃ dhātutvavacanaṃ. pratisaṃdhiṃ dadhata iti dhātavaḥ. anāsravās tu dharmā naivam iti. na janmaniśrayā janmanirodhitvāt.
