Just as the continuance of a shot arrow — its arising in successive spatial locations — is the continuation of the continuum. The time of that — the limit beyond which it ceases — its penetrating determination is the establishing of the cause. What then is that cause? A special potency produced by the wind-element generated by an extraordinary effort. Just as the penetrating determination of the duration of a shot arrow is not a separate substance, so too this penetrating determination characterized as lifespan should be viewed.

body.text: yas tu manyata iti vaiśeṣikaḥ. saṃskāro nāma guṇaviśeṣa iti. pṛthivyādīnāṃ vaiśeṣiko guṇaḥ saṃskāro nāma karmajaḥ [Tib. 156b] karmahetuś ca vegadvitīyanāmā iṣau jāyate. yadvaśād yasya guṇasya vaśād gamanam iṣor ā patanād bhavatīti. taṃ praty adṛṣṭānta eṣaḥ. yathā hi saṃskāro nāma bhāvāṃtaram asti. evam āyur syād iti. tena tan mataṃ dūṣayaty ācāryaḥ. tasyeti vistaraḥ. tasya vaiśeṣikasya tadekatvāt saṃskāraikatvāt. pratibaṃdhābhāvāc ca pratibaṃdhasya kāṣṭhapratyāghātādilakṣaṇasyābhāvāc ca. kiṃ. deśāṃtaraiḥ śīghrataratamaprāptikālabhedānupapattiḥ. śīghrā śīghratarā śīghratamā prāptiḥ śīghrataratamaprāptiḥ. kaiḥ. saha deśāṃtarair ākāśadeśādibhiḥ. tasyāḥ kālaḥ. tasya bhedaḥ. tasyānupapatti. śīghrā śīghratarā śīghratamā deśāṃtaraiḥ saha prāptir nopapadyate. pūrvoktād asmāt kāraṇadvayāt saṃskārasyāviśiṣṭatvāt patanānupapattiś ca. patanaṃ ca iṣor nopapadyate sati saṃskāre. na hy etad iṣṭam sati kāraṇe kāryaṃ na bhavatīti. vāyunā tatpratibaṃdha iti cet syān mataṃ vāyur atra pratibaṃdhaḥ. pratibaṃdhaviśeṣāc chīghrataratamaprāptikālabhedaḥ patanaṃ copapadyata iti sparśavaddravyasaṃyogād abhāvaḥ karmaṇa iti vacanāt. atrocyate arvākpatanaprasaṃgo jyāvibhāgānaṃtaram evārvāg avarata eva vāyusaṃyogāt sa iṣu patet. atha pratibadhyamāno 'pi vāyunā nārvāk patet na vā kadācit [Tib. 157a] patet na paścād api pated ity arthaḥ. kiṃkāraṇaṃ. vāyor aviśeṣāt. yathā hi samīpe vāyur evaṃ dūre 'pīti.
body.translated_text: 'But one who thinks' — the <s>Vaiśeṣika</s>. 'The formation (<s>saṃskāra</s>) is a special quality' — according to the <s>Vaiśeṣika</s>s, there is a special quality of earth and the other [elements] called <s>saṃskāra</s>, produced by action [Tib. 156b] and the cause of action, also named <s>vega</s> (impetus), which arises in the arrow. By the force of which — by the force of which quality — the movement of the arrow occurs until it falls. Against him, this is a counter-example. Just as there is a separate entity called <s>saṃskāra</s>, so too would lifespan be — [this is the analogy]. The Master refutes that view. 'Of that' — thus the elaboration. Of that <s>Vaiśeṣika</s>, because of the oneness of that — the oneness of the formation (<s>saṃskāra</s>). And because of the absence of obstruction — the absence of obstruction characterized by striking against a post and the like. What follows? 'The impossibility of differences in the time of reaching [various] spatial locations at faster and fastest speeds.' Fast, faster, and fastest reaching — this is the faster-and-fastest reaching. With what? With spatial locations — locations in space and the like. The time of that — its difference — its impossibility. Fast, faster, and fastest reaching with [respect to] spatial locations is not possible — because of the aforementioned two reasons: the non-differentiation of the formation. 'And the impossibility of falling' — the falling of the arrow is not possible when the formation exists. For this is not acceptable — that when the cause exists, the effect does not occur. 'If [you say] the wind obstructs it' — one might think the wind is the obstruction here. Because of a specific obstruction, the difference in the time of faster-and-fastest reaching and the falling become possible — [but this is wrong] because of the statement 'from the contact with a substance possessing touch, action ceases.' Here it is said: 'The consequence of falling immediately' — immediately after separation from the bowstring, the arrow would fall backward from the contact with the wind. If, though obstructed by the wind, it does not fall backward, or if it does not ever [Tib. 157a] fall — it would not fall later either, this is the meaning. For what reason? Because of the non-differentiation of the wind. For just as the wind [is present] nearby, so too far away.

body.text: caturthī viṣamāparihāreṇeti. atyaśanāder viṣamasyāparihāreṇa. kṣīṇa āyuṣi puṇyakṣayasya maraṇe nāsti sāmarthyaṃ. tena tṛtīyā koṭir na prāpnoti. tasmād ubhayakṣaye sati maraṇam ubhayakṣayād iti. ubhayakṣaye satīti yo 'rthaḥ.
body.translated_text: 'The fourth [type of death, through] non-avoidance of harmful [conditions]' — through non-avoidance of harmful things such as overeating and the like. When lifespan is exhausted, the exhaustion of merit has no power to [cause] death. Therefore the third alternative does not apply. Therefore, death occurs when both are exhausted — 'from the exhaustion of both.' The meaning of 'when both are exhausted'

body.text: so 'rtha ubhayakṣayād ity ayam artha ukto veditavyaḥ. āyurakṣayād api maraṇaṃ bhavatīti kathaṃ gamyate. sasyādisādharmyāt. sasyādīnāṃ hi bījāvedhaparikṣaye sati satsu pratyayāṃtareṣu kṣetrodakādiṣu dṛṣṭā saṃtānanivṛttir aprāpyaiva phalakālaṃ phalapākakālaṃ vā. bījasya nātisāratvāt. saty api ca sārabījākṣepe salilādisthitivṛddhipratyābhāvād dṛṣṭā saṃtānanivṛttiḥ. sārabījākṣepasthitivṛddhipratyayābhāve 'pi dṛṣṭā. yadā bījākṣepaś ca parisamāpto bhavati salilasya cābhāvaḥ. saty api ca sārabījākṣepe salilādisthitivṛddhipratyaye ca jaṃgamādyupakramakṛtā dṛṣṭā sasyādīnāṃ saṃtānanivṛttir iti. yasyāśrayopaghātād upaghātas tatsaṃtatyadhīnatvād iti. bahirdeśikamatam etat. āśrayasaṃtatipratibaddhaṃ tad āyur iti saṃtatyupanibaddham ity ucyate. kāśmīramate 'pi sa evārthaḥ. śabdamātraṃ tu bhidyate. sāṃtarāyaṃ niraṃtarāyam iti. atha vā saṃtatyupanibaddham iti svasaṃtatyupanibaddhaṃ saṃtānavarty eva tat kevalaṃ na tu sakṛd utpannaṃ tiṣṭhatīti [Tib. 157b] sāṃtarāyam ity ucyate. anenāgamena asty akālamṛtyur iti darśayann āha. sūtre 'py uktaṃ catvāra ātmabhāvapratilaṃbhā iti vistaraḥ. ātmasaṃcetanā ātmanā māraṇaṃ. parasaṃcetanā pareṇa māraṇaṃ. buddhānāṃ ceti vaktavyaṃ. kim. ātmasaṃcetanaiva kramate. svayaṃmṛtyutvāt. anupakramaṇadharmāṇo hi buddhā bhagavaṃto āyurutsargavaśitvalābhinaś ca. prāyeṇeti grahaṇaṃ caturthakoṭyabhihitanārakāṃtarābhavikādiparivarjanārthaṃ. rājarṣayaś cakravartipūrvā pravrajitāḥ. jinadūto yo buddhena bhagavatā dūtaḥ kaścit saṃpreṣitaḥ tadyathā śukaḥ kaścid bhagavatā āmrapālyāḥ preṣito licchavibhiś ca yogyāṃ kurvāṇair dṛṣṭaḥ śarajālenāpūryamāṇo 'pi mārayituṃ na śakyate. yāvad dhi sa dūtakṛtyaṃ na karoti tāvan nātmasaṃcetanā kramate na parasaṃcetanā. jinādiṣṭa iyaṃtaṃ kālam anena jīvitavyam iti ya ādiṣṭo bhagavatā. dharmilādayaḥ pūrvayogavidbhya āgamitavyāḥ. ādiśabdena cānye 'pi tata eva cāgamayitavyāḥ. teṣāṃ nātmasaṃcetanā kramate na parasaṃcetanā. caramabhavikānāṃ ca ye tasminn eva jannani arhattvaṃ prāpnuvaṃti. bodhisattvamātus tatgarbhāyā bodhisattvagarbhāyāḥ. cakravartimātuḥ cakravartigarbhāyā nātmasaṃcetanā [Tib. 158a] na parasaṃcetanā. yadi tarhi sarveṣāṃ rūpārūpyāvacarāṇāṃ nātmasaṃcetanā na parasaṃcetanā atha kasmāt sūtre uktam iti vistaraḥ. tatra cobhayaṃ nāstīti. tatra naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatane svabhūmika āryamārgo nāsti yāvad eva saṃjñāsamāpattis tāvad ājñāprativedha iti vacanāt. nāpy uparibhūmisāmaṃtaka ūrdhvabhūmyabhāvāt. parabhūmika āryamārga ity ākiṃcanyāyatanabhūmikaḥ.
body.translated_text: should be understood as expressed by 'from the exhaustion of both.' 'How is it known that death occurs from the non-exhaustion of lifespan as well?' From the analogy with crops and the like. For when the seed-penetration of crops and the like is exhausted, and when the other conditions such as field and water exist, the cessation of the continuum is observed even without reaching the time of fruition or the time of fruit-ripening — because of the seed's not having sufficient essence. And even when a seed with essence has been planted, from the absence of conditions for continuance and growth such as water, cessation of the continuum is observed. In the absence of both essential seed-planting and conditions for continuance and growth, it is also observed. And even when a seed with essence has been planted and the conditions for continuance and growth such as water exist, cessation of the continuum of crops and the like is observed due to interference by moving creatures and the like. 'Because damage to the basis causes damage to it, since it depends on the continuum of the basis' — this is the view of the outsiders (<s>bahirdeśika</s>). That lifespan is bound to the continuum of the basis — hence it is said to be 'bound to the continuum.' Even in the <s>Kaśmīra</s> view, the meaning is the same; only the wording differs. 'With interruption' and 'without interruption.' Alternatively, 'bound to the continuum' means bound to one's own continuum — it exists only in the continuum, but does not remain once arisen permanently — [Tib. 157b] hence it is called 'with interruption.' Showing by this scripture that untimely death exists, he says: 'It is also stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: there are four types of obtaining a body (<s>ātmabhāvapratilaṃbha</s>)' — thus the elaboration. Self-intention (<s>ātmasaṃcetanā</s>) is killing by oneself. Other-intention (<s>parasaṃcetanā</s>) is killing by another. 'And of <s>Buddha</s>s' — it should be said: what? Self-intention alone applies — because they die by their own will. For <s>Buddha</s>s, the Blessed Ones, are not subject to attack and have mastery over the relinquishment of lifespan. The word 'generally' is for the purpose of excluding [beings in] the fourth category — those in hells, intermediate existence, and the like. Royal sages (<s>rājarṣi</s>) are those who, having previously been universal monarchs, went forth. A messenger of the Conqueror (<s>jinadūta</s>) is someone dispatched as a messenger by the Blessed <s>Buddha</s> — for example, one named <s>Śuka</s> was sent by the Blessed One to <s>Āmrapālī</s>, and when seen by the <s>Licchavi</s>s who were making ready [to attack], even though he was being filled with a shower of arrows, he could not be killed. For as long as he has not accomplished the messenger's task, neither self-intention nor other-intention operates. 'Decreed by the Conqueror to live for such a time' — one who was decreed by the Blessed One. <s>Dharmi</s> and others should be derived from those learned in prior practice. By the word 'and so forth,' others too should be derived from that same [source]. For them, neither self-intention nor other-intention operates. And for those in their last existence (<s>caramabhavika</s>) who attain <s>Arhatship</s> in that very birth. For the mother of the <s>Bodhisattva</s>, [during] the pregnancy of the <s>Bodhisattva</s>. For the mother of a universal monarch, [during] the pregnancy of the universal monarch — neither self-intention [Tib. 158a] nor other-intention [operates]. 'If for all form-realm and formless-realm beings, neither self-intention nor other-intention [operates], then why is it stated in the <s>sūtra</s>?' — thus the elaboration. 'And there, both do not exist' — there, in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, there is no noble path of one's own ground — because of the statement 'only as far as the perception-attainment is there penetration to perfect knowledge.' Nor is there the preliminary path of a higher ground, because of the non-existence of a higher ground. The noble path of another ground means that belonging to the ground of the sphere of nothingness.

children.translated_text: 'Facing the sphere of nothingness of the noble [path], the destruction of outflows [occurs] at the peak of existence' —

body.text: iti vacanāt. paryaṃtagrahaṇāt tarhīti. tarhīty arthāṃtaravivakṣāyāṃ nipātaḥ. tadādisaṃpratyaya iti. tasya paryaṃtasya naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatanasyādiś catvāri dhyānāni trayaś ca śeṣā ārūpyāḥ. na tu kāmadhātus tadādir asamāhitatvena visādṛśyāt. samāpattito vā dhyānārūpyā eva tadādiḥ. navānupūrvasamāpattaya iti vacanāt. tatra saṃpratyayas tadādisaṃpratyayaḥ. asti kvacid anyatrāpy evaṃ dṛṣṭam iti astīty āha. kvacid ādinā paryaṃta ityādi.tadyathā devā brahmakāyikā iti. devā brahmakāyikāḥ tatparyaṃtagrahaṇāc ca brahmapurohitā mahābrahmāṇaś ca prathamā sukhopapattiḥ. tadyathā devā ābhāsvarā iti. ābhāsvarās tadādigrahānāc ca parīttābhā apramāṇābhāś ca dvitīyā sukhopapattir iti. tisra eva hi sukhopapattaya [Tib. 158b] iṣyaṃte
body.translated_text: because of this statement. 'Then, because of the word "limit" (<s>paryaṃta</s>)' — the particle 'then' (<s>tarhi</s>) indicates the intention to express another meaning. 'Beginning with that' — the beginning of that limit, the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, is the four <s>dhyāna</s>s and the three remaining formless [attainments]. But not the desire realm, because of its dissimilarity [to the limit] due to being non-concentrated. Or, from the [standpoint of] attainment, only the <s>dhyāna</s>s and formless [states] are its beginning — because of the statement 'the nine successive attainments.' Therein, 'conviction regarding that beginning' is 'conviction regarding the beginning of that.' 'Is there an example of this seen elsewhere too?' — thus he says 'there is.' 'Elsewhere' and so forth, beginning with 'limit.' For example: '<s>Brahmakāyika</s> gods' — the <s>Brahmakāyika</s> gods, and because of the inclusion of the limit [in the designation], also the <s>Brahmapurohita</s> and <s>Mahābrahmā</s> [gods] — [constitute] the first happy rebirth (<s>sukhopapatti</s>). For example: '<s>Ābhāsvara</s> gods' — the <s>Ābhāsvara</s> [gods], and because of the inclusion of the beginning [in the designation], also the <s>Parīttābha</s> and <s>Apramāṇābha</s> [gods] — [constitute] the second happy rebirth. For only three happy rebirths [Tib. 158b] are accepted —

children.translated_text: 'Three happy rebirths, nine [sub-levels] in the three <s>dhyāna</s> grounds' —

body.text: iti vacanāt. eṣa hi dṛṣṭāṃtadharma iti. etad dṛṣtāṃtacaritaṃ yad ekam api tatprakāraṃ nirdiśate na sarvaṃ śeṣasaṃpratyayaś ca bhavati. tadyathā anityaḥ śabdaḥ. kṛtakatvāt yathā ghaṭa iti paṭādīny api gṛhyaṃte. tadyathāśabdasya dṛṣṭāṃtavācakatvāt. anupasaṃhāra eṣa iti. adṛṣṭāṃta ity arthaḥ. manuṣyās tadekatyāś ca devā iti. tadeke devāḥ ṣaṭ kāmāvacarā devāḥ prathamābhinirvṛttavarjyāś ca prathamadhyānopapannā devā ity etāvaṃta eva nānātvakāyā nānātvasaṃjñinaḥ sattvā naitadvyatiriktāḥ saṃtīti nāyaṃ tadyathāśabdo dṛṣṭāṃtavācakaḥ. tasmād upadarśanārtha evāyaṃ draṣṭavyaḥ. upadarśanārthatve ca sati tad eva sthitam etat. paryaṃtagrahaṇāt tadādisaṃpratyaya iti.
body.translated_text: because of that statement. 'For this is the nature of an example' — the conduct of an example is such that even when one instance of that type is indicated, not everything [need be mentioned], and there is understanding of the remainder. Just as [in the inference]: 'sound is impermanent, because of being produced — like a pot,' cloth and the like are also grasped, because the word 'just as' (<s>tadyathā</s>) denotes an example. 'This is without complete enumeration' — meaning: without an example [covering all cases]. 'Humans and some gods' — 'some gods' are the six desire-realm gods, and gods born in the first <s>dhyāna</s> excluding those initially produced — only this many are beings with diverse bodies and diverse perceptions; there are none beyond these. So this word 'just as' does not denote an example. Therefore it should be understood as merely for illustration. And when it is for illustration, exactly that stands — 'because of the inclusion of the limit, there is understanding of those beginning [from that point].'

body.text: (II.46cd) viparyayād asaṃskṛta iti. yatraitāni na bhavaṃti. so 'saṃskṛta iti. nanu ca sthitir asaṃskṛtalakṣaṇam asti. nāsaṃskṛtasya sthitir dravyāṃtararūpāsti. dravyāṃtararūpāṇi ceha saṃskṛtalakṣaṇānīṣyaṃta ity acodyam etat. nanu ca trīṇīmānīti vistaraḥ. kathaṃ. sūtre trīṇīmāni bhikṣavaḥ saṃskṛtasya saṃskṛtalakṣaṇāni. katamāni trīṇi. saṃskṛtasya bhikṣava utpādo 'pi prajñāyate. vyayo 'pi prajñāyate. sthityanyathātvam apīti. caturtham apy atra vaktavyaṃ syād iti vaibhāṣikāḥ. kiṃ cātra noktam iti codakaḥ. sthitir iti vaibhāṣikāḥ. yat tarhīdaṃ sthityanyathātvam apīti [Tib. 159a] sthitiśabdo 'tra śrūyate. katham idam ucyate sthitir nokteti codakābhiprāyaḥ. jarāyā eṣa paryāya iti. jareyam uktā sthiter anyathātvaṃ sthityanyathātvam iti. tadyathā jāter utpāda iti paryāyaḥ. anityatāyāś ca vyayaḥ. tathā jarāyāḥ
body.translated_text: (II.46cd) 'By the reverse, [it is] unconditioned' — where these [characteristics] do not exist, that is unconditioned. 'But surely duration (<s>sthiti</s>) is a characteristic of the unconditioned?' — the unconditioned does not have duration in the form of a separate substance. And here the conditioned characteristics are accepted as being in the form of separate substances — so this is not an objection. 'But surely there are three' — thus the elaboration. How? In the <s>sūtra</s>: 'There are, monks, three conditioned characteristics of the conditioned. What three? Of the conditioned, monks, arising is discerned, passing away is discerned, and alteration while persisting is also [discerned].' 'A fourth too should be stated here' — say the <s>Vaibhāṣika</s>s. 'What is not stated here?' — asks the objector. 'Duration' — say the <s>Vaibhāṣika</s>s. 'But then this [sūtra says] "alteration while persisting" — [Tib. 159a] the word "duration" (<s>sthiti</s>) is heard here. How then can it be said that duration is not mentioned?' — this is the objector's intent. 'This is a synonym for aging (<s>jarā</s>)' — aging is expressed here: the alteration of duration is 'alteration-while-persisting' (<s>sthityanyathātva</s>). Just as 'arising' (<s>utpāda</s>) is a synonym for birth (<s>jāti</s>), and 'passing away' (<s>vyaya</s>) for impermanence (<s>anityatā</s>), so too of aging

body.text: sthityanyathātvaṃ paryāya iti. kasmāt punar lakṣaṇacatuṣṭe sati bhagavatā trīṇy evoktānīti. ata āha. ye hi dharmā iti vistaraḥ. udvejanārthaṃ vineyānāṃ jātijarānityatā iti dharmāṇāṃ lakṣaṇāny uktāni. ābhiprāyiko hi sūtranirdeśo na lākṣaṇiko yathābhidharmaḥ. jarānityate punaḥ pratyutpannād atītam iti. saṃcārayati ity adhikāro 'nuvartate. jarānityate pratyutpannād adhvano 'tītam adhvānaṃ saṃcārayataḥ. kasmāt. durbalīkṛtya vighātāt. jarā durbalīkaroti. anityatā nihaṃtīti kṛtvā. nanu cānityataiva dharmaṃ pratyutpannād adhvano 'tītam adhvānaṃ saṃcārayati. na jarā. jarā hi kevalaṃ dharmaṃ durbalīkaroti. kasmād evam ucyate. jarānityate pratyutpannād atītaṃ saṃcārayata iti. āha. durbalīkaraṇaṃ api tadadhvasaṃcārāyaiva vartate. na hy adurbalīkṛtasyādhvasaṃcāro 'stīti jarāpi tatsaṃcāre vyavasthāpyate. asaṃskṛtasyāpi ca svalakṣaṇasthitibhāvād iti. svalakṣaṇe sthitiḥ. sthityā bhāvaḥ. tasmāt sthitibhāvāt. asau sthitiḥ saṃskṛtalakṣaṇaṃ na vyavasthāpitā. sthitir hy asaṃskṛtāvasthāviśeṣalakṣaṇayā sthityā [Tib. 159b] sadṛśīti tasyāsaṃskṛtasya saṃskṛtatvaprasaṃgaparijihīrṣayā na lakṣaṇam uktam ity abhiprāyo bhagavato dharmasvāminaḥ.
body.translated_text: 'alteration-while-persisting' is a synonym. 'But why did the <s>Bhagavān</s> state only three when there are four characteristics?' Therefore he says: 'for those <s>dharma</s>s...' — thus the elaboration. For the purpose of causing alarm in the disciples, birth, aging, and impermanence were stated as characteristics of <s>dharma</s>s. For the <s>sūtra</s> teaching is intentional, not definitional like the <s>Abhidharma</s>. 'Aging and impermanence [transfer] from the present to the past' — the governing verb 'transfer' continues. Aging and impermanence transfer [a <s>dharma</s>] from the present time-period to the past time-period. Why? 'By weakening and destroying.' Aging weakens; impermanence destroys — this is the intent. 'But surely it is impermanence alone that transfers a <s>dharma</s> from the present to the past time-period, not aging. For aging merely weakens a <s>dharma</s>. Why then is it said: "aging and impermanence transfer from present to past"?' He replies: the weakening too operates precisely for the transfer to that time-period. For there is no time-period transfer of what has not been weakened — therefore aging too is established as [contributing to] that transfer. 'And because the unconditioned too has persistence in its own characteristic' — persistence in its own characteristic; the state of that persistence. Because of that persistent state, that duration is not established as a conditioned characteristic. For duration, [Tib. 159b] being similar to the unconditioned state-characteristic of persistence — wishing to avoid the unwanted consequence that the unconditioned would become conditioned, it was not stated as a [separate] characteristic. This is the intent of the <s>Bhagavān</s>, the Lord of <s>Dharma</s>.

body.text: anye punaḥ kalpayaṃtīti. sūtre 'pi sthitir ukteti kathayaṃti. sthitiṃ jarāṃ cābhisamasya sthitiś ca sthityanyathātvaṃ ca sthityanyathātvam iti abhisamasya ekaṃ lakṣaṇam uktaṃ sūtre. na vibhāgaśaḥ. kasmāt. trīṇīmāni saṃskṛtalakṣaṇānīti vacanavirodhaprasaṃgāt. kim atra prayojanam ity ata āha. eṣā hy eṣu saṃgāspadam iti vistaraḥ. eṣā hi sthitir eṣu jātyādiṣu saṃgāspadaṃ saṃgasthānaṃ dharmo 'nayā tiṣṭhatīty abhiprāyaḥ śriyam ivaināṃ sthitiṃ kālakarṇīsahitāṃ alakṣṃīsahitāṃ darśayāmāsa bhagavān tasyāṃ sthityām asaṃgārthaṃ. nāsyām āsaṃgaḥ kartavyo yasmād iyam anitatayānubaddhā lakṣmīr ivālakṣmyeti tad ekīyaṃ vyākhyānaṃ. apare tu vyācakṣate. nāsyām āsaṃktavyaṃ yasmād iyaṃ jarayānubaddhā lakṣmīr ivālakṣmyeti. jarayā hy anyathātvalakṣaṇayā asyā ekīkaraṇaṃ nānityatayeti. ataś catvāry eva saṃskṛtalakṣaṇānīti. ubhayor api pakṣayor ayam upasaṃhāraḥ.
body.translated_text: 'Others, however, conceive [differently]' — they say that duration too is mentioned in the <s>sūtra</s>. Having combined duration and aging — 'duration and alteration-while-persisting' — having combined [them], one characteristic was stated in the <s>sūtra</s>, not separately. Why? Because of the unwanted consequence of contradicting the statement 'there are three conditioned characteristics.' 'What purpose does this serve?' — therefore he says: 'for this [duration] is a basis for attachment among these...' — thus the elaboration. For this duration is a basis for attachment — a ground for attachment — among these [characteristics] beginning with birth. The intent is: by this [duration] the <s>dharma</s> persists. The <s>Bhagavān</s> showed this duration accompanied by death, like fortune accompanied by misfortune, for the purpose of non-attachment to that duration. 'One should not be attached to it, because it is accompanied by impermanence, like fortune by misfortune' — this is one interpretation. Others explain: 'one should not be attached to it, because it is accompanied by aging, like fortune by misfortune.' For the unification [of duration] with aging, which has the characteristic of alteration, [was made for this purpose], not with impermanence. Therefore there are exactly four conditioned characteristics — this is the conclusion for both positions.

body.text: (II.47ab) anyair jātyādibhir bhavitavyam iti. jātisāmarthyāt kaścit saṃskṛto dharmo jāyate. jātir api saṃskṛtā. tasmāt tasyā api anyayā jātyā bhavitavyaṃ svātmani vṛttivirodhāt.
body.translated_text: (II.47ab) 'There must be other [characteristics] such as birth, etc.' — by the power of birth, a certain conditioned <s>dharma</s> is born. Birth too is conditioned. Therefore it too must have another birth, because of the contradiction of operating upon itself.

body.text: iti ca siddhaṃtāt. evaṃ jarādayo [Tib. 160a] 'pi yojyāḥ.
body.translated_text: from this established principle as well. Thus aging and the rest [Tib. 160a] should also be applied [in the same way].

body.text: iti. jātijātyādayaś ca teṣām iti caśabdo luptanirdiṣṭo draṣṭavyaḥ. nanu caikaikasyeti vistaraḥ. ekaikasya lakṣaṇasya caturlakṣaṇī caturṇāṃ lakṣaṇānāṃ samāhāraḥ caturlakṣaṇī prāpnoti. aparyavasānadoṣaś ca aniṣṭhādoṣaś ca. teṣām anulakṣaṇānāṃ punar anyajātyādiprasaṃgāt. jāter jāter jātijāter yāvad antiyatāyā anityatāyā anityatānityatāyāś ca prasaṃgāt.
body.translated_text: thus. 'And the birth-of-birth, etc., of those' — the word 'and' (<s>ca</s>) should be understood as elided in the statement. 'But for each one...' — thus the elaboration. Each characteristic would require a set of four characteristics — a collection of four characteristics — leading to the fault of non-termination, the fault of endlessness. Because of the further entailment of other births, etc., for those sub-characteristics — from the birth of birth, the birth-of-the-birth-of-birth, up to the impermanence of impermanence, the impermanence-of-the-impermanence-of-impermanence.

children.translated_text: 'Those [operate on] eight <s>dharma</s>s in a single occurrence' —

body.text: te iti puṃliṃganirdeśo dharmābhisaṃbaṃdhāt. te jātyādijātijātyādisvabhāvā dharmā yathākramam aṣṭadharmaikavṛttayaḥ. jātyādīnām aṣṭāsu dharmeṣu vṛttiḥ. jātijātyādīnāṃ caikadharme. ātmanavamā hīti lakṣaṇānulakṣaṇāpekṣa evam uktaṃ. na hi yathāsaṃbhavaṃ tatra prāptyādayo bhūtāni bhautikāni vā notpadyaṃte.
body.translated_text: the masculine pronoun 'those' is used because of the connection with <s>dharma</s>s. Those <s>dharma</s>s whose nature is birth, etc. and birth-of-birth, etc., respectively operate on eight <s>dharma</s>s in a single occurrence. Birth, etc. operate on eight <s>dharma</s>s; birth-of-birth, etc. operate on a single <s>dharma</s>. For 'being ninth with respect to itself' — this is stated with reference to characteristics and sub-characteristics. For it is not that <s>prāpti</s>s and the like, or primary and secondary elements, do not arise there as appropriate.

children.translated_text:
'In the desire [realm], without sound, [a dharma consists of] eight substances.
Everything [is marked] by conditioned characteristics, or by <s>prāpti</s>' —

body.text: caivamādivacanāt. jātir ātmānaṃ virahayyeti vistaraḥ. svātmani vṛttivirodha ity ataḥ ātmānam virahayya muktvāṣṭau dharmān janayati. katamān aṣṭau. taṃ dharmaṃ rūpaṃ cittaṃ vā sthitiṃ jarām anityatāṃ jātijātiṃ sthitisthitiṃ jarājarām anityatānityatāṃ ca janayati. jātijātis tu tām eva jātiṃ janayati. evaṃ jarānityate api yathāyogaṃ yojye iti. [Tib. 160b] jarā ātmānaṃ virahayya aṣṭau dharmān jarayati. jarājarā punas tām eva jarāṃ. anityatā ātmānaṃ virahayya aṣṭau dharmān vināśayati. anityatānityatā punas tām evānityatām iti.
body.translated_text: from such statements as these. 'Birth, excluding itself...' — thus the elaboration. Because of the contradiction of operating upon itself, birth, excluding itself — setting itself aside — produces eight <s>dharma</s>s. Which eight? It produces that <s>dharma</s> (form or mind), duration, aging, impermanence, birth-of-birth, duration-of-duration, aging-of-aging, and impermanence-of-impermanence. But birth-of-birth produces that birth alone. Thus aging and impermanence should also be applied as appropriate. [Tib. 160b] Aging, excluding itself, ages eight <s>dharma</s>s. Aging-of-aging, in turn, ages that aging alone. Impermanence, excluding itself, destroys eight <s>dharma</s>s. Impermanence-of-impermanence, in turn, destroys that impermanence alone.

body.text: tad etad ākāśaṃ pāṭyata iti. vibhidyata ity abhiprāyaḥ. sapratighadravyābhāvamātram ākāśaṃ. nākāśaṃ nāma kiṃcid asti. tad vibhaktuṃ yathā na śakyate na yujyate vā. evam ime jātyādayaḥ asaṃto dharmā vibhaktuṃ na śakyaṃte na yujyaṃte vā. tata āha. na hy eta iti vistaraḥ. na hy ete dravyataḥ svalakṣaṇataḥ saṃvidyaṃte yathā vibhajyaṃte. jātir ātmānaṃ virahayyāṣṭau dharmān janayatīty evaṃ vistareṇa vibhajyaṃte yathā rūpādīnāṃ dharmāṇām iti. atrādiśabdena śabdādivedanādicakṣurādīnāṃ grahaṇaṃ. tatra rūpaśabdādi tāvat pratyakṣeṇa cakṣurvijñānādilakṣaṇena pramāṇenopalabhyate. vedanādy api pratyakṣeṇaivopalabhyate svasaṃvedyatvāt. cakṣurādi tu cakṣurvijñānādinānumānenānumīyate. cakṣurvijñānādisaṃniśrayo rūpaprasādaś cakṣurādīni tadbhāvabhāvayos tdbhāvābhāvāt. āgamo 'pi cakṣuṣā rūpāṇi dṛṣṭveti vistaraḥ. evaṃ śrotreṇa śabdāṃ cchrutveti vistareṇa evaṃ gandhādiṣv api yojyaṃ. [Tib. 161a] tathā yatkiṃcid rūpam atītanāgatapratyutpannam
body.translated_text: 'This space (<s>ākāśa</s>) is being split' — the intent is: 'is being divided.' Space is merely the absence of resistant substance. There is nothing called 'space' [as an entity]. Just as that cannot be divided — or it is not proper [to divide it] — so too these [characteristics] beginning with birth, being non-existent <s>dharma</s>s, cannot be divided — or it is not proper [to divide them]. Therefore he says: 'for these are not...' — thus the elaboration. For these are not found as real substances — with own-characteristics — such that they could be analyzed: 'birth, excluding itself, produces eight <s>dharma</s>s' and so on in detail, in the way that <s>dharma</s>s such as form, etc. [are found]. Here the word 'etc.' (<s>ādi</s>) includes sound, etc., feeling, etc., and the eye, etc. Therein, form, sound, and the like are first apprehended by direct perception — by the valid means of knowledge characterized as visual consciousness, etc. Feeling and the like too are apprehended by direct perception alone, because of being self-cognized. But the eye and the like are inferred by inference through visual consciousness, etc.: 'the support of visual consciousness, etc. — the material clarity — is the eye, etc.,' [established] from the presence and absence [of consciousness] given the presence and absence of that [organ]. Scripture too [states]: 'having seen forms with the eye' — thus the elaboration. Similarly, 'having heard sounds with the ear' — and so on in detail; the same should be applied [Tib. 161a] for odors, etc. Likewise, 'whatever form — past, future, or present'

body.text: iti vistaraḥ. evaṃ vedanādiṣv api yojyaṃ. pārasāṃtānikānāṃ tv arūpiṇāṃ vedanādīnām astitvānumānam ātmīyavac charīravikāraṃ dṛṣṭvā tatsaṃpratipatteḥ. āgamo 'pi cakṣuḥ pratītya rūpāṇi cotpadyate cakṣurvijñānaṃ sahajātā vedānā saṃjñā cetaneti vistaraḥ. jātyādayas tu na cakṣurindriyādipratyakṣā bhavaṃti. na caiṣām astitve samartham anumānam asti. na cāpy āgamo dravyato 'stitve. yat tarhi sūtra uktam iti vistaraḥ. nanu cāyam āgamo 'sti saṃskṛtasyotpādo 'pi prajñāyate iti vistaraḥ. arthaś ca pratisaraṇam uktaṃ bhagavateti. catvārīmāni bhikṣavaḥ pratisaraṇāni. katamāni catvāri. dharmaḥ pratisaraṇaṃ na pudgalaḥ. arthaḥ pratisaraṇaṃ na vyaṃjanaṃ. nītārthasūtraṃ pratisaraṇaṃ. na neyārthaṃ. jñānaṃ pratisaraṇaṃ na vijñānam iti. tathārthapratisaraṇo bhavati. na vyaṃjanapratisaraṇa iti. kaḥ punaḥ asyārtha iti. asyopanyastasya saṃskṛtalakṣaṇasūtrasya. tam artham āha. avidyāṃdhā hi bālā iti vistaraḥ. saṃskāraprabandham ātmata ātmīyataś cādhimuktāḥ kṛtarucayo 'bhiṣvajaṃte ity arthaḥ. saṃskṛtatvaṃ pratītyasamutpannatvam iti paryāyāv etau. sametya saṃbhūya pratyayaiḥ kṛtaṃ saṃskṛtaṃ. taṃ [Tib. 161b] taṃ pratyayaṃ pratītya samutpannaṃ pratītyasamutpannam iti. na tu kṣaṇasyeti. pravāhasyaiva saṃskṛtatvaṃ dyotayitukāma idam āha. na tu kṣaṇasya saṃskṛtatvaṃ. na hi kṣaṇasyotpādādaya utpādavyayasthityanyathātvalakṣaṇā dharmāḥ prajñāyaṃte kṣaṇasya duravadhāratvāt. brūyās tvam aprajñāyamānā apy ete lakṣaṇaṃ bhavitum arhaṃtīty ata āha. na cāprajñāyamānā ete lakṣaṇaṃ bhavitum arhaṃtīti. prajñāyamānam eva hi lakṣaṇaṃ bhavati. tadyathā jalasya balāketi. ata evātreti. ata evātra sūtre prajñāyata iti padagrahaṇam. anyathā hi saṃskṛtasyotpādo 'pi vyayo 'pi sthityanyathātvam apīty evāvakṣyat. saṃskṛtatve lakṣaṇānīti. saṃskṛtam iti lakṣaṇānīty arthapratigrahārthaṃ punaḥ saṃskṛtagrahaṇaṃ. jalabalākāvad iti. vaidharmadṛṣṭāṃto 'yaṃ yathā balākā jalāstitve lakṣaṇaṃ na punar jalasya jalatve lakṣaṇaṃ. maivaṃ vijñāyi. kiṃ. saṃskṛtasya vastunaḥ astitve 'mūni lakṣaṇāni. sādhvasādhutve vā kanyālakṣaṇavad iti. yathā kanyāyāḥ śubhāśubhāni lakṣaṇāni yathākramaṃ sādhvasādhutve lakṣaṇānīti. yadi hy amūni tathā saṃskṛtasya vastuno 'stitve sādhvasādhutve vā lakṣaṇānīṣyeran trīṇīmāni saṃskṛtalakṣaṇānīty ucyeta. saṃskṛtasya saṃskṛtalakṣaṇānīti na kriyeta. kṛtam ca. tena jñāyate saṃskṛtatve lakṣaṇānīti. [Tib. 162a] kathaṃ punar avidyamānā jātyādayaḥ pravāhe vyavasthāpyaṃte prajñāyaṃte vā. na brūmo jātyādayo na saṃvidyaṃta iti. yathā tu dravyarūpeṇa vibhajyaṃte. tathā na saṃvidyaṃta iti brūmaḥ. yathā tarhi bhavatāṃ
body.translated_text: ...and so forth in detail. The same should be applied to <s>vedanā</s> (feeling) and the rest as well. The inference of the existence of formless <s>vedanā</s> and other [mental factors] belonging to other continua (<s>pārasāṃtānika</s>) is established by observing bodily changes, just as with one's own [mental states], through understanding their correspondence. Scripture also [supports this]: 'Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises; feeling, perception, and volition are co-born,' and so forth in detail. But <s>jāti</s> (birth) and the rest are not perceptible through the eye-faculty and so on. Nor is there a valid inference for their existence as substances. Nor does scripture [establish] their existence as substances. As for what is stated in the sūtra, and so forth in detail. 'But is this not scripture: the arising of the conditioned is also perceived,' and so forth in detail. And meaning is the refuge, as stated by the Blessed One: 'These four, O monks, are the refuges. What four? <s>Dharma</s> is the refuge, not the person. Meaning is the refuge, not the letter. The sūtra of definitive meaning is the refuge, not that of provisional meaning. Knowledge (<s>jñāna</s>) is the refuge, not consciousness (<s>vijñāna</s>).' Thus one takes meaning as refuge, not the letter. What then is its meaning? Of this presented sūtra on the characteristics of the conditioned. He states that meaning: 'For the foolish are blinded by ignorance,' and so forth in detail. The meaning is that, devoted to and taking delight in the continuum of <s>saṃskāras</s> (formations) as self and as belonging to self, they cling to it. Conditionedness (<s>saṃskṛtatva</s>) and dependent origination (<s>pratītyasamutpannatva</s>) are synonyms. That which is made (<s>kṛta</s>) by conditions coming together is conditioned (<s>saṃskṛta</s>). That which has arisen dependent on this or that condition is dependently originated (<s>pratītyasamutpanna</s>). 'But not of a momentary instant' — wishing to illuminate the conditionedness of the continuum (<s>pravāha</s>) alone, he says this. But the conditionedness is not of the momentary instant, for the characteristics of the conditioned — arising, decay, duration, and alteration — are not perceived for a single instant, since an instant is difficult to discern. You might say that even though not perceived, these could still be characteristics; therefore he says: 'Nor are these fit to be characteristics when not perceived.' For only what is perceived can be a characteristic, just as a crane [is a sign] of water. 'Therefore in this' — therefore in this sūtra the word 'is perceived' is used. Otherwise it would have been said merely: 'The conditioned has arising, decay, and duration-alteration.' 'The characteristics of the conditioned' — the repetition of 'conditioned' is for the purpose of grasping the meaning that these are characteristics. 'Like a crane and water' — this is an illustration by dissimilarity: just as a crane is a sign of the existence of water, but not a sign of water being water. It should not be understood thus. Rather, these characteristics indicate the existence of a conditioned thing, or its good and bad nature, like the marks of a maiden. Just as auspicious and inauspicious marks of a maiden indicate respectively good and bad [qualities]. For if these were considered characteristics of the existence or good/bad nature of a conditioned thing, it would be said 'These three are characteristics of the conditioned,' and the expression 'characteristics of conditionedness' would not be used. What has been done? By that it is known that these are 'characteristics of conditionedness.' How then can <s>jāti</s> (birth) and the rest, being non-existent [as substances], be established in the continuum or be perceived?

body.text: saṃvidyaṃte. tathā kathyatāṃ. ata āha. pravāhasyādir utpāda iti vistaraḥ. nivṛttir vyaya iti. pravāhasyoparatir vyayaḥ. sa eva pravāho 'nuvartamāna iti. sadṛśakṣaṇānuvṛtter anuvartamānaḥ pravāhaḥ. sthitir iti ucyate. tasyāḥ pūrvāparaviśeṣa iti. pūrvasmād aparasya kṣaṇasya viśeṣaḥ. pūrvāparayoḥ kṣaṇayor vā viśeṣaḥ pūrvāparaviśeṣaḥ. evaṃ ca kṛtvoktam iti. pravāharūpān evotpādādīn kṛtvānityopasthitasmṛtitām āyuṣmataḥ suṃdaranandasyārabhyoktaṃ. pravāhagatā hi vedanās tasya viditā ivotpadyaṃte viditā iva tiṣṭhaṃte viditā iva parikṣayaṃ paryādānaṃ gacchaṃti na kṣaṇagatāḥ. kṣaṇasya duravadhāratvād iti. viditasya ca kṣaṇasyāvasthānāsaṃbhavāt. etam evārthaṃ ślokadvayena saṃgṛhṇann āha.
body.translated_text: We do not say that <s>jāti</s> and the rest do not exist at all; rather, we say they do not exist in the manner of being analyzable as separate substances. How then do they exist according to you? — Let that be explained. Therefore he says: '<s>Jāti</s> (birth) is the beginning of the continuum,' and so forth in detail. 'Cessation is decay' — the cessation of the continuum is decay. 'That very continuum continuing' — the continuum continuing by following similar successive instants is called duration (<s>sthiti</s>). 'Its difference between earlier and later' — the difference of a later instant from an earlier one, or the difference between earlier and later instants, is the earlier-later difference. 'Having thus construed' — having construed arising and the rest as forms of the continuum, the statement beginning with <s>Sundara-Nanda</s> was spoken with the impermanence of memory attended to: 'For the feelings occurring in the continuum arise as if known, endure as if known, and go to exhaustion and consumption as if known — not those occurring in a single instant, since an instant is difficult to discern.' And because it is impossible for a known instant to remain. Summarizing this very meaning in two verses, he says:

children.translated_text: '<s>Jāti</s> (birth) is the beginning of the continuum' —

body.text: ādi sarvam uktaṃ.
body.translated_text: the beginning; all has been stated.

body.text: iti. sa eva pravāhaḥ sthitiḥ.
body.translated_text: that very continuum is duration.

body.text: tasyaiva pravāhasya.
body.translated_text: of that very continuum.

body.text: prabandhocchedaḥ.
body.translated_text: the cessation of the continuum.

body.text: ślokaḥ. kṣaṇiko hi dharmaḥ.
body.translated_text: this is a verse. For a <s>dharma</s> is momentary.

body.text: vinaśyed ity arthaḥ. sthitir astīti manyase cet. sa ca dharmo vyety eva satyām api sthitau. vinaśyaty eva kṣaṇikatvāt. vināśahetvabhāvāt.
body.translated_text: it would perish, is the meaning. If you think duration exists — even if there were duration, that <s>dharma</s> still passes away, since it is momentary and because there is no cause of destruction.

body.text: niṣprayojanā sthitiparikalpanenety arthaḥ. dvitīyādikṣaṇāvasthānena [Tib. 162b] hi sthitiparikalpanā na vṛthā bhavet. tasmāt pravāha eva sthitiḥ. yasmāt kṣaṇikasya hi dharmasya sthitiparikalpanā vyartheti. evaṃ ca kṛtvāyam apīti. pravāha eva sthitir iti kṛtvety arthaḥ. na hi kṣaṇasyotpannasyāvināśo 'stīti. atra kasyacid evam abhiprāyo bhavet. sthitisadbhāvād ekaṃ kṣaṇam avināśo dharmasyotpannasya. yadi hi sthitir na syāt. so 'py ekaḥ kṣaṇo na syād iti. na. hetupratyayapūrvakatvāt tadastitvasya. asmin satīdaṃ bhavatīti vacanāt. sthitir upagṛhṇātīti cet. syān mataṃ hetupratyayebhya utpadyamānaṃ dharmaṃ sthitir upagṛhṇātīti. yadi sthitir nopagṛhṇīyāt kiṃ syāt. ātmasattā dharmasya na bhavet.
body.translated_text: the meaning is that the conception of duration is purposeless. For the conception of duration would not be vain only if there were remaining for a second or further instant. Therefore duration is the continuum alone, since the conception of duration for a momentary <s>dharma</s> is pointless. And 'having thus construed' means having construed duration as the continuum alone. For there is no non-destruction of something that has arisen in a single instant. Here someone might hold the view: because duration truly exists, there is one instant of non-destruction for an arisen <s>dharma</s>; for if there were no duration, that single instant too would not exist. No — because its existence is preceded by causes and conditions, as stated: 'When this exists, that comes to be.' If you say duration supports [the dharma] — the thought might be that duration supports a <s>dharma</s> as it arises from causes and conditions. If duration did not support it, what would happen? The <s>dharma</s> would not have its own existence.

body.text: janikā tarhi sthitiḥ prāpnoti na sthāpikā. saṃtānam avasthāpayatīti cet. hetupratyayeṣu sthityākhyā prasajyate. hetupratyayānāṃ saṃtānahetutvāt. nikāyasabhāgacittaṃ yujyata iti. ekasmiṃ nikāyasabhāge 'nekam api cittaṃ ekam ity ucyate. ekanikāyasabhāgasaṃbhūtatvād ity abhiprāyaḥ. tac cittaṃ yujyata ekasmiṃś citta iti vaktum. anyathā hi katham ekasyaiva cittakṣaṇasya jātiś ca maraṇaṃ cānyathātvaṃ ca syāt.
body.translated_text: Then duration would be a producer, not a sustainer. If you say it sustains the continuum — then the designation 'duration' would apply to causes and conditions [themselves], since causes and conditions are the causes of the continuum. 'The mind in a <s>nikāyasabhāga</s> (homogeneous class) is fitting' — even many minds within a single <s>nikāyasabhāga</s> are called 'one,' with the intention that they belong to a single homogeneous class. That mind is fit to be called 'within a single mind.' Otherwise, how could birth, death, and alteration all belong to a single mind-instant?

body.text: uttarottarakṣaṇānubandhaḥ sthitir iti. pūrvasya kṣaṇasya uttaraḥ kṣaṇaḥ pratinidhibhūtaḥ sādṛśyāt. ataḥ sa pūrvaḥ kṣaṇo 'dyāpi avatiṣṭhata iveti kṛtvottaraḥ kṣaṇaḥ sthitir ucyate. yadā tarhi sadṛśā utpadyante iti. yadā sadṛśā utpadyante. tadā visadṛśatvaṃ [Tib. 163a] nāsti. visadṛśatvaṃ ca sthityanyathātvam uktam. ataḥ sadṛśotpattau sthityanyathātvaṃ nāstīti avyāpilakṣaṇaṃ syād ity abhiprāyaḥ. kṣiptākṣiptabalidurbalakṣiptasyeti vistaraḥ. kṣiptaṃ ca tad akṣiptaṃ ca kṣiptākṣiptaṃ. balidurbalābhyāṃ kṣiptaṃ balidurbalakṣiptaṃ. kṣiptākṣiptaṃ ca tad balidurbalakṣiptaṃ ca kṣiptākṣiptabalidurbalakṣiptaṃ. kiṃ tat. vajrādi. ādigrahaṇena lohapāsāṇāder grahaṇaṃ. apare punar evaṃ vigrahaṃ kurvanti. kṣiptaś cākṣiptaś ca kṣiptākṣiptau. balidurbalābhyāṃ kṣiptau balidurbalakṣiptau. kṣiptasyaivāyaṃ dvidhābhedaḥ. kṣiptākśiptau ca balidurbalakṣiptau ca kṣiptākṣiptabalidurbalakṣiptaṃ. vajrādir asya vajrādiḥ. asmin vijrahe vajrādi viśeṣaṇaṃ. kṣiptākṣiptabalidurbalakṣiptaṃ viśeṣyaṃ. tasya vajrāder evaṃvidhasya yathāsaṃbhavaṃ cirāśutarapātaḥ. kṣiptasya ciraṃpātaḥ. akṣiptasya cirataraḥ pātaḥ. durbalakṣiptasyāśupātaḥ. balikṣiptasyāśutaraḥ pātaḥ. tasya kālaḥ. kālasya bhedaḥ. cirāśutarapātakālabhedāt. [Tib. 163b] tadbhūtānāṃ vajrādimahābhūtānāṃ. pariṇāmaviśeṣaḥ kṣiptasyānyathāpariṇāmo yena ciraṃpātaḥ. evaṃ yāvad balikṣiptasyānyathāpariṇāmo yenāśutaraḥ pātaḥ. tasya pariṇāmaviśeṣasya siddhiḥ. tasyāḥ pariṇāmaviśeṣasiddheḥ na te nirviśeṣā bhavantīty adhikṛtaṃ. antimasya tarhīti vistaraḥ. śabdasyārciṣaś ca dīpāder yo 'ntyaḥ kṣaṇaḥ saṃtānoparatikāle. nirupadhiśeṣanirvāṇakāle vārhataḥ. tasya ṣaḍāyatanasya uttarakṣaṇābhāvāt sthitir nāsti. sthiter abhāvāt sthityanyathātvaṃ nāstīti avyāpinī lakṣaṇavyavasthā prāpnoti. yeyam uktā tasyā visadṛśatvam sthityanyathātvam iti. yasyāsti sthitiḥ. tasyāvaśyam anyathātvaṃ bhavati. yasya nāsti sthitiḥ. tasya nāsti sthityanyathātvam ity uktaṃ bhavati. saṃbhavaṃ hi praty evam uktaṃ sūtre trīṇīmāni saṃskṛtalakṣaṇānīti. tasmād aṃtyaśabdārciḥkṣaṇaprabhṛtīnām utpādavyayāv eva dve lakṣane iti abhiprīyete. tadanyeṣāṃ tu sthityanyathātvam apīti. apara āha.
body.translated_text: 'The succession of subsequent instants is duration' — a subsequent instant, being a representative of the prior instant, is similar [to it]; therefore that prior instant is as if still standing even now, and thus the subsequent instant is called 'duration.' When similar [instants] arise — when similar ones arise, there is no dissimilarity. And dissimilarity has been called 'duration-alteration.' Therefore, when similar ones arise, there is no duration-alteration, so the characteristic designation would be non-pervasive — this is the intended objection. 'Thrown and not-thrown, strong and weak, thrown' — and so forth in detail. What is both thrown and not-thrown is 'thrown-and-not-thrown.' What is thrown by strong and weak [forces] is 'strong-weak-thrown.' What is thrown-and-not-thrown and also strong-weak-thrown is 'thrown-not-thrown-strong-weak-thrown.' What is that? A diamond (<s>vajra</s>) and the like. The word 'and the like' includes iron chains and similar objects. Others analyze it thus: the thrown and the not-thrown are a pair; those thrown by strong and weak [forces] are the strong-weak-thrown pair — this is a twofold division of the thrown alone. The thrown-not-thrown and the strong-weak-thrown together are the thrown-not-thrown-strong-weak-thrown. A diamond and the like is its example. In this analysis, the diamond and the like are the qualifier; thrown-not-thrown-strong-weak-thrown is the qualified. For such diamonds and the like, there is a corresponding duration of fast or slow fall: slow fall for the thrown, slower for the not-thrown, fast for the weak-thrown, faster for the strong-thrown. Its time — the division of time — is according to the division of fast-and-slow fall durations. The transformation-difference of the great elements constituting those [objects like] diamonds — the different transformation of a thrown object that causes its slow fall; similarly up to the different transformation of a strongly-thrown object that causes its faster fall. The establishment of that transformation-difference — regarding the establishment of that transformation-difference, the topic is that they are not without difference. 'Of the final one, then' — and so forth in detail. For the final instant of sound, flame, lamp, and the like — at the time of cessation of the continuum, or at the time of <s>nirupādhiśeṣanirvāṇa</s> (nirvāṇa without remainder) for an <s>Arhat</s> — because there is no subsequent instant for those six sense-bases, there is no duration; and because there is no duration, there is no duration-alteration, so the characteristic designation would be non-pervasive. What was stated — 'dissimilarity is duration-alteration' — for that which has duration, there necessarily is alteration; for that which has no duration, there is no duration-alteration. This has been stated. Only in accordance with possibility was it stated in the sūtra: 'These three are the characteristics of the conditioned.' Therefore, for the final instants of sounds, flames, and the like, only two characteristics — arising and decay — are intended. But for others, duration-alteration also [applies]. Another [commentator] says:

body.text:
aṃtyānām api śabdārciḥkṣaṇaprabhṛtīnāṃ sthitir asti yat svāvasthānaṃ. tasyāś cānyathātvaṃ pūrvakṣaṇāpekṣam iti. teṣām api trīṇi saṃskṛtalakṣaṇāni vyavasthāpyaṃta iti. katham idānīṃ sa eva dharṃo lakṣyaḥ. tasyaiva ca lakṣaṇam iti. lakṣyalakṣaṇayor [Tib. 164a] jalabalākāvat anyatvaṃ paśyaṃtaś codayaṃti. tad vyabhicārayaṃtaḥ sautrāṃtikā āhuḥ. kathaṃ tāvan mahāpuruṣalakṣaṇānītyādi. mahāpuruṣalakṣaṇāni mahāpuruṣasaṃgṛhītatvān nāto 'nyāni. brūyān na mahāpuruṣalakṣaṇamātraṃ mahāpuruṣaḥ. dharmamātraṃ tv abhūtvā bhavati bhūtvā ca na bhavatīti adṛṣṭāṃta eṣaḥ. atra brūmaḥ. samam evaitat. yathā hi mahāpuruṣalakṣaṇāni mahāpuruṣākhyāni mahāpuruṣalakṣaṇākhyāni ca bhavaṃti. evaṃ saṃskṛto dharmaḥ saṃskṛtaṃ coyate saṃskṛtalakṣaṇaṃ ca. utpādādilakṣaṇena hy avasthāviśeṣeṇa sa dharmo lakṣyate. yadā ca pravāhalakṣaṇavyavasthā kriyate. tadā samudāyibhiḥ samudāyo laṣyate. yathā mahāpuruṣasaṃjñaḥ samudāyo mahāpuruṣalakṣaṇaiḥ samudāyibhir iti. etena sāsnādīni lakṣaṇāni vyākhyātāni. kūṭhinyādīni ceti vistaraḥ. ubhayasiddho 'yaṃ dṛṣṭāṃtaḥ pravacanasiddhatvāt. kaṭhinalakṣaṇo hi pṛthivīdhātur ucyate. na ca pṛthivīdhātor anyat kāṭhinyam. evaṃ sarvatra yojyaṃ. sa eva hi pṛthivīdhātuḥ kaṭhinalakṣyamāṇaḥ kaṭhinalakṣaṇa ucyate. etad eva saṃskṛtam abhūtvābhavadbhūtvācābhavallakṣyamāṇaṃ saṃskṛtalakṣaṇam ucyate.
lakṣyata iti lakṣaṇam iti kṛtvā. na ca tat tasmād anyat. yathā cordhvagamaneneti vistaraḥ. ksaṇikavādino vaibhāṣikasya dhūmasyordhvagamanaṃ [Tib. 164b] nānyad asti. sa evordhvadeśāṃtareṣu niraṃtaram utpadyamāna ūrdhvagamanākhyāṃ labhate. tad ūrdhvagamanaṃ tato bhinnam iva lakṣyate. na ca dhūmasya ūrdhvagamanatvam anyad iṣyate. na ca tat tasmād anyat. na ca tad ūrdhvagamanaṃ tasmād dhūmāt anyat. sa evātra nyāya iti. evam utpādo vināśo 'nyathātvaṃ ca tato bhinnam iva lakṣyate. na ca saṃskṛtasya saṃskṛtam anyad bhavatīti. na ca saṃskṛtānāṃ rūpādīnāṃ tāvat saṃskṛtatvaṃ lakṣyate gṛhṇatāpi svabhāvaṃ gṛhṇatāpi rūpādīnāṃ svabhāvaṃ. yāvat prāgabhāvo na jñāyate. yāvat teṣāṃ rūpādīnāṃ prāgutpattyabhāvo na jñāyate. paścāc ca. kim. abhāvaḥ. prāgabhāvaś ca pradhvansābhāvaś ca yāvan na jñāyate. saṃtateś ca viśeṣo yāvan na jñāyate iti vartate. tasmān na tenaiva tal lakṣitaṃ bhavati. na tenaiva saṃskṛtatvena saṃskṛtatvaṃ lakṣyate. kiṃ tarhi. prāgabhāvādibhis tat saṃskṛtatvaṃ lakṣyate. yadi hi rūpādīnāṃ svabhāvaṃ gṛhṇan saṃskṛtam iti gṛhṇīyāt prāgabhāvaṃ paścādabhāvaṃ ca saṃtateś ca viśeṣaṃ ajñātvā tenaiva tal lakṣitaṃ syāt. na tv evaṃ jānīta iti na tenaiva tal lakṣitaṃ bhavati. na ca tebhyo 'pi rūpādibhyo dravyāṃtarāṇy eva jātyādīni vidyaṃte.
body.translated_text:
Even for final [entities] such as sound-moments, flame-moments, and so forth, there is duration — namely, their abiding in their own state. And the alteration of that [duration] is with reference to the preceding moment. Thus, even for those, three conditioned characteristics (<s>saṃskṛtalakṣaṇa</s>) are established. 'How now is the very same <s>dharma</s> the characterized (<s>lakṣya</s>), and the characteristic (<s>lakṣaṇa</s>) also belongs to it?' — Those who see the otherness of the characterized and the characteristic [Tib. 164a] like water and a crane raise this objection. Refuting that deviation, the <s>Sautrāntikas</s> say: 'How then, with regard to the marks of a great man (<s>mahāpuruṣalakṣaṇa</s>)' — and so forth. The marks of a great man are not other than the great man, because they are included in the great man. One might say: 'A great man is not merely the marks of a great man.' But [in the case of] a <s>dharma</s> alone — 'it comes to be not having been, and having been, ceases to be' — this is [said to be] without precedent. Here we say: This is exactly the same. For just as the marks of a great man are called both 'great man' and 'marks of a great man,' so too a conditioned <s>dharma</s> is called both 'conditioned' and 'conditioned characteristic.' For that <s>dharma</s> is characterized by the characteristics of arising and the rest — which are distinctions of state. And when the establishment of continuum-characteristics is made, the aggregate is characterized by its constituents — just as the aggregate designated as 'great man' [is characterized] by its constituents, the marks of the great man. By this, the characteristics of dewlap (<s>sāsnā</s>) and so forth are explained — 'and hardness and so forth' — and so on in detail. This illustration is established for both sides, because it is established in the authoritative teaching. For the earth-element is said to be characterized by hardness. And hardness is not other than the earth-element. This should be applied everywhere. For that very earth-element, being characterized as hard, is called 'the hardness-characteristic.' This very conditioned [dharma], being characterized as 'not having been, it comes to be; and having been, it ceases to be,' is called 'the conditioned characteristic.'
[This is so] because 'that which is characterized is a characteristic.' And that [characteristic] is not other than it [the characterized]. 'Just as with upward movement [of smoke]' — and so forth in detail. For the momentariness-proponent (<s>kṣaṇikavādin</s>) <s>Vaibhāṣika</s>, the upward movement of smoke [Tib. 164b] does not exist [as something separate]. That very [smoke], being produced uninterruptedly in successively higher locations, receives the designation 'upward movement.' That upward movement appears as if different from it [the smoke]. Yet the upward-moving nature of smoke is not accepted as something separate. And that upward movement is not other than that smoke. The same reasoning [applies] here. Thus, arising, destruction, and alteration too appear as if different from it [the conditioned dharma]. Yet the conditioned nature of conditioned [dharmas] — form and the rest — is not [something separate]. And the conditioned nature of conditioned [dharmas] such as form and the rest is not characterized [as such] even when one grasps — even when one grasps the intrinsic nature of form and the rest — so long as the prior non-existence is not known — so long as the prior non-existence of those forms and the rest before arising is not known; and afterwards too — what? — the non-existence — so long as the prior non-existence and the cessational non-existence are not known; and so long as the distinction of the continuum is not known. Therefore, it is not the case that [the conditioned] is characterized by that very [conditioned nature]. That conditioned nature is not characterized by conditioned nature itself. Rather, that conditioned nature is characterized by prior non-existence and the rest. For if, in grasping the intrinsic nature of form and the rest, one were to grasp 'this is conditioned' — without knowing prior non-existence, subsequent non-existence, and the distinction of the continuum — then it would be characterized by that very [conditioned nature]. But since one does not know thus, it is not characterized by that very [conditioned nature]. And yet there are no substances separate from form and the rest that are birth (<s>jāti</s>) and so forth.

children.translated_text: 'Birth is the beginning of a continuum' —

body.text: vistareṇa vacanāt. eṣāṃ sahabhūtatvāt jātyādīnāṃ samānakālotpādatvāt. na. kāritrakālabhedād iti. naitad evaṃ. kasmāt. kāritrakālabhedāt. puruṣakārakālabhedād ity arthaḥ. tat pratipādayann āha. anāgatā hi jātiḥ kāritraṃ karotīti vistaraḥ.
body.translated_text: because of the statement in detail. 'Because of their being co-existent' — because birth and the rest arise at the same time. [Objection:] No — 'because of the difference in the time of functioning.' This is not so. Why? Because of the difference in the time of functioning — meaning the difference in the time of operative activity. Explaining that, he says: 'For birth, being future, performs its function' — and so forth in detail.

body.text: kim anāgataṃ [Tib. 165a] dravyato 'sti nāstīti. anāgatam eva tāvad dravyato nāstīti pratipādayiṣyate. kuto 'nāgatā jātiḥ kāritraṃ karotīty abhiprāyaḥ. saty api tu tasminn iti. saty api tu dravyato 'nāgate jātir anāgatāvasthāyāṃ kāritraṃ kurvatī katham anāgatā sidhyati. aprāptakāritraṃ hi anāgatam iti siddhāṃtaḥ. sa virudhyeta. tasmāt tad vaktavyaṃ. kathaṃ vartamānā sidhyatīti. uparatakāritro 'tīta iṣyate. jātiś cānāgataiva. uparatakāritre hi vartamānāvasthāyām evātītā prāpnotīti na vartamānā bhaved iti vartamānalaṣaṇaṃ vaktavyam iti. aparisamāptakāritro vartamāna iti cet. atīto 'py vartamānaḥ syāt. atītasyāpi hi phaladānakāritram iṣyate. yadaivaṃ hy enaṃ sthitir iti vistaraḥ. sthitijarāvināśavṛttayo hy anyonyavipratiṣiddhāḥ. na hi sa eva dharmas tiṣṭhati ca jīryati ca vinaśyati ceti yukto vyavasthāpayituṃ. tasya kṣaṇikatvaṃ bādhyata iti. prathamaṃ sthitiḥ sthāpayati. tato jarā jarayati. tato 'nityatā vināśayati. kṣaṇatrayāvasthānāt. kṣaṇikatvaṃ bādhyata iti. eṣa eva hi naḥ kṣaṇa iti. kāryaparisamāptilakṣaṇo na tūtpattyanaṃtaravināśalakṣaṇa ity arthaḥ. evam apīti vistaraḥ. sahotpannānāṃ krameṇa kāritraṃ na yujyate. kuta etat. sthitis tāvat sthāpayati. na tu tasmin kāle jarā jarayati nāpy anityatā vināśayatīti. punaḥ kenābalīyastvaṃ [Tib. 165b] paścāt kenābalīyastvaṃ yad enāṃ yasmād enāṃ sthitiṃ saha dharmeṇa yasyāsau sthitiḥ. tena dharmeṇa sahānityatā nihaṃti. kṛtakṛtyā punaḥ kartuṃ notsahate jātivad iti. yathā jātiḥ kṛtakṛtyā janyaṃ janayitvā parikṣīṇaśaktir na punar janayati. tathā sthitir api tadvad eva na punaḥ sthāpayatīti. na hi śakyam iti vistaraḥ. na vartamānatām ānītaṃ janyaṃ punar ānetuṃ śakyate 'navasthāprasaṃgāt. śakyaṃ tu khalu sthityā sthāpyam atyaṃtaṃ sthāpayituṃ. sthiter vināśapratibandhalakṣaṇatvāt. te eva jarānityate iti. te eva jarānityate pratibandhaḥ. yena sthitiḥ sthāpyam atyaṃtaṃ sthāpayituṃ na śaknoti. jarā hi sthitiṃ durbalīkaroti durbalām anityatā nihaṃtīti.
body.translated_text: 'Does the future [Tib. 165a] exist substantially or not?' — [The reply:] First, it will be demonstrated that the future does not exist substantially. How then can 'future birth perform its function?' — this is the intent. 'But even if that [future] exists' — but even if the future exists substantially, how is birth established [as performing its function] in the future state? For 'that which has not attained its function is future' — this is the established doctrine. That would be contradicted. Therefore, that must be stated — 'How is the present established?' [For the Vaibhāṣikas:] 'the past is that whose function has ceased.' And birth is precisely future. For when the function has ceased, already in the present state it [the dharma] reaches pastness — so it would not be present, and thus the characteristic of the present must be stated. 'If [the reply is:] the present is that whose function is incomplete' — then the past too would be present. For even the past is accepted as having the function of giving results. If thus [the dharma] has duration — and so forth in detail. For the functions of duration, decay, and destruction are mutually contradictory. It is not reasonable to establish that the very same <s>dharma</s> endures, decays, and is destroyed. Its momentariness (<s>kṣaṇikatva</s>) would be contradicted. For first, duration stabilizes; then decay decays; then impermanence destroys — [requiring] abiding through three moments. Momentariness would be contradicted. 'For this is our [understanding of a] moment' — meaning a moment characterized by the completion of a function, not by destruction immediately after arising. 'Even so' — and so forth in detail. For co-arisen [characteristics], sequential functioning is not reasonable. How so? Duration stabilizes first — but at that time, decay does not decay, nor does impermanence destroy. Then, 'by what weakness' — [Tib. 165b] by what subsequent weakness, by what [cause] is that duration, together with the <s>dharma</s> to which it belongs, destroyed by impermanence? '[Duration], having completed its function, is unable to act again — like birth.' Just as birth, having completed its function — having generated the generable — is exhausted in capacity and does not generate again, so too duration similarly does not stabilize again. 'For it is not possible' — and so forth in detail. It is not possible to bring the generable into the present state again, because of the consequence of infinite regress. But indeed, duration could stabilize the stabilizable completely — because duration has the characteristic of preventing destruction. 'Decay and impermanence are precisely the obstacle' — those very decay and impermanence are the obstacle — by which duration is unable to stabilize the stabilizable completely. For decay weakens duration; and impermanence, weakened, destroys it.

body.text: ācārya āha. yadīti sarvaṃ. yadi hi te jarānityate balīyasyau syātāṃ pūrvam eva syātāṃ sthitikāritrakāle. yataḥ sā sthitir na labhate kāritraṃ kartuṃ. nivṛttakāritrāyām iti vistaraḥ. yadā nivṛttakāritrā sthitiḥ. tadā te 'pi jarānityate na tiṣṭhataḥ. sa cāpi dharmaḥ. sthitikāritrād dhi teṣāṃ sthitiḥ kalpate.
body.translated_text: The <s>Ācārya</s> [<s>Vasubandhu</s>] says: 'If' — and everything [that follows]. If those decay and impermanence were more powerful, they would be so even earlier — at the very time of duration's functioning. Because then duration would not be able to perform its function. 'When the function of duration has ceased' — and so forth in detail. When duration's function has ceased, then those decay and impermanence too do not persist — nor does that <s>dharma</s> [itself]. For their persistence is possible only through duration's functioning.

body.text: tasmāt te 'pi na tiṣṭhataḥ. katham atiṣṭhantyau jarānityate kutra vā dharmiṇy atiṣṭhati kāritraṃ kartum utsahiṣyete. kiṃ vā punas tābhyāṃ jarānityatābhyāṃ kartavyaṃ. sthitisāmarthyād dhi sa dharma utpannamātro na vinaṣṭo 'bhūt. sa tayā uparatakāritrayā sthityāpy upekṣyamāṇo 'sthāpyamāno dhruvaṃ na sthāsyatīti. ayam evāsya vināśo yad idam anavasthānaṃ. kiṃ punar jarānityatābhyāṃ [Tib. 166a] kāryam ity abhiprāyaḥ. na ca tasmād eva tasyānyaprakāratā yujyata iti. yadi sa eva nāsāv anyathā. athānyathā na sa eva. yayor hi anyathātvaṃ. tayor anyatvaṃ dṛṣṭaṃ tadyathā devadattayajñadattayoḥ.
body.translated_text: Therefore, those two [decay and impermanence] too do not persist. How will decay and impermanence, not persisting, undertake to perform their function — and in what <s>dharmin</s> (bearer of properties) that does not persist? Or further, what is there for those two — decay and impermanence — to do? For by the power of duration, that <s>dharma</s>, having just arisen, did not perish. That [dharma], being abandoned by that very duration whose function has ceased — not being stabilized — will certainly not persist. This very non-persisting of it is its destruction. What then is there for decay and impermanence [Tib. 166a] to do? — this is the intent. 'And the otherness of that very [dharma] is not reasonable either.' If it is the same, then it is not otherwise; and if it is otherwise, then it is not the same. For wherever there is otherness, there otherness is seen — as in the case of <s>Devadatta</s> and <s>Yajñadatta</s>.

body.text: yo 'py āha nikāyāṃtarīya iti āryasaṃmatīyaḥ. sa ghaṭāder mudgarādikṛto vināśa iti manyate kālāṃtarāvasthāyi hi tasya rūpaṃ. cittacaittānāṃ tu kṣaṇikatvaṃ. ata ucyate. cittacaittānāṃ ca kṣaṇikatvābhyupagamāt tadanityatāyāś cittacaittānityatāyā vināśakāraṇānapekṣatvāt svayaṃ vinaśvaratvāt sthityanityate kāritraṃ yugapat kuryātāṃ. ata ekasya cittasya caittasya vā yugapatsthitivinaṣṭatā anyonyaviruddho 'pi saṃprasajyate. evam etat sūtraṃ sunītam iti. yad etat trīṇīmāni bhikṣavaḥ saṃskṛtasya saṃskṛtalakṣaṇānīti.
body.translated_text: 'One who belongs to another school also says' — [this refers to] the <s>Āryasaṃmatīya</s>. He holds that for pots and the like, destruction is caused by a hammer-blow and the like — for their form persists for some time. But mind and mental factors are momentary. Therefore it is said: 'Since the momentariness of mind and mental factors is conceded, and since the impermanence of mind and mental factors — their destruction — does not require a [separate] cause of destruction, being self-destructing, duration and impermanence would perform their functions simultaneously.' Thus, even the simultaneous duration and destruction of a single mind or mental factor — though mutually contradictory — would follow. 'Thus this <s>sūtra</s> is well-conducted' — namely, the [sūtra] which states: 'There are three conditioned characteristics of the conditioned, O monks.'

body.text: (II.47cd) sati sāmagrye bhāvāt. asati cābhāvād iti. sati hetupratyayānāṃ sāmagrye bhāvāt janyasya. asati cābhāvāt. na jāteḥ. kiṃ. sāmarthyaṃ paśyāma ity adhikṛtaṃ. na hi hetupratyayasāmagrye 'pi taj janyaṃ kadācid bhavati kadācin na bhavati. atra bhadaṃtānaṃtavarmā āha. yathā cakṣur na vinā ālokādibhiś cakṣurvijñānaṃ janayati. na cātas tadutpattau na kāraṇaṃ. evaṃ jātir na vinā hetupratyayair dharmaṃ janayati. na cātas tadutpattau na kāraṇam iti. atrocyate. [Tib. 166b] asamānam etat. cakṣur hi dṛṣtasāmarthyam satsv ālokādiṣu andhānandhayoś cakṣurvijñānasyānutpattyutpattidarśanāt. na tv evaṃ jātir iti. sūkṣmā api hi dharmaprakṛtaya iti. tadyathā sparśādīnāṃ caitasikānāṃ prakṛtayaḥ svabhāvā duḥparicchedyatvāt sūkṣmāh. asty etad evaṃ. adṛśyamāno 'pi kaścid dharmaḥ kāritreṇa nirdhāryate. na tv evaṃ jātiḥ kāritreṇa nirdhāryate. sparśasya hi kāritraṃ bhagavataivanirdhāritaṃ. yaḥ kaścid vedanāskaṃdhaḥ saṃjñāskaṃdhaḥ saṃskāraskaṃdhaḥ. sarvas sa sparśaṃ pratītyeti vistaraḥ. jātam ity eva tu na syāt asatyāṃ jātāv iti. svalakṣaṇāpekṣā rūpe rūpabuddhiḥ. na tu jātam iti svalakṣaṇāpekṣā jātabuddhiḥ. vedanādiṣv api bhāvāt. tasmād arthāṃtarabhūtajātidravyāpekṣeyaṃ jātabuddhir iti nirdhāryate. ṣaṣṭhīvacanaṃ ca na syāt rūpasyotpāda iti. vaiyadhikaraṇye hi ṣaṣṭhīnirdeśo na sāmānādhikaraṇye. tenāha. yathā rūpasya rūpam iti. vaidharmadṛṣṭāṃta eṣaḥ. yathā rūpaṃ rūpād ananyad iti kṛtvā ṣaṣṭhīnirdeśo na bhavati
body.translated_text: (II.47cd) 'Because of existence when the aggregate is present, and non-existence when it is absent.' When the aggregate of causes and conditions is present, the produced [dharma] exists; when it is absent, [the produced dharma] does not exist. Not because of birth (<s>jāti</s>). What [do we see]? 'We see the capacity [of the aggregate alone]' — this is the subject. For when the aggregate of causes and conditions is present, that produced [dharma] sometimes exists and sometimes does not exist — this is not [the case]. Here the Venerable <s>Anantavarman</s> says: 'Just as the eye does not generate visual consciousness without light and the rest, yet it is not therefore not a cause of its arising — so too birth does not generate a <s>dharma</s> without causes and conditions, yet it is not therefore not a cause of its arising.' To this it is replied: [Tib. 166b] This is not analogous. For the eye has a demonstrable capacity — because, given the presence of light and the rest, visual consciousness is observed not to arise for the blind but to arise for those who are not blind. But birth is not thus [demonstrated]. 'Even subtle natural properties of <s>dharmas</s>' — just as the natural properties, the intrinsic natures, of mental factors such as contact (<s>sparśa</s>) and the rest are subtle, being hard to discern — this is so. An imperceptible <s>dharma</s> too is determined by its function. But birth is not thus determined by its function. For the function of contact has been determined by the Blessed One himself: 'Whatever feeling-aggregate, perception-aggregate, or formation-aggregate there is — all of that is dependent on contact' — and so forth in detail. 'But [the cognition] "it is born" would not arise in the absence of birth' — [Response:] The cognition 'form' depends on the own-characteristic of form. But the cognition 'it is born' does not depend on the own-characteristic [of birth] in the same way. Because it exists in the case of feeling and the rest too. Therefore, this cognition 'it is born' is determined to depend on a substance that is birth, which is of a different nature [from the dharma itself]. 'And the sixth-case [genitive] expression would not obtain — "the arising of form"' — for the sixth-case designation is used in the case of non-co-referentiality (<s>vaiyadhikaraṇya</s>), not in the case of co-referentiality (<s>sāmānādhikaraṇya</s>). Therefore he says: 'Just as [one does not say] "the form of form."' This is a counter-example (<s>vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta</s>). Just as, because form is not other than form, the genitive designation does not occur [in "the form of form"]

body.text: rūpasya rūpam iti. tathā rūpasyotpāda iti na syāt. tasmāj jātinimitto 'yaṃ ṣaṣṭhīnirdeśa iti gamyate. evaṃ yāvad anityatā yathāyogaṃ vaktavyeti. sthitam eva tu na syāt asatyāṃ sthitau. ṣaṣṭhīvacanaṃ ca rūpasya sthitir iti yathā rūpasya rūpam iti. jīrṇam ity eva tu na syāt asatyāṃ jarāyāṃ. ṣaṣṭhīvacanaṃ ca rūpasya [Tib. 167a] jareti yathā rūpasya rūpam iti. tathā vinaṣṭam ity eva tu na syāt asatyām anityatāyāṃ. ṣaṣṭhīvacanaṃ ca rūpasya vināśa iti yathā rūpasya rūpam iti.
body.translated_text: 'the form of form.' Likewise, 'the arising of form' would not [be possible]. Therefore, it is understood that this genitive expression is occasioned by birth (<s>jāti</s>). Similarly, up to impermanence (<s>anityatā</s>), should be stated as appropriate. 'But "it has persisted" itself would not [be possible] in the absence of duration (<s>sthiti</s>).' And the genitive expression 'the duration of form' is like 'the form of form.' 'But "it has aged" itself would not [be possible] in the absence of aging (<s>jarā</s>).' And the genitive expression 'the aging of form' [Tib. 167a] is like 'the form of form.' Likewise, 'but "it has perished" itself would not [be possible] in the absence of impermanence.' And the genitive expression 'the destruction of form' is like 'the form of form.'

body.text: tena tarhīti vistaraḥ. yadi jātamityevamādibuddhisiddhyarthaṃ ṣaṣṭhīvidhānārthaṃ ca jātyādayaḥ kalpyaṃte anātmatvam apy eṣṭvyaṃ. na hi nirnimittā anātmabuddhir bhavitum arhati. athānātmatvaṃ prajñaptisad iṣyate. tannimittānātmabuddhiḥ. jātyādy api prajñaptisad eṣṭavyaṃ. tannimittā ca jātyādibuddhir iti. sādhanaṃ cātra. prajñaptisat jātyādi. dravyasad apekṣya gṛhyamāṇatvād. anātmatvavad iti. sattādayo 'pīti. ādiśabdena dravyatvarūpaghaṭatvādi gṛhyate. ekaṃ rūpaṃ dve rūpe mahad aṇu pṛthak saṃyuktaṃ vibhaktaṃ param aparaṃ sadrūpam iti. tathā dravyam etad rūpam idaṃ ghaṭo 'yam ity evamādibuddhisiddhārthaṃ saṃkhyādayo 'pi vaiśeṣikaparikalpitā abhyupagaṃtavyāḥ. ṣaṣthīvidhānārthaṃ ca rūpasya saṃyoga iti. saṃyogagrahaṇam udāharaṇamātraṃ. rūpasya vibhāgaḥ paratvāparatvam ityevamādy api yojyaṃ. eṣā ca ṣaṣṭhī kathaṃ kalpyate rūpasya svabhāva iti. na hi vaibhāṣikāṇāṃ [Tib. 167b] rūpād anyo rūpasya svabhāva iṣṭaḥ. jātam iti. jātam eva na vinaṣṭam ity abhūtvābhāvajñāpanārthaṃ kriyate prajñaptiḥ. bahuvikalpa iti. bahubhedo rūpavedanādibhedāt. tasya viśeṣaṇārthaṃ rūpasyotpāda iti na vedanādīnām utpāda iti viśeṣaṇārthaṃ ṣaṣṭhīṃ kurvaṃti. mānyaḥ pratyāyi rūpasaṃjñaka evotpādo na vedanādisaṃjñaka iti. dṛṣṭāṃtaṃ kathayaṃti. candanasya gandhādayaḥ śilāputrakasya śarīram iti. anarthāṃtarabhāve 'pi ṣaṣṭhīnirdeśaḥ kriyate. gandhādisamūhamātraṃ hi candanam iti bauddhasiddhāntaḥ. vaiśeṣikasiddhāntāpekṣayā tu asiddhaś candana ity aparo dṛṣṭānta upanyasyate. śilāputrakasya śarīram iti. śilāputrakaśarīrayor vaiśeṣikāṇām api siddhānte nārthāntarabhāvo bhavati ca ṣaṣṭhīnirdeśaḥ. arthāntaraparikalpakṛto hi tathā nirdeśaḥ. evaṃ sthityādayo 'pi yathāyogaṃ veditavyā iti. tasmāt prajñaptimātram evedaṃ pravāhāvasthānajñāpanārthaṃ kriyate sthitam iti. sā ca pravāhāvasthānalakṣaṇā sthitir bahuvikalpā. tasyā viśeṣaṇārthaṃ rūpasya sthitir iti ṣaṣṭhīṃ kurvanti. yathā rūpasaṃjñakaiva [Tib. 168a] sthitiḥ pratīyeta mānyā pratyāyīti. tathā prajñaptimātram evaitat pūrvaparaviśeṣajñāpanārthaṃ
body.translated_text: 'Therefore, then' — and so on in detail. If birth and the rest are posited for the purpose of establishing cognitions such as 'it has been born' and for the purpose of the genitive construction, then selflessness (<s>anātmatva</s>) too must be accepted [as a real entity]. For a cognition of selflessness cannot arise without a basis. If selflessness is accepted as existing by convention (<s>prajñaptisat</s>), and the cognition of selflessness is [explained as] occasioned by that — then birth and the rest too should be accepted as existing by convention, and the cognition of birth and so forth as occasioned by that. And the proof here [is]: birth and the rest exist by convention, because they are apprehended in dependence upon what exists substantially (<s>dravyasat</s>), like selflessness. 'Existence (<s>sattā</s>) and the rest too' — by the word 'and the rest,' substance-hood (<s>dravyatva</s>), formness (<s>rūpatva</s>), pot-ness (<s>ghaṭatva</s>), and the like are included. 'One form, two forms, large, small, separate, conjoined, divided, far, near, similar' — likewise, 'this is a substance, this is form, this is a pot' — for the purpose of establishing such cognitions, the numbers (<s>saṃkhyā</s>) and the rest posited by the <s>Vaiśeṣikas</s> would also have to be accepted. And for the purpose of the genitive construction: 'the conjunction of form.' The mention of conjunction is merely an illustration. 'The disjunction of form,' 'the farness and nearness [of form]' — these too should be applied. But how is this genitive conceived — 'the intrinsic nature (<s>svabhāva</s>) of form'? For the <s>Vaibhāṣikas</s> [Tib. 167b] do not accept an intrinsic nature of form that is different from form. 'It has been born' — the convention is made for the purpose of indicating [the state of] having come into being without having existed previously — '[it has been] born, [and has] not yet perished.' 'Being of many varieties' — of many divisions, due to the divisions of form, feeling, and so forth. For the purpose of qualifying that, they employ the genitive: 'the arising of form' — not 'the arising of feeling and the rest' — for the purpose of qualification. The venerable commentator [says]: an arising designated by form alone, not one designated by feeling and the rest. They give illustrations: 'the fragrance and the rest of sandalwood,' 'the body of a stone statue.' Even when there is no real difference, a genitive expression is made. For sandalwood is nothing but an aggregate of fragrance and the rest — this is the Buddhist established doctrine. But since the illustration of sandalwood is unestablished with respect to the <s>Vaiśeṣika</s> doctrine, another illustration is presented: 'the body of a stone statue.' For even in the <s>Vaiśeṣika</s> doctrine, there is no real difference between a stone statue and its body, yet the genitive expression is [still] made. For such an expression is made by one who conceives a real difference. Similarly, duration and the rest too should be understood as appropriate. Therefore, 'it has persisted' is merely a convention, made for the purpose of indicating the continuity of the stream. And that duration, characterized as the continuity of the stream, is of many varieties. For the purpose of qualifying it, they employ the genitive: 'the duration of form' — just as [Tib. 168a] the duration designated by form alone is understood as the venerable [commentator intends]. Likewise, 'it has aged' is merely a convention, made for the purpose of indicating the difference between earlier and later states.

body.text: kriyate jīrṇam iti. sā ca pūrvāparaviśeṣalakṣaṇā jarā bahuvikalpā. tasyā viśeṣaṇārthaṃ rūpasya jareti ṣaṣṭhīṃ kurvanti. yathā rūpasaṃjñakaiva jarā pratīyeta mānyā pratyāyīti. tathā prajñaptimātram evaitat pravāhanivṛttijñapanārthaṃ kriyate vinaṣṭam iti. sa ca pravāhanivṛttilakṣaṇo vināśo bahuvikalpaḥ. tasya viśeṣaṇārthaṃ rūpasya vināśa iti ṣaṣṭhīṃ kurvanti. yathā rūpasaṃjñaka eva vināśaḥ pratīyeta mānyaḥ pratyāyīti. sarvatra ca dṛṣṭāntadvayaṃ vaktavyaṃ. tadyathā candanasya gandhādayaḥ śilāputrakasya śarīram iti.
body.translated_text: And that aging, characterized as the difference between earlier and later, is of many varieties. For the purpose of qualifying it, they employ the genitive: 'the aging of form' — just as the aging designated by form alone is understood as the venerable [commentator intends]. Likewise, 'it has perished' is merely a convention, made for the purpose of indicating the cessation of the stream. And that destruction, characterized as the cessation of the stream, is of many varieties. For the purpose of qualifying it, they employ the genitive: 'the destruction of form' — just as the destruction designated by form alone is understood as the venerable [commentator intends]. And everywhere, both illustrations should be stated — namely: 'the fragrance and the rest of sandalwood,' 'the body of a stone statue.'

body.text: yathā ca dharmatayeti. dharmatā dharmaprakrtiḥ dharmasvabhāvo dharmaśailīty arthaḥ. dharmatā dharmaprakṛtir iti kuta etat. cakṣuḥ samṛddhe śūnyaṃ nityena dhruveṇa śāśvatena avipariṇāmadharmeṇa ātmanātmīyena ca. tat kasya hetoḥ. prakṛtir asyaiṣeti. yathā ca dharmatayā na sarvaṃ jātimad iṣyate ākāśādi. tathā dharmatayā na sarvaṃ jāyata ity eṣṭavyam. na hy atra kiṃcit kārāṇam asti. yat saṃskṛtam eva jātimad bhavati nāsaṃskṛtam iti anyatra dharmatāyāḥ. evam asatyām api jātau saṃskṛtam evotpadyate. nāsaṃskṛtam iti. yathā ca tulyajātimatāṃ keṣāṃcid rūpavedanādīnāṃ tadanye pratyayās tebhyo rūpotpattipratyayebhyo 'nye vedanādyutpattipratyayās tadanye. te tadanye pratyayās tadanyasyotpādane na samarthā bhavanti. tebhyo vedanādibhyo 'nyat tadanyat [Tib. 168b]. kiṃ tad. rūpaṃ. tasya. tadanyasya te vedanādipratyayā utpādane yathā na samarthā bhavanti. evam asaṃskṛtasyākāśāder utpādane sarve 'pi rūpavedanādipratyayā na samarthāḥ syur iti. pūrvaṃ svabhāvaniyamenoktam idānīṃ śaktiniyameneti.
body.translated_text: 'And as by nature (<s>dharmatā</s>)' — <s>dharmatā</s> means the nature of <s>dharmas</s>, the intrinsic nature of <s>dharmas</s>, the way of <s>dharmas</s>. '<s>Dharmatā</s> is the nature of <s>dharmas</s>' — from what [is this known]? 'The eye is thoroughly empty of a permanent, stable, eternal [self], of a nature not subject to change, of self or what belongs to self. For what reason? This is its nature.' And just as by nature, not everything that has birth is accepted [as real] — space and the rest [do not]. So too, by nature, it should be accepted that not everything arises. For there is no reason here — other than nature — why the conditioned alone has birth but not the unconditioned. Similarly, even in the absence of [a real entity called] birth, the conditioned alone arises, not the unconditioned. And just as, among things equally possessing birth, the conditions for the arising of some — form, feeling, and so forth — are different from the conditions for the arising of others — the conditions for the arising of feeling and the rest are different from those — those different conditions are not capable of producing something different from those. What is different from those — feelings and the rest — is what? [Tib. 168b] Form. The conditions for feelings and the rest are not capable of producing that different thing [i.e., form]. Similarly, all conditions whatsoever — those of form, feeling, and the rest — would not be capable of producing the unconditioned — space and the rest. 'Previously stated by way of restricting the intrinsic nature, now stated by way of restricting the capacity' —

body.text: na hi dūṣakāḥ santīti vistaraḥ. yathā na mṛgāḥ santīti yavā nopyaṃte upyanta evety arthaḥ. dvau pratiṣeḍhau prakṛtam arthaṃ gamayataḥ. yathā na makṣikāḥ patantīti modakā na bhakṣyante. kiṃ tarhi. bhakṣyanta eva. tathā na dūṣakās santīti āgamo 'bhidharmaśāstrāṇy apāsyante. tasmād doṣeṣu pratividhātavyaṃ. doṣeṣu paravyavasthāpiteṣu parihāraḥ kartavyaḥ. siddhāntaś cānusartavyo na parityājya ity abhiprāyaḥ.
body.translated_text: 'For there are no destroyers' — and so on in detail. Just as 'there are no deer' [does not mean] that barley is not sown — rather, it is indeed sown — the two negations convey the intended meaning. Just as 'flies do not land [on them]' [does not mean] that sweets are not eaten — rather, they are indeed eaten. So too, 'there are no destroyers' [does not mean] that the scriptures and <s>Abhidharma</s> treatises are to be cast aside. Therefore, the faults should be remedied. When faults have been pointed out by the opponent, a response must be given, and the established doctrine must be followed, not abandoned — this is the intent.

body.text:
(II.48ab) nāmakāyādayaḥ saṃjñāvākyākṣarasamuktaya
