'For the purpose of the evening meal' — for the purpose of afternoon eating. 'For the purpose of the morning meal' — for the purpose of morning eating. 'Storing' (<s>saṃnidhikāra</s>) — hoarding. 'Dividing fields' — through arranging their livelihood with self-grown rice (<s>akṛṣṭopta śāli</s>) after dividing fields. The establishment of the designations <s>Kṣatriya</s> and the rest is through the etymological method.

body.text: iti parisamāptiḥ. adharmarāgaraktā iti. kāmamithyācārarāgādhyavasitāḥ. viṣamalobhābhibhūtā iti. viṣamalobhaḥ parakīyasvīkaraṇecchā cauryād balād vā. tenābhibhūtāḥ. mithyādharmaparītā iti viparītadharmaparidīpakāḥ. amātṛjñā apitṛjñā iti vistaraḥ. punaḥ kalpasya niryāṇakāla iti. kalpasya niryāṇāni trīṇy ucyante. śastrarogadurbhikṣāṇi. kim ekasya daśavarṣāyuḥkalpasya trīṇi niryāṇāni krameṇa bhavaṃti. āhosvid ekaikasya ekaikaṃ krameṇeti. eka tāvad āhuḥ. ekaikam iti. apare punar āhuḥ. ekasya krameṇa trīṇi bhavaṃti. pūrvaṃ durbhikṣaṃ tadanantaro rogaḥ tadanaṃtaraṃ śastram iti. pūrvakas tu pakṣa iṣṭa iti paśyāmaḥ. tair eva doṣair iti adharmādirāgādibhiḥ. amanuṣyāḥ piśācādaya ītiṃ vyādhyādikām utsṛjaṃti. ojo vā haraṃti. prabhāvato vā puṣpaphalauṣadhiprabhṛtīnāṃ mahābhūtāni dūṣayaṃti. [Tib. 326a] yatas teṣām asādhyā vyādhayaḥ prādurbhavanti. yato mriyante. tadā ceti vistaraḥ. yadeha. jambūdvīpe
body.translated_text: means completion. 'Impassioned with unrighteous desire' — those given over to the desire of sexual misconduct (<s>kāmamithyācāra</s>). 'Overcome by uneven greed' — uneven greed is the desire to appropriate what belongs to others, whether by theft or by force; overcome by that. 'Encompassed by wrong <s>dharma</s>' — those who illuminate perverted teachings. 'Not knowing mother, not knowing father' — and so forth in detail. Again, the time of the termination of the <s>kalpa</s> — three terminations of the <s>kalpa</s> are spoken of: by weapons, by disease, and by famine. Does a single ten-year-lifespan <s>kalpa</s> have three terminations in sequence? Or does each one have one each in sequence? Some say: each one has one each. But others say: a single one has three in sequence — first famine, immediately after that disease, immediately after that weapons. But we consider the former view to be preferred. 'Through those very faults' — through unrighteousness (<s>adharma</s>), desire (<s>rāga</s>), and the like. Non-humans — <s>piśāca</s>s and the like — release calamities such as diseases. Or they steal vitality. Or through their power they corrupt the great elements of flowers, fruits, herbs, and the like, so that incurable diseases arise for them, and they die. 'Then' — and so forth in detail. Here, in <s>Jambudvīpa</s>

body.text: śastrakaḥ prāṇātipātaḥ. tadā dvayor dvīpayoḥ pūrvavidehāvaragodānīyayor vyāpāda udrekaprāpto bhavati. yadeha rogaḥ. tadā tayor daurbalyaṃ. yadeha durbhikṣaṃ. tadā tayor jighatsāpipāse.
body.translated_text: when there is a weapon-[calamity], the killing of living beings — at that time in the two continents, <s>Pūrvavideha</s> and <s>Avaragodānīya</s>, ill-will reaches its peak. When here there is disease, there in those two there is weakness. When here there is famine, there in those two there is hunger and thirst.

body.text: (III.98, 99) tīrthakārāḥ. kaṇabhukprabhṛtayaḥ. vāyur bījam uktam iti. bahuvidhaprabhāvabhinnair vāyubhir abhimathyamānā iti vacanāt. tasya nimittam iti. rūpāvacaro vāyur avinaṣṭaḥ kāmāvacarasya vivartakāle prathamakṣaṇotpannasya vāyor nimittaṃ. bījāny āhriyaṃte iti. paṃca bījajātāni mūlabījādīni. mūlabījaṃ phalubījaṃ bījabījaṃ agrabījaṃ skaṃdhabījaṃ. evam apīti. yady apy āhriyante bījāni na te sthūlabhāvānāṃ bījādibhyo bījāṃkuragaṇḍādibhyo 'ṃkurādīnām aṃkurakāṇḍādīnām utpattim icchanti. bījādīni hi teṣāṃ nimittakāraṇāni na samavāyikāraṇāni. samavāyikāraṇaiś ca bhavitavyaṃ. ata āha. kiṃ tarhi. svebhya evāvayavebhya iti vistaraḥ. tadyathāṃkurādyavayavī aṃkurādyavayavebhyaḥ. teṣām api aṃkurādyavayavānāṃ svebhya evāvayavebhyaḥ. teṣām api svebhya eveti evaṃ yāvat paramāṇubhyaḥ. anyatra paramāṇūpasarpaṇād iti. na janane bījādīnāṃ sāmarthyaṃ kiṃcid asti. aṃkurādiparamāṇūpasarpaṇāt tu teṣāṃ sāmarthyam iṣyata ity abhiprāyaḥ. aniyamo [Tib. 326b] hi syād iti. tantvādibhyo 'pi kaṭādyutpattiḥ syād ity arthaḥ. śaktiniyamād iti. yathā bījādīnāṃ sāmarthyaniyamān na aniyamo bhaviṣyati. śabdapākajotpattivat. yathā śabdo 'bhighātādibhyo vijātīyebhya utpadyate. atha ca na yataḥ kutaścid gandharasāder vijātīyād utpadyate. abhighātādīnām eva vijātīyānāṃ tadutpādane sāmarthyāt. tathā pākajā rūpādayo vijātīyād agnyāder utpadyaṃte. atha ca na yataḥ kutaścid vijātīyāc cakṣurāder utpadyaṃte. agnyāder eva tadutpādane sāmarthyāt. vaiśeṣika āha. citro vai guṇadharmaḥ svajātīyebhyo vijātīyebhyaś cotpadyate. svajātīyebhyas tāvat. rūparasagandhasparśādayaḥ kāraṇapūrvāḥ rūparasagandhasparśādibhya evotpadyaṃte. vijātīyebhyo 'pi saṃyogavibhāgapākajādayaḥ karmādibhyaḥ. tad evaṃ guṇadharmo dravyadharmaṃ prati anudāharaṇaṃ. ta eva hi te tatheti vistaraḥ. vīraṇādaya eva hi te tathā tena prakāreṇa kaṭādirūpeṇa saṃniviṣṭā vyavasthitāḥ. tāṃ kaṭasaṃjñāṃ labhante. pipīlikādipaṃktivat. yathā pipīlikāḥ. tathā saṃniviṣṭāḥ paṃktir iti saṃjñāṃ labhante. na ca tābhyo 'nyat paṃktidravyam asti bhavatām api siddhānte. kathaṃ gamyate tāni vīraṇādīni tathāsaṃniviṣṭāni kaṭādisaṃjñāṃ labhante. na punas tebhyo dravyāntarāṇīti. ata āha. ekatantusaṃyoge paṭasyānupalaṃbhāt. ārabdhakārye hy ekasmiṃ taṃtau cakṣuḥsaṃsparśābhyāṃ
body.translated_text: (III.98, 99) The founders of [non-Buddhist] schools (<s>tīrthakāra</s>) — <s>Kaṇabhuj</s> (Kaṇāda) and others. It has been stated that wind is the seed — because of the statement: 'churned by winds differentiated by manifold potencies.' 'Its efficient cause' (<s>nimitta</s>) — the wind belonging to the Form Realm, which has not perished, is the efficient cause of the wind produced at the first moment of the evolution of the Desire Realm. 'Seeds are brought' — the five kinds of seeds beginning with root-seeds: root-seed, fruit-seed, seed-seed, tip-seed, and trunk-seed. 'Even so' — even though seeds are brought, they do not accept that gross entities — sprouts and the like — arise from seeds and the like, from seed-sprout-stems and the like, from sprout-stems and the like. For seeds and the like are their efficient causes (<s>nimittakāraṇa</s>), not their inherent causes (<s>samavāyikāraṇa</s>). And there must be inherent causes. Therefore he says: 'What then? From their own parts alone' — and so forth in detail. Just as a sprout-and-so-on composite [arises] from sprout-and-so-on parts; and those sprout-and-so-on parts from their own parts; and those from their own parts — thus down to atoms (<s>paramāṇu</s>). 'Except through the approach of atoms from elsewhere' — seeds and the like have no power in generation. But their power is accepted through the approach of atoms of sprouts and the like — this is the intent. 'For there would be indeterminacy' — the meaning is: from threads and the like too, mats and the like would arise. 'Because of the determinacy of potency' — just as through the determinacy of the potency of seeds and the like, there will be no indeterminacy. Like the production of sound and heat-produced [qualities]. Just as sound arises from dissimilar [causes] such as striking and the like, yet it does not arise from any and every dissimilar [source] such as smell, taste, and the rest — because only those dissimilar [causes] like striking and the like have the potency to produce it. Similarly, heat-produced [qualities] such as form and the rest arise from dissimilar [causes] such as fire and the rest, yet they do not arise from any and every dissimilar [source] such as the eye-faculty and the rest — because only fire and the rest have the potency to produce them. The <s>Vaiśeṣika</s> says: the nature of qualities (<s>guṇadharma</s>) is indeed variegated — they arise from those of the same kind and also from those of different kind. From those of the same kind: form, taste, smell, touch, and the rest arise from form, taste, smell, touch, and the rest as their prior causes. From those of different kind too: [qualities] produced by conjunction, disjunction, heat, and the like [arise] from action and the like. Thus, this quality-nature provides no counter-example against substance-nature. 'For those very ones are thus' — and so forth in detail. For those very <s>vīraṇa</s> grasses and the like, arranged and established in that manner, in the form of a mat and the like, receive the designation 'mat.' Like a row of ants. Just as ants, arranged in that way, receive the designation 'row.' And there is no separate substance called 'row' apart from them, even in your own doctrine. How is it known that those <s>vīraṇa</s> grasses and the like, arranged in that manner, receive the designation 'mat' and the like, and that there are no separate substances apart from them? Therefore he says: because in the conjunction of a single thread, cloth is not perceived. For when the work has begun and a single thread is conjoined with the sense of sight and contact

body.text:
[Tib. 327a] saṃyukte bhavanmatena paṭo 'pi ca tābhyāṃ saṃnikṛṣṭa iti asāv api tathaivopalabhyeta. yadi brūyāt. pratibandhāt tasyānupalabdhir iti. ata āha. ko hi tadā sato vidyamānasya paṭasyopalabdhau pratibandha iti. nāsti pratibandha ity abhiprāyaḥ. tasmān na paṭo nāma dravyāntaram astīti. syān mataṃ. ekaikasmin tantau pradeśena paṭo vartate na sarvātmanā vartata iti. ata ucyate. akṛtsnavṛttav iti vistaraḥ. akṛtsnavṛttau paṭasya kalpamānāyāṃ paṭabhāgo 'traikaikasmin tantau syān na paṭas tataḥ. kim iti cet. ata āha. samūhamātraṃ ca paṭaḥ syād iti vartate. ekasmin tantāv eko bhāgo aparasminn apara iti tantuvartināṃ bahūnāṃ bhāgānāṃ samudāyaḥ paṭa iti ca prāpnoti. na ceṣyate. kaś ca tantubhyo 'nyaḥ paṭabhāga iti. kaṇabhugbhaktāḥ praṣṭavyāḥ yena bhāgenāyam indriyasaṃnikṛṣṭe tantau varteta. tasmād etām api kalpanāṃ kalpayitvā nāto 'nyaḥ paṭaḥ sidhyati. syān matam. ekaikasminn api tantau paṭo vartate. paṭopalabdhes tu paṭendriyasaṃnikarṣaḥ. paṭasyānekāśrayasaṃyogāpekṣo nimittam iti. ato 'nekāśrayasaṃyogāpekṣāyām upalabdhau kalpyamānāyāṃ daśāmātrasaṃghāte gṛhyamāṇe paṭa upalabhyeta. na tūpalabhyate. paṭamadhyabhāgādyadarśanāt. atha mataṃ. naiva tadānīm apīndriyeṇa madhyādibhāgāḥ saṃprayujyanta iti. ato daśāmātrasaṃhāte paṭopalabdhir na bhavatīti. tata idam abhidhīyate. na vā kadācid iti vistaraḥ. na vā kadācit paṭopalabdhiḥ syāt. madhyaparabhāgānām indriyeṇāsaṃnikarṣāt. [Tib. 327b] naiva hi saṃbhavo 'sti yat tadāraṃbhakāḥ madhyaparabhāgāḥ sarva evendriyeṇa saṃnikṛṣyeran. tathā ca sati tantvādiṣv apy eṣa prasaṃga iti na ca kiṃcid api kāryam upalabhyeta. kiṃ ca kramasaṃnikarṣe ceti vistaraḥ. yadā krameṇa cakṣuḥ saṃsparśanendriyaṃ vā paṭaṃ gṛhṇīyāt. tadā paṭagrahaṇaṃ na syāt.
yugapad anekāśryasaṃyogabhāvāc cakṣuḥsparśanendriyayoḥ. evam anyeṣām api avayavānāṃ grahaṇaṃ na syāt. tasmād iti vistaraḥ. yasmāt krameṇa paṭabuddhiḥ kaṭabuddhir vā. tasmād avayaveṣv eva paṭāvayaveṣu kaṭāvayaveṣu vā tadbuddhiḥ paṭabuddhiḥ kaṭabuddhir vā vikalpavaśād bhavati. alātacakravat. yathālāte śīghrasaṃcārāt tatratatrotpadyamāne alātacakrabuddhir bhavati. tadvat. sādhanaṃ cātra. na dravyasat paṭaḥ. avayavagrahaṇasṝāpekṣagrahaṇatvāt. alātacakravat. bhinnarūpajātikriyāsv iti vistaraḥ. bhinnarūpeṣu tantuṣu nīlapītādibhedāt. bhinnajātiṣu dukūlakarpāsādibhedāt. bhinnakriyeṣūrdhvadhogamabhedāt. paṭasya rūpādyasaṃbhavāt. kīdṛśaṃ tatra rūpaṃ bhavatu
body.translated_text: according to your view, the cloth too is in proximity with those [senses], so it too should be perceived in the same way. If one were to say: it is because of obstruction that it is not perceived — therefore he says: for what obstruction could there be to the perception of cloth that exists, that is present, at that time? The intent is: there is no obstruction. Therefore there is no separate substance called cloth. One might think: the cloth exists in each thread partially, not in its entirety. Therefore it is said: 'If it does not exist in its entirety' — and so forth in detail. If the cloth's not-existing-in-its-entirety is posited, then in each single thread there would be a part of cloth, not the cloth itself. Why? Therefore he says: and the cloth would be a mere collection — this is the continuation. In one thread one part, in another thread another part — the aggregate of the many parts existing in the threads would then be the cloth. And this is not accepted. And what part of cloth is there other than the threads? The followers of <s>Kaṇabhuj</s> (Kaṇāda) should be asked: by what part would this [cloth] exist in a thread that is in proximity with the sense-faculty? Therefore, even having devised this contrivance, no cloth separate from these [threads] is established. One might think: the cloth exists even in each single thread. But the perception of cloth requires the proximity of the cloth's sense-faculty. And the cloth depends on conjunction with multiple supports. Therefore, when a conjunction with multiple supports is posited for perception, cloth should be perceived when only about ten [threads] are grasped. But it is not perceived — because the middle portions and the like of the cloth are not seen. Now if one thinks: at that time too, the middle and other portions are not conjoined with the sense-faculty, and therefore cloth is not perceived in a collection of only about ten [threads] — to this, the following is said: 'Or never' — and so forth in detail. Or there would never be perception of cloth — because the middle and outer portions are not in proximity with the sense-faculty. For there is no possibility that all the middle and outer portions that constitute it could all be in proximity with the sense-faculty. And if that were the case, this consequence would apply to threads and the like too — and nothing at all would be perceived. Moreover, 'in sequential proximity' — and so forth in detail. When the eye or the tactile sense-faculty would grasp the cloth sequentially, then there would be no grasping of the cloth, because of the impossibility of simultaneous conjunction with multiple supports for the eye and the tactile sense-faculty. Likewise, there would be no grasping of other parts either. 'Therefore' — and so forth in detail. Since the cognition of cloth or mat arises sequentially, therefore, it is in the parts alone — the parts of cloth or the parts of mat — that the cognition of cloth or mat arises through the force of conceptual construction (<s>vikalpa</s>). Like a fire-wheel (<s>alātacakra</s>). Just as when a firebrand is rapidly moved, with [perceptions] arising here and there, the cognition of a fire-wheel arises — so too. And the proof here is: cloth is not a real substance, because its grasping depends on the sequential grasping of parts, like a fire-wheel. 'In different forms, kinds, and actions' — and so forth in detail. In threads of different forms — because of the distinction of blue, yellow, and the like. Of different kinds — because of the distinction of silk, cotton, and the like. Of different actions — because of the distinction of upward and downward movement. Because form and the rest of the cloth are impossible — what kind of form

body.text: jātiḥ kriyā vā. syād eṣā buddhiḥ citram asya rūpādīti. tad evaṃ citrarūpāditve kalpyamāne vijātīyāraṃbho 'pi syāt. tantuvīraṇayor api kaṭāraṃbhaḥ syāt. tathā sati dharmaviśeṣaviparyayaḥ prāpnoti. atyantavijātīyāraṃbhakatvaṃ dravyāṇāṃ [Tib. 328a] prāpnotīty arthaḥ. avicitre ca pārśvāntare ekapārśvavicitrasya paṭasyādarśanaṃ syāt. tasya citrarūpābhimatatvāt. rūpadarśane hi tadāśrayadravyopalabdhir iṣyate vaiśeṣikaiḥ. mahaty anekadravyavattvād rūpāc copalabdhiḥ. rūpasaṃskārābhāvāt vāyor anupalabdhir iti vacanāt. cittrarūpadarśanaṃ vā acitre pārśve syāt yadi paṭo dṛśyeta. citraṃ hi tasya rūpam iṣyate. kriyāpi citrety aticitram iti. ekaṃ tad dravyaṃ vicitrakriyam iti na yujyate. kriyāvaicitrye hi kriyāvad abhimatānāṃ dravyāṇām anyatvam iṣyate.
body.translated_text: , universal (<s>jāti</s>), or action could belong to it? One might have the notion: its form and the rest are variegated. But then, if variegated form and the rest are posited, there would also be production from dissimilar [causes]. From threads and <s>vīraṇa</s> grasses too, there would be the production of mats. If that were so, it would entail the reversal of the specific properties of substances — the meaning is: it would entail that substances could produce things utterly dissimilar [to themselves]. And on the non-variegated other side, a cloth that is variegated on one side would not be seen — because the cloth is held to have variegated form. For the <s>Vaiśeṣika</s>s accept that upon seeing a form, the substance that is its substratum is perceived. And a great [substance] is perceived through its form because of possessing multiple substances. And because of the statement: 'wind is not perceived because of the absence of form and saṃskāra.' Or, variegated form would be seen on the non-variegated side, if the cloth were seen [as a whole] — for its form is held to be variegated. 'And action too is variegated' — thus 'exceedingly variegated' — it is not fitting that a single substance has variegated action. For when there is diversity of action, distinctness of the substances held to possess action is accepted.

body.text: tāpaprakāśabhede ceti vistaraḥ. agniprabhālakṣaṇasya avayavina ādimadhyānteṣu āraṃbhakeṣu tāpaprakāśabhede sparśanabhedo dṛṣṭaḥ. sa ca tadbhedas tatra yathākramaṃ tīvramadhyamandatā. tasyāvayavinaḥ prabhādravyasya tau rūpasparśau nopapadyete. na hy ekasyāvayavina anekaṃ rūpaṃ sparśo vā yujyate. tena nāvayavebhyo 'vayavi dravyam anyad astīti. atha mataṃ. yadi tantvādibhyo 'vayavebhyo na paṭādyavayavī vyatirikto 'sti. paramāṇūnām atīndriyatvāt. na ca tair avayavaiḥ aindriyaka ārabdha iti. kṛtsnaṃ jagad apratyakṣaṃ syāt. pratyakṣaṃ ca gavādi dṛśyate. tasmād atīndriyaiḥ paramāṇubhir arthāntaram anyad aindriyakam ārabdham iti siddham ity atrocyate. paramāṇvatīndriyatve 'pīti [Tib. 328b] vistaraḥ. yathā bhavatāṃ vaiśeṣikāṇām atīndriyatve 'pi samastānāṃ kāryāraṃbhakatvaṃ na vyastānām. evam asmākam api samastānām eva pratyakṣatvaṃ na vyastānāṃ asaty apy avayavini arthāntarabhūte. yathā cakṣurādīnāṃ cakṣūrūpālokamanaskārāṇāṃ samastānāṃ cakṣurvijñānotpattau kāraṇatvaṃ naikaikasya. evaṃ paramāṇūnām atīndriyatve 'pi samastānāṃ pratyakṣatvaṃ naikaikasya. taimirikāṇāṃ ca puruṣāṇāṃ vikīrṇānām asaṃyuktānāṃ keśānāṃ samūha upalabhyate anārabdhe 'py avayavini. na tv ekaikaḥ keśaḥ. teṣāṃ taimirikāṇāṃ paramāṇuvad ekaḥ keśo 'tīndriyaḥ. ity ato nāsti te 'nyad dravyaṃ.
body.translated_text: In the distinction of heat and luminosity — and so forth in detail. In the parts — beginning, middle, and end — that constitute the composite (<s>avayavin</s>) defined as fire-light, a distinction of touch and light is observed. And that distinction therein is, respectively, intense, moderate, and mild. Those two — form and touch — are not possible for that composite substance of light. For it is not fitting that a single composite has multiple forms or touches. Therefore there is no substance called 'composite' (<s>avayavin</s>) that is different from the parts. Now one might think: if there is no composite (<s>avayavin</s>) distinct from the parts such as threads and the like, then, since atoms are beyond the range of the senses, and since no sensible [object] is produced by those parts — the entire world would be imperceptible. But cows and the like are seen to be perceptible. Therefore it is established that something else, a sensible [entity], is produced by imperceptible atoms — to this, the following is said: 'Even though atoms are beyond the senses' — and so forth in detail. Just as for you <s>Vaiśeṣika</s>s, even though [atoms] are beyond the senses, only the aggregate of them has the capacity to produce effects, not individual [atoms] — similarly for us too, only the aggregate has perceptibility, not individual [atoms], even without a composite substance that is a separate entity. Just as for the eye and the rest — the eye, form, light, and mental attention — only the aggregate of them has causal power for the production of visual consciousness, not each one individually. Similarly, even though atoms are beyond the senses, only the aggregate has perceptibility, not each one individually. And for persons with eye-disease (<s>taimirika</s>), a collection of scattered, unconjoined hairs is perceived even without a composite being produced — but not each individual hair. For those with eye-disease, a single hair, like an atom, is beyond the senses. Therefore there is no separate substance for you.

body.text: tad evam avayavinaṃ pratiṣidhya rūpādibhyo guṃebhyaḥ arthāntaraṃ guṇināṃ pratiṣeddhukāma āha. rūpādiṣv eva ceti vistaraḥ. rūpādiṣv eva paramāṇur iti saṃjñāviniveśaḥ. tadvināśe rūpādivināśe siddhaḥ paramāṇuvināśa iti. vaiśeṣikā āhuḥ. dravyaṃ hi paramāṇuḥ. anyac ca rūpādibhyo dravyaṃ. rūpagandharasasparśavatī pṛthivī ity evamādisiddhāntavacanāt. aprayuktam
body.translated_text: Having thus refuted the composite (<s>avayavin</s>), wishing to refute the substance-possessor (<s>guṇin</s>) as something separate from qualities such as form and the rest, he says: 'In form and the rest alone' — and so forth in detail. The designation 'atom' (<s>paramāṇu</s>) is applied to form and the rest alone. Upon their destruction — upon the destruction of form and the rest — the destruction of the atom is established. The <s>Vaiśeṣika</s>s say: the atom is a substance (<s>dravya</s>). And substance is different from form and the rest. Because of doctrinal statements such as: 'Earth possesses form, smell, taste, and touch.' This is not applicable

body.text: asyānyatvaṃ yasmān na kenacit paricchidyante imāni pṛthivyaptejāṃsi. ime eṣāṃ pṛthivyādīnāṃ rūpādayo rūparasagandhasparśā guṇā iti. brūyāt atīndriyāṇi tāny ato na nirdhāryanta [Tib. 329a] ity ata āha. cakṣuḥsparśanagrāhyāṇi ca tāni pṛthyvyādīni pratijñāyanta iti. dagdheṣu ceti viṣtaraḥ. ūrṇādīny avayavidravyāṇi na dahyanta iti pailukāḥ. tad uktaṃ bhavati. prāktanaguṇanivṛttau pākajaguṇotpattau tadāśrayās tu dravyāṇi tadavasthānāny eva bhavantīti. tathaivorṇādibuddhiḥ syāt. na ca bhavati. tasmāt taddravyabuddhyabhāvāt. rūpādiṣv eva tadbhuddhir na dravye arthāntarabhūta iti. yadi hi ūrṇādidravyaṃ rūpādibhyo 'nyat syāt tat tadavasthānaṃ bhavatīti rūpādīny evāgnisaṃbandhād uṣṇena niruddhānīty ūrṇādibuddhiḥ syāt. na ca bhavati. tasmād rūpādiṣv evorṇādibuddhiḥ. vaiśeṣikā āhuḥ. yadi rūpādimātraṃ ghaṭaḥ syād agnisaṃbandhād rūpādīni pākajādīny anyāny utpadyanta iti sa evāyaṃ ghaṭa iti na parijñāyeta. yasya tu pākād rūpādīny evotpadyante nirudhyante ceti sa eva ghaṭas tadavasthāno bhavatīti tasya tatparijñānaṃ yujyata ity ata idam ucyate. pākajotpattau ghaṭaparijñānaṃ. saṃsthānasāmānyād iti. rūpādyākṛtisāmānyād ity arthaḥ. paṃktivat. yathā na vas tat pipīlikānāṃ tadvyatiriktaṃ paṃktidravyaṃ nāmāsti. atha ca pūrvapaṃktisaṃsthānasāmānyād anyasyām iti tatparijñānaṃ bhavati. saiveyaṃ pipīlikānāṃ paṃktir iti. [Tib. 329b] āha. katham etad gamyate. saṃsthānasāmānyāt parijñānaṃ na tu tādavasthyād iti. atrocyate. cihnam apaśyato 'parijñānād iti. yasmāt khaṇḍanimnonnatādicihnam apaśyatas tatparijñānaṃ na bhavati. ataḥ saṃsthānasāmānyād iti siddhaṃ.
body.translated_text: its otherness — because no one can determine: these are earth, water, and fire [elements]; these are the qualities of form, taste, smell, and touch belonging to those earth elements and the rest. One might say: they are beyond the senses, therefore they cannot be ascertained. To this he says: and those earth elements and the rest are acknowledged to be graspable by sight and touch. 'When burned' — and so forth in detail. The composite substances (<s>avayavidravya</s>) such as wool and the rest are not burned — [say] the <s>Pailuka</s>s (Vaiśeṣikas). This amounts to saying: upon the cessation of the prior qualities and the arising of heat-produced qualities, the substances that are their substrata remain in the same condition. If so, the cognition of wool and the rest should persist. But it does not. Therefore, because of the absence of cognition of that substance, the cognition of 'that' pertains only to form and the rest, not to a substance that is a separate entity. For if the substance of wool and the rest were different from form and the rest, then, since it remains in the same condition, one should still have the cognition of wool and the rest — since the form and the rest alone have been destroyed by heat through contact with fire. But one does not. Therefore, the cognition of wool and the rest pertains to form and the rest alone. The <s>Vaiśeṣika</s>s say: if a pot were merely form and the rest, then since through contact with fire other heat-produced forms and the rest arise, one could not recognize 'this is the same pot.' But for one whose forms and the rest alone arise and cease through heating, that same pot remains in the same condition, and its recognition is fitting — therefore this is said: the recognition of the pot upon the arising of heat-produced [qualities] is due to the similarity of configuration. The meaning is: due to the similarity of the shape of form and the rest. Like a row [of ants]. Just as for you there is no separate row-substance apart from those ants, yet from the similarity of configuration with the former row, one recognizes 'this is the very same row of ants' even for another [row]. He asks: how is this known — that the recognition is from similarity of configuration and not from the persistence of the same thing? To this it is said: because of non-recognition by one who does not see the distinguishing mark. Since for one who does not see the distinguishing marks such as being chipped, concave, convex, and the like, the recognition does not occur. Therefore, it is established that [recognition arises] from similarity of configuration.

body.text: sā ceti vistaraḥ. sā ca prītiḥ prasrabdhiyogena. prīter manasaḥ prasrabdhir jāyata. iti prasrabdhiyogenāśrayamṛdukaraṇāt apkalpā. ata eva ceti vistaraḥ. āśrayamṛdukaraṇāt. tasmin dvitīye samāpattidhyāne kṛtsnasya kāyasthairyasyāpagamāt. duḥkhendriyanirodha uktaḥ. sukhasya ca prahāṇāt. duḥkhasya ca prahāṇāt. pūrvam eva saumanasyadaurmanasyayor astaṃgamād aduḥkhāsukham upekṣāsmṛtipariśuddhaṃ caturthaṃ dhyānam upasaṃpadya
body.translated_text: 'That' — and so forth in detail. And that joy (<s>prīti</s>), through the application of tranquility (<s>prasrabdhi</s>) — from joy arises mental tranquility, and through the application of tranquility, by making the basis pliant, it is water-like (<s>apkalpa</s>). 'For this very reason' — and so forth in detail. Because of making the basis pliant. Because in that second meditative attainment (<s>samāpattidhyāna</s>), with the departure of the entire bodily stability, the cessation of the pain-faculty (<s>duḥkhendriya</s>) has been stated. And because of the abandonment of pleasure, and because of the abandonment of suffering — 'with the prior disappearance of mental pleasure and displeasure, one enters and abides in the fourth <s>dhyāna</s>, which is neither-suffering-nor-pleasure, with equanimity and mindfulness purified'

body.text: viharatīti vacanāt. ādhyātmikāpakṣālarahitatvād iti. ye vitarkavicārādayo 'ṣṭāv ādhyātmikāpakṣālāḥ. vitarkavicārau cāsū ca sukhādi ca catuṣṭayam iti. tadrahitatvād ity arthaḥ. ānejyam iti. ejṛ kampana ity asya dhātor etad rūpam ānejyam iti. yadā tv āniṃjyam iti pāṭhaḥ. tadā igeḥ prakṛtyantarasyaitad rūpam draṣṭavyaṃ. na taiḥ śuddhāvāsakāyikaiḥ śakyam ārūpyān praveṣṭuṃ. vipaśyanācaritatvāt. śamathacaritāś cārūpyāḥ. nāpy anyatra gantum adharāṃ bhūmiṃ. viśeṣagāmitvāt. etena krameṇeti. yathoktena saptānāṃ tejaḥsaṃvartanīnāṃ anantaram adbhiḥ saṃvartanī bhavaty ekā. punaḥ saptānāṃ tejaḥsaṃvartanīnām anaṃtaram adbhiḥ [Tib. 330a] saṃvartanī bhavati dvitīyā. evaṃ yāvat saptamy adbhiḥ saṃvartanī.
body.translated_text: — thus from the statement. 'Because of being free from internal impurities' — the eight internal impurities that are <s>vitarka</s>, <s>vicāra</s>, and the rest: <s>vitarka</s> and <s>vicāra</s>, and pleasure (<s>sukha</s>) and the rest — a set of four. Because of being free from those — this is the meaning. '<s>Ānejya</s>' (imperturbable) — from the root <s>ejṛ</s> meaning 'to tremble,' this form is <s>ānejya</s>. But when the reading is <s>āniñjya</s>, then it should be seen as a form from another root <s>ig</s>. 'Those <s>Śuddhāvāsa</s> deities cannot enter the formless [attainments]' — because of being practitioners of insight (<s>vipaśyanā</s>), while the formless [attainments] are practiced through calm (<s>śamatha</s>). 'Nor can they go elsewhere to a lower ground' — because of being progressive. 'In this sequence' — in the sequence as stated: after seven fire-dissolutions, there is one water-dissolution. Then after another seven fire-dissolutions, there is a second water-dissolution. Thus up to the seventh water-dissolution.

children.text:
evaṃ gate 'dbhiḥ saptake punaḥ
tejasā saptakaḥ.
children.translated_text:
After seven sets of water-dissolutions have thus passed,
again a set of seven by fire.

body.text: tataḥ paścād ekā vāyusaṃvartanī bhavati. kiṃkāraṇaṃ yathāvarṇitaṃ bahunā kālaprakarṣaṇenāpsaṃvartanī bhavati. tato 'pi bahutareṇa vāyusaṃvartanīty ata idam ucyate. yathaiva hi teṣām iti vistaraḥ. yathā prathamadhyānāt dvitīyadhyānasamāpattiviśeṣāt ātmabhāvānāṃ dvitīyadhyānabhūmikānāṃ sthitiviśeṣaḥ. ardhamahākalpārdhaṃ prathamadhyānopapannānām āyuḥpramāṇaṃ. kalpadvayaṃ dvitīyadhyānopapannānām iti. tathā bhājanānām api. kiṃ. sthitiviśeṣa iti. evaṃ dvitīyād api tṛtīyadhyānasya viśeṣo vaktavyaḥ. evaṃ ca kṛtveti. yasmād aṣṭakṛtvas tejaḥsaṃvartanīsaptakā iti ṣaṭpaṃcāśat tejaḥsaṃvartanyo bhavanti saptāpsaṃvartanyaḥ ekā vāyusaṃvartanīti catuḥṣaṣṭisaṃvartanyo bhavanti. tasmād yad uktaṃ prajñaptibhāṣye catuḥṣaṣṭiḥ kalpāḥ śubhakṛtsnānām āyuhpramāṇam iti. tat sūktaṃ bhavati. yathā
body.translated_text: After that there is one wind-dissolution. Why does a water-dissolution occur after such a long period of time as described? And a wind-dissolution after an even longer period? Therefore this is said: 'Just as for those' — and so forth in detail. Just as from the first <s>dhyāna</s>, through the distinction of attainment of the second <s>dhyāna</s>, there is a distinction in the lifespan of beings born in the second <s>dhyāna</s> ground — the lifespan measure of those born in the first <s>dhyāna</s> is half a great <s>kalpa</s>, and for those born in the second <s>dhyāna</s> it is two <s>kalpa</s>s — similarly for the vessels (world-containers) too. What? There is a distinction in lifespan. Similarly, the distinction of the third <s>dhyāna</s> from the second should be stated. 'And having done so' — since eight times the sets of seven fire-dissolutions make fifty-six fire-dissolutions, seven water-dissolutions, and one wind-dissolution — there are sixty-four dissolutions. Therefore what is stated in the <s>Prajñaptibhāṣya</s> — 'sixty-four <s>kalpa</s>s is the lifespan measure of the <s>Śubhakṛtsna</s> [gods]' — that is well said. As

children.translated_text:
'Above, the basis is distinguished as small and the rest,
doubling and doubling' —

body.text: ity atroktaṃ śubhakṛtsnānāṃ catuḥṣaṣṭiyojanānāṃ śarīrapramāṇaṃ. śarīrapramāṇena ca teṣām āyuḥpramāṇam uktaṃ.
body.translated_text: thus it is stated here: the body-measure of the <s>Śubhakṛtsna</s> [gods] is sixty-four <s>yojana</s>s. And their lifespan measure is stated in accordance with body measure.

children.translated_text: 'But lifespan is [measured] in <s>kalpa</s>s according to one's own basis' —

body.text: iti vacanāt. ekaikā saṃvartanī mahākalpa iti kṛtvā. iyatā hi kālena teṣām āyuṣah parisamāptir iti.
body.translated_text: thus from the statement. Each dissolution being reckoned as a great <s>kalpa</s> — for in that much time, the completion of their lifespan occurs.

body.text: ācāryayaśomitrakṛtāyāṃ sphuṭarthāyām abhidharmakośe vyākhyāyāṃ tṛtīyaṃ kośasthānaṃ. 3.
body.translated_text: In the <s>Sphuṭārthā</s>, the commentary on the <s>Abhidharmakośa</s> composed by <s>Ācārya Yaśomitra</s>, the third <s>kośasthāna</s> [is complete]. 3.

body.text: IV karmanirdeśa
body.translated_text: IV. Exposition of <s>Karma</s>

body.text: (IV.1) [Tib. 1b] tīrthakaravipratipattyā samutpāditasaṃdehaḥ pṛcchati. atha yad etad iti vistaraḥ. tatra sattvavaicitryaṃ dhātugatiyonyādibhedena. bhājanavaicitryaṃ merudvīpādibhedena. vyāmiśrakāriṇām iti. kuśalākuśalakarmakāriṇāṃ. atha kasmāt teṣām āśrayā ramyā na bhavanti [Tib. 2a] bhogās tu ramyā iti. sati caivaṃ viṣayopabhogaḥ saṃbhavati. āśrayaramyatve hi kasya pratīkārasya viṣayopabhogaḥ syāt. avyāmiśrakāriṇām iti. rūpāvacarāṇāṃ. kāmāvacarā api devā avyāmiśrakārikalpā āśrayaviṣayaramyāḥ. ramyatā hetukarmadvayakāritvāt.
body.translated_text: (IV.1) One whose doubt has been raised by the conflicting views of the founders of [non-Buddhist] schools (<s>tīrthakara</s>) asks: 'Now, this which' — and so forth in detail. Therein, the variety of beings is through the distinctions of element (<s>dhātu</s>), destiny (<s>gati</s>), birth-mode (<s>yoni</s>), and the rest. The variety of the vessel [world] is through the distinctions of <s>Meru</s>, continents, and the rest. 'Of those who perform mixed [actions]' — of those who perform both wholesome and unwholesome <s>karma</s>. Then why are their bases not delightful while their enjoyments are delightful? Because in such a case, the enjoyment of sense-objects is possible. For if the basis were delightful, what remedy would [require] the enjoyment of sense-objects? 'Of those who perform unmixed [actions]' — those of the Form Realm. Even the gods of the Desire Realm who are like performers of unmixed [actions] have delightful bases and objects — because of performing the two kinds of causal <s>karma</s> for delightfulness.

body.text: cetayitvā ceti. evaṃ cedaṃ kariṣyāmīti. [Tib. 2b] svabhāvataś ced vākkarmaikam iti. vā eva karmeti kṛtvā. itarayos tu na karmatvaṃ. kāyena kāyasya vā karma kāyakarma. evaṃ manaskarma. iti na svabhāvataḥ karma. tribhiḥ kāraṇair iti. āśrayataḥ svabhāvataḥ samutthānataś ceti. trayāṇām iti. kāyavāṅmanaskarmaṇām. āśrayataḥ kāyakarma. kāyāśrayaṃ karma kāyakarmeti. svabhāvato vākkarma. vāg eva karmeti. samutthānato manaskarma. manaḥsamutthitam iti kṛtvā.
body.translated_text: 'Having willed' (<s>cetayitvā</s>) — thus: 'I shall do this.' 'By its own nature, vocal <s>karma</s> is one' — because speech itself is <s>karma</s>. But for the other two, there is no <s>karma</s>-nature [by own nature]. Bodily <s>karma</s> is <s>karma</s> of the body or belonging to the body. Similarly, mental <s>karma</s>. Thus [they are] not <s>karma</s> by own nature. 'Through three reasons' — from the basis, from own nature, and from origination. 'Of the three' — bodily, vocal, and mental <s>karma</s>s. From the basis, bodily <s>karma</s> — <s>karma</s> having the body as its basis is bodily <s>karma</s>. From own nature, vocal <s>karma</s> — because speech itself is <s>karma</s>. From origination, mental <s>karma</s> — because it originates from the mind.

body.text: (IV.2cd-4) gatir ity apara iti. vātsīputrīyāḥ. ātmalābho 'nantaravināśīti. kṣaṇasyānantarakṣaṇa [Tib. 3a] iti nairuktena vidhinā ātmalābho 'nantaravināśī kṣaṇaśabdenābhidhīyate. atha vā kālaparyantaḥ kṣaṇaḥ. svāvasthānaḥ. so 'syāstīti ksaṇikaḥ. ata iniṭhanāv iti ṭhan. saṃskṛtasyāvaśyaṃ vyayād iti. utpattyanantaravināśirūpaṃ. cittacaittavat. ākasmiko hi bhāvānāṃ vināśa iti. akasmādbhava ākasmikaḥ ahetuka ity arthaḥ. sādhanaṃ cātra. ahetuko vināśaḥ. abhāvatvāt. atyantabhāvavat. dṛṣṭo vai kāṣṭhādīnām iti vistaraḥ [Tib. 3b] ādiśabdena
body.translated_text: (IV.2cd-4) 'Movement (<s>gati</s>), according to others' — the <s>Vātsīputrīya</s>s. 'Self-existence perishes in the immediately following [moment]' — the moment immediately following a moment — by etymological derivation, self-existence that perishes immediately is designated by the word 'moment' (<s>kṣaṇa</s>). Or alternatively, a <s>kṣaṇa</s> is a limit of time, a duration in its own state. That which possesses this is momentary (<s>kṣaṇika</s>). Therefore the <s>ṭhan</s> suffix by the rule 'ata iniṭhan.' 'Because of the necessary perishing of the conditioned' — having the nature of perishing immediately after arising, like mind and mental factors. 'For the destruction of entities is uncaused' — <s>ākasmikaḥ</s> means arising without reason, meaning: without cause. And the proof here is: destruction is uncaused, because of being a non-entity (<s>abhāva</s>), like absolute non-existence (<s>atyantābhāva</s>). 'For it is seen that of wood and the like' — and so forth in detail. By the word 'and the like'

body.text: rūpādīnāṃ grahaṇaṃ. dṛṣṭo 'gnisaṃyogād vināśa iti. pratyakṣadvārāpatito dharmasvarūpaviparyaya iti pratijñādoṣaṃ darśayati. ata evāha. na ca dṛṣṭād gariṣṭhaṃ pramāṇam iti. na pratyakṣād gurutamaṃ pramāṇam astīty arthaḥ.
body.translated_text: form and the rest are included. 'Destruction is seen from contact with fire' — [to this] he shows the fault of the thesis as a reversal of the true nature of things that falls into the domain of direct perception. For this very reason he says: 'And there is no means of valid knowledge weightier than what is seen' — the meaning is: there is no means of valid knowledge more authoritative than direct perception.

body.text: ācāryaḥ pratyakṣābhimānaṃ pareṣāṃ darśayann āha. kathaṃ tāvad bhavān yāvan manyata iti. na hi kāṣṭhādivināśo rūpādivat pratyakṣata upalabhyate. akṣaṇikavādinas ta āhuḥ. teṣāṃ punar adarśanād iti. teṣāṃ kāṣṭhādīnām adarśanāt. tad evam anumānataḥ siddhiṃ darśayati. agnisaṃyogahetukaḥ kāṣṭhādivināśaḥ. tadāpāte bhāvāt. yasya yadāpāte bhāvaḥ. sa taddhetukaḥ. tadyathā bījāpāte bhāvyo 'ṃkuraḥ. saṃpradhāryaṃ tāvad etad iti. naikāntikatām udbhāvayati. na hi yasyāpāte [Tib. 4a] yo vināśo bhavati. sa taddhetuka iti. vāyusaṃyogapāte hi sati pradīpasya vināśaḥ. na ca sa vināśo vāyusaṃyogakṛtaḥ. kṣaṇikatvābhyupagamād dhi pradīpasyākasmiko vināśa iṣyate. sa hi utpannapradhvaṃsitatvāt svayaṃ vinaṣṭaḥ pradīpaḥ. vāyupratibandhād anyasyānutpattau na dṛśyate. na tena vināśa iti. tathā ghaṇṭāśabdakṣaṇika iṣyate. pāṇisaṃyogapāte ca sati ghaṇṭāśabdasya vināśaḥ. na sa tatkṛtaḥ. kṣaṇikatvād dhi svayaṃ vinaṣṭo ghaṇṭāśabdaḥ. tatpratibandhatvād anyasyānutpattau na dṛśyate. na tena vināśa iti. tasmād anumānasādhyo 'yam arthaḥ. na pratyakṣasiddha ity abhiprāyaḥ. tasmād anaikāntikam etat. yasya pāte yaḥ kaścid vināśaḥ. sa tatkṛta iti. kiṃ punar atrānumānam iti. atrāhetuko vināśa ity etasminn arthe kim anumānam iti. uktaṃ tāvad akāryatvād abhāvasyeti. ahetuko vināśaḥ. akāryatvāt. ākāśavat. akāryaś cāsau. abhāvasvabhāvatvāt. [Tib. 4b] atyantābhāvavat.
body.translated_text: The <s>Ācārya</s>, showing the opponents' presumption of direct perception, says: 'How indeed do you consider' — and so forth. For the destruction of wood and the like is not perceived by direct perception like [the destruction of] form and the like. The proponents of non-momentariness then say: 'Because of their non-perception thereafter' — because of the non-perception of those pieces of wood and the like. Thus he shows establishment through inference: the destruction of wood and the like is caused by contact with fire, because of its occurrence upon the advent of that. Whatever occurs upon the advent of something else is caused by that — just as a sprout, which occurs upon the advent of a seed. 'This should be carefully considered' — he brings out the non-conclusiveness. For it is not the case that whatever destruction occurs upon the advent of something is caused by that. For the destruction of a lamp occurs upon the advent of contact with wind, yet that destruction is not caused by contact with wind — because, by accepting momentariness, the destruction of the lamp is held to be uncaused. For that lamp, being of the nature of perishing immediately after arising, has perished by itself. Due to the obstruction by wind of the arising of another [flame], it is not seen — it is not that destruction is caused by that. Similarly, the sound of a bell is held to be momentary. And the destruction of the bell-sound occurs upon the advent of contact with the hand, yet it is not caused by that — because, being momentary, the bell-sound has perished by itself. Because of the obstruction by that [hand-contact] of the arising of another [sound], it is not perceived — it is not that destruction is caused by that. Therefore this matter is to be established by inference, not established by direct perception — this is the intent. Therefore this is inconclusive: whatever destruction occurs upon the advent of something is caused by that. What then is the inference here? In this matter — that destruction is uncaused — what inference [is there]? It has been stated: because of being a non-effect (<s>akārya</s>), since it is a non-entity. Destruction is uncaused, because of being a non-effect, like space (<s>ākāśa</s>). And it is a non-effect, because of having the nature of non-existence (<s>abhāva</s>), like absolute non-existence.

body.text: iti. na kasyacid akasmād ity arthaḥ. utpādavad iti viparītopamānaṃ. yathotpāda ātmalābhalakṣaṇaḥ sahetuka eva. nāhetukaḥ. tadvināśaḥ syāt. na caivaṃ bhavati. katham ity āha. kṣaṇikānāṃ ca buddhiśabdārciṣāṃ dṛṣṭa ākasmiko vināśaḥ. tad evam anumānāpatito dharmasvarūpaviparyayaḥ. ākasmikaḥ kāṣṭhādīnāṃ vināśaḥ. vināśasvābhāvyāt. buddhyādivināśavad iti.
body.translated_text: the meaning is: of nothing, without reason. 'Like arising' — this is an inverted analogy. Just as arising, characterized by the obtaining of self-existence, is invariably with a cause, not without cause — so too should destruction be. But it is not so. How? He says: for of momentary cognitions (<s>buddhi</s>), sounds (<s>śabda</s>), and flames (<s>arciṣ</s>), uncaused destruction is seen. Thus, a reversal of the true nature of things that falls into the domain of inference [is shown]: the destruction of wood and the like is uncaused, because of being destruction by its very nature, like the destruction of cognitions and the like.

body.text: yas tu manyata iti vaiśeṣikāḥ. pūrvā buddhir uttarayā buddhyā utpannayā vināśyate. anyā tu buddhiḥ pūrvayā buddhyā vināśyate. evaṃ śabdo 'pi vācyaḥ. āha. na yuktam etat. kasmāt. buddhyor asamavadhānāt. ayugapadbhāvād ity arthaḥ. na hy asantaṃ nāśyaṃ hetur vināśayatīti. kathaṃ gamyate buddhyor asamavadhānam iti. ata āha. na hi saṃśayaniścayajñānayor yuktasamavadhānam iti
body.translated_text: 'But one who thinks' — the <s>Vaiśeṣika</s>s. The prior cognition is destroyed by the arising of the subsequent cognition. But another cognition is destroyed by the prior cognition. Similarly, sound too should be stated. He says: this is not correct. Why? Because of the non-coincidence of the two cognitions — the meaning is: because of their non-simultaneity. For a cause does not destroy a thing-to-be-destroyed that does not [yet] exist. How is it known that the two cognitions do not coincide? Therefore he says: for it is not fitting that a cognition of doubt and a cognition of certainty coincide

body.text: vistaraḥ. svasaṃvedyam etat. yadā saṃśayajñānam. na tadā niścayajñānam. yadā niścayajñānaṃ. na tadā saṃśayajñānam iti. evaṃ sukhaduḥkhayo rāgadveṣayoś cāsamavadhānam iti yojayaṃ. yathā ca viruddhayor asamavadhānam. evam [Tib. 5a] aviruddhayor api jñānayor asamavadhānaṃ bhavatīti. yadā ceti vistaraḥ. athāpi samavadhānaṃ syād iti. tathāpy apaṭubuddhiśabdau paṭū na hiṃsyātāṃ. durbalasamānajātīyatvāt. na hi durbalasamānajātīyo balavantaṃ hiṃsan dṛṣṭaḥ. asamānas tu durbalo 'pi hiṃsyāt. tadyathā udakaṃ tejaḥ.
body.translated_text: this is the elaboration. This is self-evident. When there is doubtful knowledge, there is no certain knowledge at that time. When there is certain knowledge, there is no doubtful knowledge at that time. Thus the non-coincidence of pleasure and pain, and of desire and aversion, should be connected. And just as there is non-coincidence of contradictory [states], so too [Tib. 5a] there is non-coincidence even of non-contradictory cognitions. 'And when' — this is the elaboration. 'Even if there were coincidence' — even so, the dull intelligence and sound would not harm the sharp ones, because of being of the same kind as the weak. For a weak one of the same kind is not seen to harm a strong one. But one of a different kind, even if weak, could harm — just as water [harms] fire.

body.text: yo 'py arciṣaṃ avasthānahetvabhāvād iti. avasthānahetvabhāvād bhāvānāṃ vināśa iti. sthaviravasubandhuprabhṛtibhir ayaṃ hetur uktaḥ. sa cāyuktaḥ. na hy abhāvaḥ kāraṇaṃ bhavitum arhatīti. dharmadharmavaśād veti vaiśeṣikaḥ. taṃ pratyāha. na cāpy utpādavināśahetvor iti. utpādavināśahetvor adharmasya. kṣaṇa eva kṣaṇa iti. mukhye kṣaṇe. naupacārike kṣaṇa ity arthaḥ. atha vā kṣaṇa eva kṣaṇa iti. kṣaṇe kṣaṇa evety arthaḥ. vṛttilābhapratibandhau vṛttilābho vṛttipratibandhaś ca kṣaṇekṣaṇe bhavituṃ nārhataḥ. kathaṃ kṛtvā. yasyārciṣaḥ utpattāv anugraho bhavati caitrasya maitrasya vā. tasya dharma utpalabdhavṛttiḥ tad utpādayatīty evam utpādahetuḥ. vināśahetur api. yadi tadvināśas tasyānugrahaṃ karoti andhakārāvasthāyām. evam adharmo 'pi. yasyārcirutpattāv apakāro bhavati. [Tib. 5b] tasyādharmo labdhavṛttis tad utpadayati. vināśahetur api. yadi tadvināśas tasyāpy apakāraṃ karoti andhakārāvasthāyām. iti tayor vṛttilābhād arciṣām utpattir bhavati. na ca vṛttilābhaṃ tayor apratibadhya tābhyām eva tasminn eva kṣaṇe teṣāṃ vināśa iti. kṣaṇekṣaṇe vṛttilābhapratibandhau na dvayor yujyete. śakyaś caiṣa kāraṇaparikalpa iti vistaraḥ. dharmādharmavināśa iti kāraṇaparikalpaḥ sarvatra saṃskṛte dvyaṇukādau anityeṣu rūpādiṣu karmaṇi ca śakyate kartuṃ. ato na vaktavyam etat. agnisaṃyogāt kāṣṭhādīnāṃ vināśa ity evamādi. tataś ca sarvasaṃskṛtasya kṣaṇikasiddhiḥ. dharmādharmayos tadvināśakāraṇāntarānapekṣatvād ity alaṃ vivādena.
body.translated_text: As for the one [who argues] that flame [perishes] because of the absence of a cause for persistence — 'because of the absence of a cause for persistence, entities perish' — this reason was stated by the elder <s>Vasubandhu</s> and others. And it is inappropriate, for non-existence cannot be a cause. 'Or because of <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s>' — says the <s>Vaiśeṣika</s>. He replies to that: 'Nor of the cause of arising and destruction' — of the cause of arising and destruction, that is, of <s>adharma</s>. 'In a moment itself, in a moment' — in the primary sense of moment, not in the figurative sense of moment — this is the meaning. Or alternatively, 'in a moment itself, in a moment' means: in a moment, in a moment itself — this is the meaning. The obtaining of function and its obstruction cannot occur in moment after moment. How so? For whichever [person] — <s>Caitra</s> or <s>Maitra</s> — there is benefit at the arising of the flame, the <s>dharma</s> (merit) of that person, having obtained function, produces that — thus it is the cause of arising. It is also the cause of destruction, if the destruction of that [flame] benefits that person in the state of darkness. Similarly with <s>adharma</s> (demerit): for whichever person there is harm at the arising of the flame, [Tib. 5b] the <s>adharma</s> of that person, having obtained function, produces that. It is also the cause of destruction, if the destruction of that [flame] also harms that person in the state of darkness. Thus from the obtaining of function by those two, there is the arising of flames. But without obstructing the obtaining of function of those two, there cannot be destruction of those [flames] by those very [dharma and adharma] in that very moment. The obtaining of function and its obstruction in moment after moment is not tenable for the two. 'And this imagination of causes is possible' — this is the elaboration. The imagination of causes through the destruction of <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s> can be applied everywhere in the conditioned — in dyads of atoms and the rest, in impermanent forms and the rest, and in action. Therefore this should not be said: 'From contact with fire, the destruction of wood and the rest' — and so forth. And consequently, the momentariness of all conditioned things is established — because of the non-dependence of <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s> on another cause for their destruction. Enough of this dispute.

body.text: tat eva tādṛśād veti. yadi agnisaṃyogaḥ śyāmatāṃ ghaṭasya nivartya raktatāṃ janayati. sa eva raktatāṃ nivartya raktataratāṃ janayatīti kalpyate.
body.translated_text: 'From that very [cause], from one of such a kind' — if the contact with fire, having removed the dark color of the pot, produces redness, then that very [contact] is imagined to remove the redness and produce a deeper redness.

body.text: hetur eva vināśakaḥ syāt. atha jvālānāṃ kṣaṇikatvād anyas tatsaṃyogo janako 'nyo 'pi vināśaka iti kalpyate. hetvaviśiṣṭo vināśakaḥ syāt. na ca yuktam iti sarvaṃ. jvālāntareṣu ca tāvad dhetubhede 'pi parikalpanāṃ parikalpayeyuḥ vaiśeṣikāḥ. kṣaṇikatvāt. jvālānām anyā janikāḥ. [Tib. 6a] anyā vināśikā iti. kṣārayāvadbhūmisambandhāt tu pākajaviśeṣotpattau kāṃ kalpanāṃ kalpayeyuḥ. na hi teṣāṃ kṣārādayaḥ kṣaṇikāḥ. tatra hetur eva vināśakaḥ syāt. yat tarhi āpa iti vistaraḥ. yady agnisaṃyoge 'py āpo na vināśyante. kathaṃ tarhy āpaḥ kvāthyamānāḥ kṣīyanta ity abhiprāyaḥ. tejodhātur iti. tadavinirbhāgasaṃvardhanaṃ. yasya prabhāvād apāṃ saṃhātaḥ kṣāmakṣāmo jāyata iti. kāraṇaviśeṣāt kāryaviśeṣa iti. kṣāmakṣāmataro jāyate. yāvad atikṣāmatāṃ gato 'nte na punaḥ saṃtānaṃ saṃtanoti. kāryaṃ karoti na tv abhāvaṃ karotīty arthaḥ. bhaṃguratvād iti vistaraḥ. bhaṃgaśīlatvāt svayaṃ vinaśyanto 'nyenājanitā vināśāḥ. santa utpannamātrād ekakṣaṇalabdhātmāno bhavanto vinaśyanti. tṛṇajvālāvad iti. yathā tṛṇajvālāyāḥ kṣaṇikatve 'pi deśantareṣu nirantarotpattau gatyabhimānaḥ. tṛṇaṃ dahantīti. jvālā gacchantīti. tadvat. sādhanaṃ ca. avidyamānagatayo deśāntare nirantaram utpadyamānā rūpādayo bhāvāḥ. kṣaṇikatvāt. tṛṇajvālāvat [Tib. 6]. saṃsthānaṃ kāyavijñāptir iti vaibhāṣikavacanaṃ.
body.translated_text: The cause itself would be the destroyer. But if, because of the momentariness of flames, one imagines that one contact produces while another destroys — the destroyer would be indistinguishable from the cause. And none of this is reasonable. The <s>Vaiśeṣikas</s> might indeed, even with respect to different flames, [Tib. 6a] imagine such an imagination despite the difference of causes — because of the momentariness of flames, some produce and others destroy. But with respect to the production of special heat-produced [qualities] through the connection with alkali-water-earth, what imagination could they devise? For alkalis and the rest are not momentary according to them. In that case, the cause itself would be the destroyer. 'As for what [you say about] water' — this is the elaboration. If water is not destroyed even through contact with fire, then how is it that water being boiled diminishes? — this is the intent. 'The fire-element' — the growth of the [fire-element that is] inseparable [from the water] — by whose power the mass of water becomes progressively drier and drier. 'From the specificity of the cause, the specificity of the effect' — it becomes even drier, until having reached extreme dryness, it finally no longer continues the continuum. It produces an effect but does not produce non-existence — this is the meaning. 'Because of being breakable' — this is the elaboration. Because of having a nature that tends to break, perishing by themselves, destructions are unproduced by another — being existent, having obtained existence for merely a single moment, they perish. 'Like a grass-flame' — just as even though a grass-flame is momentary, through uninterrupted arising in successive locations, there is the impression of movement — 'it burns the grass,' 'the flame moves' — so too. And the proof: forms and the rest, though having no actual motion, arising uninterruptedly in successive locations, [appear to move] — because of momentariness, like a grass-flame [Tib. 6b]. 'Configuration (<s>saṃsthāna</s>) is bodily intimation (<s>kāyavijñapti</s>)' — this is the <s>Vaibhāṣika</s> statement.

body.text: iti. ekā diṅ mukham asyeti ekadiṅmukhaṃ. tasmin. bhūyasi bahutare. evaṃ sarvam iti. ūrdhvaikadiṅmukhe bhūyasi utpanna unnatam iti prajñapyate. adho bhūyasy avanatam iti. eṣā dik. tadyathā alātam iti. na dravyasat saṃsthānaṃ. varṇagrahaṇāt pakṣagrahaṇatvāt. alātacakravad iti. atha vā na dravyaṃ saṃsthānam. anyarūpagrahaṇāt pakṣagrahaṇatvāt. dhānyarāśivad iti. dvābhyām asaya grahaṇaṃ prāpnuyād ity ukte vaibhāṣiko brūyāt. na dīrghatvādeḥ kāyendriyeṇa grahaṇaṃ. kiṃ tarhi. spraṣṭavyāvayaveṣv eva. tathā saṃniviṣṭeṣu dīrghādigrahaṇaṃ bhavati. ato na dvābhyām asya grahaṇaṃ prāpnotīty ata idam ucyate. yathā vā spraṣṭavya iti vistaraḥ. ko 'rthaḥ. yathā
body.translated_text: thus. That whose face is one direction — facing one direction. In that. 'Preponderant' means in greater quantity. 'Thus everything' — when color or tangible [matter] facing one direction is grasped in a preponderant quantity, the conceptual cognition 'long' arises; when in lesser quantity, the conceptual cognition 'short' — and so on should be understood. 'By means of a painting' — this is the elaboration. Or by means of a painting — by a multicolored configuration being seen in many ways — multiple configurations such as long and so forth are seen. Therefore, from the seeing of multiple configurations

body.text: spraṣṭavye dīrghahrasvādigrahaṇaṃ. na ca spraṣṭavyāyatanasaṃgṛhītaṃ saṃsthānaṃ. tathā varṇe 'pi saṃbhāvyatāṃ dīrghādigrahaṇaṃ. na ca rūpāyatanasaṃgṛhītaṃ saṃsthānam. arthāntarabhūtaṃ syād ity arthaḥ. punar vaibhāṣika āha. smṛtimātraṃ tatra iti vistaraḥ. smṛtimātraṃ tatra saṃsthāne. sparśasāhacaryāt ślakṣṇatvādibhiḥ sparśaiḥ sahacarabhāvāt. [Tib. 7a] na tu sākṣādgrahaṇaṃ dīrghādisaṃsthānasya. yathāgnirūpaṃ dṛṣṭvā tasyāgner uṣṇatāyāṃ smṛtir bhavati. sāhacaryāt. puṣpasya ca caṃpakasya ca gandhaṃ ghrātvā tadvarṇe 'pi smṛtiḥ. sāhacaryāt. āha. yuktam atreti vistaraḥ. yuktam atrāgnāv avyabhicārāt uṣṇatāyāś ca varṇasya ca. anyenānyasmaraṇam agnirūpeṇoṣṇatāyāḥ. puṣpagandhena ca tadvarṇasya. na tu kiṃcid iti vistaraḥ. na tu kiṃcit spraṣṭavyaṃ ślakṣṇatvādi kvacid iti saṃsthāne dīrghādau niyataṃ. yato 'tra saṃsthāne spraṣṭavyaṃ spṛṣṭvā samaraṇaṃ niyamena syāt. yatra hy agnirūpaṃ. tatra taduṣṇatayā bhavitavyaṃ. yatra ca campakagandhaḥ. tatra tadrūpeṇa bhavitavyaṃ. na tu yatra ślakṣṇatvaṃ karkaśatvaṃ vā tatra dīrghatvena hrasvatvena vā bhavitavyaṃ. tasmād taduṣṇatārūpayor niyamena yujyate saṃsthāne tu niyamena smaraṇaṃ na prāpnoti. tathāsaty api sāhacaryaniyame spraṣṭavyasaṃsthānayoḥ saṃsthāne smaraṇaṃ niyamena syāt. varṇe 'pi syāt smaraṇaṃ niyameneti vartate. tad evaṃ spraṣṭavyaṃ spṛṣṭvā smared ity arthaḥ. athāniyamena varṇasmaraṇaṃ bhavati varṇavad vā saṃsthāne 'py aniyamena syāt. dīrghe hrasvam iti. hrasve dīrgham iti. kiṃkāraṇaṃ. varṇe hy aniyamena smaraṇaṃ bhavati spraṣṭavyāt. kadācid rakte pītam iti pīte [Tib. 7b] raktam iti. na caivaṃ bhavati. katham evaṃ na bhavati. yathā varne saṃsmaraṇaṃ na niyamena bhavati. tathā saṃsthāne 'py aniyameneti. kiṃ tarhi. varṇe smaraṇaṃ na niyamena bhavati. saṃsthāne punar niyamenety ayuktam asya saṃsthānasya spraṣṭavyāt smaraṇaṃ. kathaṃ tarhi dīrghabuddhir hrasvabuddhir vā bhavati. uktam etat. ekadiṅmukhe bhūyasi varṇe vā spraṣṭavye vā gṛhyamāṇe dīrghavikalpabuddhir alpīyasi hrasvavikalpabuddhir ity evamādy avagantavyaṃ. citrāntareṇa veti vistaraḥ. citrāntareṇa vānekavarṇasaṃsthāne bahubhiḥ prakārair dṛśyamānenānekasaṃsthānaṃ dṛśyate dīrghādi. ato 'nekasaṃsthānadarśanād
body.translated_text: just as in the tangible there is the grasping of long, short, and so forth, yet configuration is not included in the tangible sense-base — so too, in color also, the grasping of long and so forth should be considered possible, yet configuration is not included in the visible-form sense-base — it would be a separate thing, is the meaning. Again the <s>Vaibhāṣika</s> says: 'It is merely recollection there' — this is the elaboration. It is merely recollection with respect to that configuration — because of association with touch, because of being accompanied by touches such as smoothness and the rest. [Tib. 7a] But there is no direct grasping of long and other configurations. Just as upon seeing the form of fire, there arises recollection of that fire's heat — because of association. And upon smelling the fragrance of a <s>campaka</s> flower, there is recollection of its color too — because of association. He says: 'This is appropriate here' — this is the elaboration. This is appropriate here with fire, because of the invariable connection of heat and color. The recollection of one thing from another — of heat from the form of fire, and of the flower's color from its fragrance. 'But nothing' — this is the elaboration. But no tangible such as smoothness and the rest is invariably [connected] with any particular configuration such as long and the rest, such that upon touching the tangible in this configuration, there would necessarily be recollection. For wherever there is the form of fire, there must be its heat. And wherever there is <s>campaka</s>-fragrance, there must be its color. But it is not the case that wherever there is smoothness or roughness, there must be length or shortness. Therefore, recollection is rightly connected with those — heat and color — in a necessary way, but recollection does not necessarily apply to configuration. Even if there were such a necessary association between touch and configuration, recollection of configuration would necessarily arise. 'It would also be recollection of color' — necessarily, is continued. That is: from touching the tangible, one would recollect — this is the meaning. But if recollection of color from [touch] occurs without necessity, then for configuration too, it would occur without necessity — short for long, long for short. Why? Because recollection of color from the tangible occurs without necessity — sometimes red from yellow, sometimes [Tib. 7b] yellow from red. And this does not happen. How does it not happen thus? Just as recollection of color from touch does not occur necessarily, so too for configuration there should be no necessity. But rather: recollection of color does not occur necessarily, yet recollection of configuration does occur necessarily — this is unreasonable, this recollection of configuration from touch. How then does the cognition 'long' or 'short' arise? This has been stated: when color or tangible facing one direction is grasped preponderantly, the conceptual cognition 'long' arises; when in lesser quantity, the conceptual cognition 'short' — and so on should be understood. 'Or by means of a painting' — this is the elaboration. Or by means of a painting — by a multicolored configuration being seen in many ways — multiple configurations such as long and the rest are seen. Therefore, from seeing multiple configurations

body.text:
bahūnāṃ saṃsthānānām ekadeśaṃ prāpnuyāt. yatraiva dīrghatvaṃ. tatraiva hrasvādigrahaṇāt. tac cāyuktaṃ varṇavat. yathā hi varṇaḥ sapratighatvād ekadeśo na bhavati. tathā saṃsthānam apīti. tathā ca sati dravyato 'sti saṃsthānam iti sapakṣālaḥ pakṣo bhavati. dharmiviśeṣaviparyayāt. na cāṇau tad iti. yathā nīlādirūpaṃ aṣṭadravyakādāv aṇau vidyate. na caivam aṇau saṃsthānaṃ dīrghādi vidyate. kathaṃ punar gamyate. saṃsthānaṃ paramāṇau nāstīti. dīrghasaṃsthāne 'pacīyamāne dīrghabuddhyabhāvāt. dīrghaṃ hi daṇḍam upalabhya tasminn evāpacīyamāne dīrghabuddhir na nivartet. na hi nīlādidravyam upalabhyapacīyamāne tasmin pītabuddhir bhavati. dīrghadravye tv apacīyamāne hrasvabuddhir bhavati. na dīrghabuddhiḥ. na ca yuktaṃ vaktuṃ. tad eva saṃsthānaṃ dīrghādihrasvādibuddhiṃ janayatīti. [Tib. 8a] tasmād bahuṣv eveti sarvaṃ. atha matam iti vistaraḥ. saṃsṭhānaparamāṇava eva tathā saṃniviṣṭā ekadiṅmukhādikrameṇa dīrghādisaṃjñā bhavanti. na hy atatsvabhāvāḥ tathā saṃniviṣṭhāḥ samānās tāṃ saṃjñām upalabdhum arhatīty abhiprāyaḥ. na ca saṃsthānāvayavānāṃ varṇādivat svabhāvaḥ siddha iti. varṇāvayavāḥ prasiddhasvabhāvāḥ. pratyavayavaṃ nīlāditvato grahaṇāt. na caivaṃ saṃsthānaparamāṇavaḥ pratyavayavaṃ dīrghāditvato gṛhyante. tasmān na prasiddhasvabhāvāḥ. yadi tu naiva te dīrghādisvabhāvāḥ. saṃniveśaviśeṣāt tu dīrghādibuddhihetavo bhavanti. varṇādiparamāṇava eva saṃniveśaviśeṣā dīrghādibuddhihetavo bhavantīti kiṃ neṣyate. yat tarhi varṇatvābhinna iti.
yadi varṇasaṃniveśamātraṃ saṃsthānaṃ syāt. varṇābhede saṃsthānabhedo na syāt. mṛdbhājanānāṃ kuṇḍādīnām anarthāntarabhāvāt. nanu coktam iti vistaraḥ. yathā saṃniviṣṭavarṇe dīrghādisaṃjñā prajñapyate. ekadiṅmukhe ca varṇa iti vistareṇa. yathā ca pipīlikādīnām iti vistaraḥ. yathā ca pipīlikādaya [Tib. 8b] ekarūpā bhavanti. teṣāṃ ca paṃktir ity asmin deśe 'nyādṛśy anyasminn anyādṛśī. evaṃ cakrādīnāṃ bheda ity evamādi. tathā varṇābhede 'pi saṃsthānabhedaḥ syāt. tarhi tamasīti vistaraḥ. yat tarhi tamasi varṇam apaśyaṃtaḥ sthāṇupuruṣahastyādīnāṃ dīrghahrasvatva parimaṇḍalādīni paśyanti. tat katham iti vākyaśeṣaḥ. yadi tarhi varṇāj jātyantaraṃ saṃsthānaṃ na syāt. yathā varṇaṃ nīlaṃ pītam iti vā na paśyanti. tathā saṃsthānam api dīrghaṃ hrasvam iti na paśyeyuḥ. paśyanti ca kadācit. ato jātyantaraṃ saṃsthānam iti. paṃktisenāparikalpavad iti. yathā tamasy avyaktaṃ
body.translated_text: it would be a portion of many shapes. For wherever there is length, right there short and the rest are also grasped. And that is not fitting, like color. For just as color, because of having resistance (<s>sapratighatva</s>), is not a portion [of multiple colors], so too shape. And that being so, the thesis 'shape exists as a substance' would have a defective example — because of the reversal of the property of the subject. 'And it is not [found] in the atom' — just as blue and other forms exist in a minimal atom of eight substances and so on, shape such as length and the rest does not similarly exist in the atom. But how is it known that shape does not exist in the atom? Because of the absence of the cognition of length when the long-shaped [object] is diminished. For having perceived a long stick, when that very [stick] is diminished, the cognition of length would not cease [if length were intrinsic]. For when a blue substance is perceived and diminished, the cognition of yellow does not arise. But when a long substance is diminished, the cognition of shortness arises, not the cognition of length. And it is not fitting to say that the very same shape generates the cognition of length and shortness. Therefore, [shape exists] only in the many [atoms together] — this is everything. 'Now if one thinks' — and so forth in detail. Shape-atoms themselves, arranged in that way, in a sequence facing one direction and the like, become [designated as] long and the rest. The intent is: those not having that nature, when arranged in that way, would not equally deserve to receive that designation. 'And the own-nature of the parts of shape, like color and the rest, is not established' — the parts of color have a well-known own-nature, because each part is grasped as blue and the like. But shape-atoms are not thus grasped part-by-part as long and the like. Therefore their own-nature is not well-known. But if they do not have the nature of long and the rest, yet become causes of the cognition of length and the rest through a particular arrangement, then why is it not accepted that color-atoms and the rest themselves, through a particular arrangement, become causes of the cognition of length and the rest? 'Then [the objection]: it would be non-different from color' — if shape were merely the arrangement of colors, then there would be no difference of shape when there is no difference of color — because clay vessels such as pots and the like would not be separate things. 'But has it not been said' — and so forth in detail. Just as the designation of long and the like is conventionally applied to arranged colors, and color facing one direction — and so on in detail. 'And just as with ants and the like' — and so forth in detail. Just as ants and the like are of one form, and their row, in one place is of one kind and in another place of another kind — similarly, the distinction of wheels and the like [is understood]. And thus even without difference of color, there can be difference of shape. 'Then, in darkness' — and so forth in detail. Since in darkness, not seeing colors, they see the length, shortness, roundness, and the like of posts, persons, elephants, and the like — how [can shape be reduced to color]? This is the completion of the sentence. If shape were not of a different universal from color, then just as they do not see color as blue or yellow, they should likewise not see shape as long or short. Yet sometimes they do see [shape]. Therefore shape is of a different universal. 'Like the imagining of a row or an army' — just as in darkness, having indistinctly seen

body.text: pakṣiṇaḥ pipīlikā vā dṛṣṭvā dīrghā paṃktir iti parikalpayaṃti yathā vā tamasy eva hastyādīn avyaktaṃ dṛṣṭvā parimaṇḍala iyaṃ senā vyavasthiteti parikalpayanti. tadvat. veviditaṃ caitad evam iti. yathedānīm uktam asaty api jātyantare saṃsthāne varṇam eva te tatrāvyaktaṃ dṛṣṭvā dīrghādiparikalpaṃ kurvanti. yat kadācid iti vistaraḥ. anirdhāryamāṇaparicchedam iti. anirdhāryamāṇasaṃsthānaṃ saṃghātamātram avyaktam alakṣyamāṇanīlatvādikaṃ dṛśyate. na ca varṇasaṃsthānavyatiriktaṃ rūpāyatanam astīti. yathā nānyat kiṃcid dravyaṃ [Tib. 9a] kalpyate. tadvat saṃsthānam api na varṇavyatiriktaṃ kalpayitavyaṃ.
body.translated_text: birds or ants, they imagine 'this is a long row'; or just as in darkness itself, having indistinctly seen elephants and the like, they imagine 'this army stands in a circle' — so too. 'And this has been understood thus' — as has now been stated: even without shape being of a different universal, having seen color indistinctly there, they make the imagination of length and the like. 'When sometimes' — and so forth in detail. What is perceived without a determinable boundary — shape that cannot be determined as a mere aggregate, indistinct, with blue-ness and the like not discernible — is seen. And there is no sense-base of form (<s>rūpāyatana</s>) other than color and shape. Therefore, just as no other substance is imagined [beyond what is perceived], so too shape should not be imagined as distinct from color.

body.text: tatra bhavanta iti. te bhavanta ity arthaḥ. itarābhyo 'pi dṛśyanta iti vacanāt. kathaṃ kāyakarma prajñāpayantīti. prajñaptisattvāt kāyakarmayoga iti manyamānaḥ pṛcchati. kāyādhiṣṭhānam iti. kāyālambanam ity arthaḥ. yasya hi kāyaḥ pravartyaḥ. tat kāyādhiṣṭhānaṃ karma. tenāha. yā cetanā kāyasya tatratatra pranetrīti. yathāyogaṃ veditavye iti. vāgadhiṣṭhānaṃ karma vākkarma. manaskarma tu manasaḥ karma. manasā vā saṃprayuktaṃ karma manaskarma. tena yathāyogam ity uktaṃ. vijñaptyabhāvād iti vistaraḥ. yadi vijñaptir na syāt. avijñaptir api kāmāvacarī na syāt. vijñaptyadhīnā hi kāmāvacary avijñaptir na cittānuparivartinīti. sā caivaṃ nāstīti. mahānto doṣā anuṣajyante. samvarāsamvarābhāvadoṣaḥ saptaupadhikapuṇyakriyāvastupuṇyavṛddhyabhāvadoṣa ity evam ādayo 'nuṣaṃgāḥ. anuṣaṃgāṇāṃ punaḥ pratyanuṣaṃgā iti. tatparihārā bhaviṣyantīti arthaḥ. kāyakarmasaṃśabditād iti. kāyādhiṣṭhānād ity arthaḥ. samāhitāvijñaptivad iti. yathā samāhitāvijñaptiś [Tib. 9b] cittānuparivartinī. evaṃ prātimokṣasamvarādilakṣaṇāpy avijñaptiḥ syāt. sautrāntikā āhuḥ. naivaṃ bhaviṣyati. na cittānuparivartinī bhaviṣyati. cetanāviśeṣeṇāsamāhitena tadākṣepaviśeṣād asamāhitāyā avijñapter ākṣepād ity arthaḥ. sāpi ca vijñaptir bhavadīyā satī vidyamānā avijñapter ākṣepe utpādanacetanāyā balaṃ sāmarthyaṃ nibhālayate apekṣate. kasmāt. jaḍatvād apaṭutvāc cetanābalam antareṇa tām avijñaptiṃ janayituṃ na śaknoti. na hy asatyāṃ samādānacetanāyāṃ yadṛcchotpannā vijñaptir avijñaptiṃ janayati.
body.translated_text: 'Therein, your honors' — meaning: those of you. 'They are seen from the other [sides] too' — because of this statement. 'How do they designate bodily action (<s>kāyakarma</s>)?' — thinking that bodily action (<s>kāyakarma</s>) exists as a conventional entity, he asks. 'Governed by the body' (<s>kāyādhiṣṭhāna</s>) — meaning: having the body as its object. For that whose body is to be directed — that action is governed by the body. Therefore he says: 'that volition (<s>cetanā</s>) which directs the body here and there.' 'To be understood as appropriate' — action governed by speech is verbal action. But mental action is action of the mind, or action associated with mind — hence mental action. Therefore it is said 'as appropriate.' 'Because of the absence of informative action (<s>vijñapti</s>)' — and so forth in detail. If informative action did not exist, non-informative action (<s>avijñapti</s>) belonging to the Desire Realm would also not exist. For non-informative action belonging to the Desire Realm depends on informative action, not following the mind. And if it thus does not exist, great faults follow — the fault of the absence of restraint and non-restraint, the fault of the absence of increase of merit in the seven bases of meritorious action (<s>aupadhikapuṇyakriyāvastu</s>) — such and other consequences. 'And the consequences have further consequences' — meaning: there will be resolutions of those [consequences]. 'From what is designated as bodily action' — meaning: from what is governed by the body. 'Like the non-informative action of concentration' (<s>samāhitāvijñapti</s>) — just as the non-informative action of concentration follows the mind, so too the non-informative action characterized by <s>prātimokṣa</s> restraint and the like would [follow the mind]. The <s>Sautrāntika</s>s say: it will not be so — it will not follow the mind. Through a specific volition in the non-concentrated [state], because of the specific impetus from that — through the impetus of the non-concentrated non-informative action — this is the meaning. And that informative action of yours, being existent, being present, looks to, depends on, the power and capacity of the undertaking volition for the production of non-informative action. Why? Because of inertness — because of incapacity, it cannot generate that non-informative action without the power of the volition. For in the absence of the undertaking volition, an informative action that has arisen spontaneously does not generate non-informative action.

body.text: iti. tuśabdo viśeṣaṇena. yathā kāyavijñaptiḥ saṃsthānātmikā na tathā vāgvijñaptiḥ. kiṃ tarhi. vāgātmako dhvanir varṇātmakaḥ śabda ity arthaḥ.
body.translated_text: the word 'but' (<s>tu</s>) indicates a distinction. Unlike bodily informative action, which has the nature of shape, vocal informative action is not so. What then? Sound (<s>dhvani</s>) having the nature of speech — meaning: a sound having the nature of articulate syllables (<s>varṇa</s>).

children.text:
avijñaptiḥ pūrvam evokteti.
te tu vijñaptyavijñapti
children.translated_text: 'Non-informative action (<s>avijñapti</s>) has been stated before' — 'those two, informative and non-informative action' —

body.text: ity uktaṃ. tatra vijñaptir uktā avijñaptir vaktavyā. sā ca pūrvam evoktā.
body.translated_text: this was stated. Therein, informative action has been explained; non-informative action is to be explained. And it was explained before [in the text].

children.translated_text: 'Of one who is distracted or without mind' —

body.text: vacanāt. sāpi dravyato nāsti sāpy avijñaptir dravyato nāsti. na kevalā vijñaptir ity apiśabdaḥ. abhyupetyākaraṇamātratvād [Tib. 10a] iti. imaṃ divasaṃ upādāya prāṇātipātādibhyaḥ prativiramāmīty abhyupetya. tasmāt pareṇa teṣām akaraṇamātram avijñaptir ity evaṃ dravyato nāstīti sautrāntikāḥ. teṣāṃ cātītānāṃ mahābhūtānāṃ. na hy atītānāṃ pratyutpannasvabhāvo 'sti. paṃcame ca kośasthāna etad darśayiṣyata iti. katham avidyamānāny asyā āśraya ity ato na dravyato 'sti. rūpalakṣaṇabhāvāc ca. rūpyata iti rūpalakṣaṇaṃ. tac cāsyā apratighatvān nāsti. tasmān na dravyato 'sti.
body.translated_text: because of this statement. That too — that non-informative action too — does not exist as a substance. Not only informative action — the word 'too' (<s>api</s>) [indicates this]. 'Because it is merely the non-performance of what has been undertaken' — having undertaken from this day onward 'I shall refrain from killing living beings and the like,' from that [moment] onward, the mere non-performance of those [acts] is non-informative action — thus it does not exist as a substance, according to the <s>Sautrāntika</s>s. 'And of those past great elements' — for past [great elements] do not have a present nature. And this will be shown in the fifth chapter (<s>kośasthāna</s>). How can non-existent [great elements] be its support? Therefore it does not exist as a substance. 'And because of the [absence of the] characteristic of form (<s>rūpa</s>)' — the characteristic of form is being affected (<s>rūpyate</s>). And this [characteristic] is absent for it because of being without resistance (<s>apratighatva</s>). Therefore it does not exist as a substance.

body.text: (IV.5ab)
body.translated_text: (IV.5ab)

body.text: vistaraḥ. trividhaṃ ca tad amalaṃ ca trividhāmalarūpaṃ. tasyoktiḥ. akurvataḥ panthā akurvatpathaḥ. pareṇa kārayataḥ svayam akurvataḥ karma ity arthaḥ. trividhāmalarūpoktiś ca vṛddhiś cākurvatpathaś cādir eṣāṃ. tānīmāni
body.translated_text: and so forth in detail. It is threefold and it is pure (<s>amala</s>) — [hence] the pure form of three kinds. Its statement — the path of one who does not act (<s>akurvatpathaḥ</s>). Action of one who does not act himself but has another perform it — this is the meaning. The statement of the pure form of three kinds, and the increase, and the path of one who does not act — these are the beginnings of those. These are:

children.translated_text: the statement of pure form of three kinds, the increase, the path of one who does not act, and the rest.

body.text: ādiśabdena dharmo bhikṣo ity atrārūpīty avacanaṃ. āryāṣṭāṃgavacanaṃ. prātimokṣasamvarasetuvacanaṃ ca gṛhyate. rūpasya rūpasaṃgraha iti. rūpasya rūpeṇaiva saṃgraho bhavati. nānyair vedanādibhiḥ. asti rūpaṃ sanidarśanaṃ sapratighaṃ. yac cakṣurvijñānavijñeyaṃ rūpam. [Tib. 10b] asty anidarśanaṃ sapratighaṃ. yāni cakṣurādīni. tat punar nava rūpyāyatanāni. asti rūpam anidarśanam apratighaṃ. yan manovijñānavijñeyaṃ avijñaptirūpaṃ dharmāyatanasaṃgṛhītaṃ. nāvijñaptiṃ virahayyeti vistaraḥ. avijñaptiṃ muktvā nāsti rūpam anidarśanam apratighaṃ yad rūpasaṃgrahasūtra uktaṃ. nāpy anāsravam asti rūpam avijñaptiviraheyyeti vartate. na hi mārgasatyasamāpannasya kāyavāgvijñaptirūpaṃ yujyate. saptabhir aupadhikair iti. upadhir ārāmavihārādiḥ. tatrabhavam aupadhikaṃ. tasyopadher abhāvān niraupadhikaṃ. satatam abhīkṣṇaṃ. samitaṃ nirantaraṃ. atra sūtraṃ. bhagavān kauśāṃbyāṃ viharati sma. ghoṣirārāme. athāyuṣmān mahācundo
body.translated_text: By the word 'and the rest,' the non-mention of 'formless' in '<s>dharma</s>, O monk' [is grasped]; the statement of the Noble Eightfold [Path]; and the statement of the <s>prātimokṣa</s> restraint as a bridge are grasped. 'The inclusion of form by form' — form is included by form alone, not by others such as feeling and the rest. There is form that is visible and has resistance — that form which is cognized by visual consciousness. There is [form that is] invisible yet has resistance — the eye and the rest. And that [latter] is the nine form sense-bases. There is form that is invisible and without resistance — the non-informative form (<s>avijñaptirūpa</s>) that is cognized by mental consciousness, included in the <s>dharma</s> sense-base. 'Not excluding non-informative action' — and so forth in detail. Excluding non-informative action, there is no form that is invisible and without resistance as stated in the <s>Rūpasaṃgraha Sūtra</s>. Nor is there outflow-free (<s>anāsrava</s>) form excluding non-informative action — this is the continuation. For it is not fitting that there be bodily or verbal informative form for one who has attained the truth of the path. 'Through seven bases' (<s>saptaupadhika</s>) — a base (<s>upadhi</s>) is a park, monastery, and the like. What belongs to such a base is <s>aupadhika</s>. Because of the absence of that base, [it is] without base (<s>niraupadhika</s>). 'Constantly' means always. 'Continuously' means without interruption. Here is a <s>sūtra</s>: the Blessed One was dwelling in <s>Kauśāmbī</s>, in the <s>Ghoṣira</s> park. Then the venerable <s>Mahācunda</s>

body.text: yena bhagavāṃs tenopasaṃkrāntaḥ. upasaṃkramya bhagavataḥ pādau śirasā vanditvā ekānte 'sthāt. ekānte sthita āyuṣmān mahācundo bhagavantam etad avocat. labhyaṃ bhadanta aupadhikaṃ puṇyakriyāvastu prajñapayituṃ mahāphalaṃ mahānuśaṃsaṃ mahādyutikaṃ mahāvaistārikaṃ. labhyaṃ cundeti bhagavāṃs tasyāvocat. saptemāni cundaupadhikāni puṇyakriyāvastūni mahāphalāni yāvan mahāvaistārikāṇi. [Tib. 11a] yaiḥ samanvāgatasya śrāddhasya kulaputrasya vā kuladuhitur vā carato vā tiṣṭhato vā svapato vā jāgrato vā satatasamitam abhivardhata eva puṇyam upajāyata eva puṇyaṃ. katamāni sapta. iha cunda śrāddhaḥ kulaputro vā kuladuhitā vā cāturdiśāya bhikṣusaṃghāyārāmaṃ pratipādayati. idaṃ cunda prathamam aupadhikaṃ puṇyakriyāvastu mahāphalaṃ yāvan mahāvaistārikaṃ. yena samanvāgatasya kulaputrasya vā vistareṇa yāvad upajāyata eva puṇyaṃ. punar aparaṃ cunda śrāddhaḥ kulaputro vā kuladuhitā vā tasminn evārāme vihāraṃ pratiṣṭhāpayati. idaṃ dvitīyam aupadhikaṃ puṇyakriyāvastu mahāphalaṃ yāvad upajāyata eva puṇyaṃ. punar aparaṃ cunda śrāddhaḥ kulaputro vā kuladuhitā vā tasminn eva vihāre śayanāsanaṃ prayacchati. tadyathā. mañcaṃ pīṭhaṃ bṛṣīṃ koccavaṃ bimbopadhānaṃ caturaśrakaṃ dadāti. idaṃ cunda tṛtīyam aupadhikaṃ puṇyakriyāvastu pūrvavat. punar aparaṃ cunda śrāddhaḥ kulaputro kuladuhitā vā tasminn eva vihāre dhruvabhikṣāṃ prajñāpayaty anukūlayajñām. idaṃ cunda caturtham aupadhikaṃ puṇyakriyāvastu mahāphalaṃ pūrvavat. punar aparaṃ cunda śrāddhaḥ kulaputro vā kuladuhitā vā āgantukāya gamikāya vā dānaṃ dadāti. idaṃ cunda paṃcamam aupadhikaṃ [Tib. 11b] puṇyakriyāvastu pūrvavat. punar aparaṃ cunda śrāddhaḥ kulaputro vā kuladuhitā vā glānāya glānopasthāyakāya vā dānaṃ dadāti. idaṃ. ṣaṣṭham aupadhikaṃ puṇyakriyāvastu pūrvavat. punar aparaṃ cunda śrāddhaḥ kulaputro vā kuladuhitā vā yās tā bhavanti śītalikā vā vaddalikā vā vātalikā vā varṣalikā vā. tadrūpāsu śītalikāsu yāvad varṣalikāsu bhaktāni vā tarpaṇāni vā yavāgūpānāni vā tāni saṃghāyābhinirhṛtyānuprayacchati. idam āryā asmākam anārdragātrāḥ anabhivṛṣṭacīvarāḥ paribhujya sukhaṃ sparśaṃ viharaṃtu. idaṃ ca cunda saptamam aupadhikaṃ puṇyakriyāvastu mahāphalaṃ. yāvad upajāyata eva puṇyam. ebhiḥ saptabhir aupadhikaiḥ puṇyakriyāvastubhiḥ samanvāgatasya śrāddhasya kulaputrasya vā kuladuhitur vā na labhyaṃ puṇyasya pramāṇam udgrahītuṃ. etāvat puṇyaṃ vā puṇyaphalaṃ vā puṇyavipākaṃ vā. api tu bahutvāt puṇyasya mahāpuṇyaskaṃdha iti saṃkhyāṃ
body.translated_text: he approached the <s>Bhagavān</s>. Having approached, he bowed his head at the feet of the <s>Bhagavān</s> and stood to one side. Standing to one side, the venerable <s>Mahācunda</s> said this to the <s>Bhagavān</s>: 'Is it possible, Venerable Sir, to designate a basis of meritorious action that is material (<s>aupadhika</s>), of great fruit, great benefit, great radiance, and great extent?' 'It is possible, <s>Cunda</s>' — thus the <s>Bhagavān</s> spoke to him. 'There are, <s>Cunda</s>, seven material bases of meritorious action, of great fruit, up to great extent, possessing which, whether walking, standing, sleeping, or waking, for a faithful son or daughter of good family, merit constantly and continuously increases, merit constantly arises. What are the seven? Here, <s>Cunda</s>, a faithful son or daughter of good family offers a monastery to the <s>Saṃgha</s> of the four directions.
