body.text: pratikūlaṃ hi duḥkham iti lakṣaṇān mārgo na duḥkham iti. kim idam anyad evocyate. pūrvam uktaṃ pratyayābhisaṃskaraṇāt sarvasaṃskārā anityāḥ. yac cānityaṃ. tad duḥkham iti. mārgaś ca pratyayābhisaṃskṛtatvād anityaḥ. tasmād duḥkham iti prasajyet. yadi hi pratikūlataiva duḥkhalakṣaṇam iṣyet. tat pūrvoktam alakṣaṇaṃ syāt. tac ced duḥkhatālakṣaṇam. idam alakṣaṇam iti. naiṣa doṣaḥ. kathaṃ. yad anityam āryāṇāṃ pratikūlaṃ. tad duḥkham ity ayam atrābhipreto 'rthaḥ. kiṃ cānityam āryāṇāṃ pratikūlaṃ yat sāsravaṃ vastu. kasmāt punar anāsravo mārgas tathaivānityo 'pi na cāryāṇāṃ pratikūla [Tib. 176b] ity ata āha. na hi tasyotpāda āryāṇāṃ pratikūlaḥ sarvaduḥkhakṣayāvāhanād iti. aviśeṣābhidhāne 'pi hi loke viśeṣapratipattir dṛṣṭā. tadyathā gamanād gauḥ na ca gamanān mahiṣo 'pi gaur bhavati. evaṃ hy arthe niyate gauḥ [kāsmiṃcid bhavati.] kasmād bhavati. yasmāt gacchatīti. evam ihāpi yat sāsravaṃ vastu. tat pratikūlam āryāṇāṃ. kasmāt. anityatvād iti. yad eva duḥkhato dṛṣṭam iti. sāsravaṃ vastu. tasyaiva nirodhaṃ śāṃtataḥ paśyaṃti. na mārgasyety avagaṃtavyaṃ. mudgādibhāve 'pi māṣarāśyapadeśavad iti. māṣarāśau mudgamasūrakalāyādisadbhāve 'py alpatvān mudgādīnāṃ māṣarāśir iti loke vyapadeśo dṛśyate. tadvat. pariṣekasukhāṇukeneti. sukhaṃ ca tad aṇukaṃ ca sukhāṇukaṃ. pariṣekeṇa sukhāṇukaṃ pariṣekasukhāṇukaṃ. tenāha khalv apīti. bhadankakaumāralātaḥ duḥkhasaṃtatyāṃ.
body.translated_text: 'For what is contrary (<s>pratikūla</s>) is suffering' — by this definition, the path is not suffering. 'Is something else being said here?' Previously it was said: 'because of being conditioned by conditions, all conditioned things are impermanent; and what is impermanent is suffering' — and the path, being conditioned by conditions, is impermanent; therefore it would follow that it is suffering. If indeed contrariness alone is accepted as the definition of suffering, then the previously stated [definition] would be no definition. And if that is no definition of suffering, this too would be no definition. 'There is no fault here.' How? 'What is impermanent is contrary to the nobles — that is suffering' — this is the intended meaning here. And what that is impermanent is contrary to the nobles? — that which is a contaminated entity (<s>sāsrava vastu</s>). 'Why then is the uncontaminated path, even though equally impermanent, not contrary to the nobles?' — therefore he says: 'For its arising is not contrary to the nobles, because it brings about the cessation of all suffering.' Even though in the world, despite a general statement, a specific understanding is seen — just as 'a cow, because of going (<s>gamana</s>)' — but a buffalo too goes, yet a buffalo does not become a cow. For 'cow' applies to a fixed referent. How does it apply? Because it goes (<s>gacchati</s>). Likewise here too: what is a contaminated entity — that is contrary to the nobles. Why? Because of impermanence. 'What was seen as suffering' — the contaminated entity. Of that very thing they see the cessation as peaceful — not of the path — this should be understood. 'Like the designation of a heap of <s>māṣa</s>-beans even when <s>mudga</s>-beans and the rest are present' — even when <s>mudga</s>-beans, lentils, peas, and the rest are present in a heap of <s>māṣa</s>-beans, because of the smallness of the <s>mudga</s>-beans and the rest, the designation 'heap of <s>māṣa</s>-beans' is seen in the world; likewise. 'With a trifle of pleasure from sprinkling' — it is pleasant and it is trifling — hence 'a trifle of pleasure.' A trifle of pleasure from sprinkling — hence 'a trifle of pleasure from sprinkling.' Therefore he says '<s>kila</s>' — Venerable <s>Kaumāralāta</s>, in the continuum of suffering,

children.translated_text: 'and because of being the cause of suffering' —

body.text: iti. sukhaṃ duḥkhasya hetur duḥkhavedanīyena karmaṇā saṃprayuktatvād iti.
body.translated_text: thus. Pleasure is the cause of suffering, because of being associated with <s>karma</s> to be experienced as suffering.

children.translated_text: And because of being accompanied by not a few sufferings.

body.text: yasmāc cātibahubhir duḥkhaiḥ parasevākṛtyādikṛtaiḥ samuditaṃ sukham [Tib. 177a] utpadyate.
body.translated_text: Because pleasure arises accompanied by extremely many sufferings caused by serving others, performing duties, and the like.

children.translated_text: And because of the desire for it when suffering exists.

body.text: yasmāc ca kṣutpipāsādikṛte duḥkhe sati. bhojanapānādikṛtaṃ sukhaṃ iṣṭaṃ. nānyathā. ata ebhyaḥ kāraṇebhyo
body.translated_text: Because when suffering caused by hunger, thirst, and the like exists, pleasure produced by food, drink, and the like is desired — not otherwise. Therefore, from these reasons,

children.translated_text: they determine that pleasure is suffering.

body.text: sahaiva tu sukheneti. tuśabdaḥ pūrvapakṣavyāvartanārthaḥ. saṃskāraduḥkhataikarasatvād iti. saṃskāṛaduḥkhataikaprakāratvāt. katham idānīṃ sukhasvabhāvām iti. katham aduḥkhasvabhāvāṃ vedanāṃ duḥkhataḥ paśyaṃti. anityatayā pratikūlatvād iti. anityatvāt pratikūlaṃ pratikūlatvād duḥkhataḥ paśyaṃtīty
body.translated_text: 'But together with pleasure itself' — the word 'but' (<s>tu</s>) is for the purpose of departing from the prior position. 'Because of being of one flavor with the suffering of conditioned things (<s>saṃskāraduḥkhatā</s>)' — because of being of one type with the suffering of conditioned things. 'How then, the one whose own-nature is pleasure' — how do they see as suffering a feeling whose own-nature is not suffering? 'Because of being adverse due to impermanence' — because of being impermanent, it is adverse; because of being adverse, they see it as suffering — this is

body.text: arthaḥ. yathā rūpasaṃjñādīny apīti. yathā rūpasaṃjñāsaṃskāravijñānāny api duḥkhataḥ paśyaṃti. na ca tāny evaṃ duḥkhāni. yathā duḥkhā vedanā. tasyā upaghātakasvabhāvatvāt. teṣāṃ vā tallakṣaṇatvāt. yas tu manyata iti bhadantakumāralātaḥ. tasya bhadantasyāsau samudayākāraḥ syān na duḥkhākāraḥ. duḥkhahetuto darśanāt. kiṃ cāryāṇāṃ cānāgāmināṃ rūpārūpyopapattau kathaṃ duḥkhasaṃjñā pravartate. naiva pravartate ity arthaḥ. na hi teṣām anāgāmināṃ duḥkhavedanāhetuḥ duḥkhāyā vedanāyā hetuḥ. [Tib. 177b] ke. skaṃdhā rūpārūpyāvacarāḥ. kasmān na hetuḥ. punar duḥkhasthānānāgamanāt. saṃskāraduḥkhata ca sūtre kim artham uktā bhaved iti. yadi duḥkhahetutvāt sukham api duḥkhataḥ paśyaṃti. yeyaṃ saṃskāraduḥkhatoktā yad anityaṃ. tad duḥkham iti. sā kiṃprayojanā duḥkhahetutvenaiva tatprayojanasiddheḥ. duḥkhahetuvādy āha. yadi tarhīti. yadi yad anityaṃ. tad duḥkham ity anityatvād duḥkhataḥ paśyaṃti na duḥkhahetutvād anityaduḥkhākārayoḥ kaḥ prativiśeṣaḥ.
body.translated_text: the meaning. 'Just as form, perception, and the rest too' — just as they see form, perception, formations, and consciousness too as suffering. Yet those are not suffering in the way that painful feeling is suffering — because that [painful feeling] has the own-nature of afflicting. Or because those [other aggregates] have that characteristic [of conditioned suffering]. 'But he who thinks' — this is Venerable <s>Kumāralāta</s>. For that Venerable, this would be an aspect of origination, not an aspect of suffering — because of seeing from the perspective of being a cause of suffering. Moreover, for Noble <s>Anāgāmins</s>, upon rebirth in the Form and Formless [Realms], how does the perception of suffering operate? It does not operate at all — this is the meaning. For their aggregates belonging to the Form and Formless Realms are not the cause of painful feeling — that is, not the cause of painful feeling. Which [aggregates]? The aggregates belonging to the Form and Formless Realms. Why are they not the cause? Because of not again reaching a place of suffering. 'And what would be the purpose of stating the suffering of conditioned things (<s>saṃskāraduḥkhatā</s>) in the <s>sūtra</s>?' — if they see even pleasure as suffering because of its being a cause of suffering, then this statement of the suffering of conditioned things — 'whatever is impermanent, that is suffering' — what purpose would it serve, since the purpose would be accomplished by being a cause of suffering alone? The proponent of 'cause of suffering' says: 'If then' — if 'whatever is impermanent, that is suffering,' [meaning] they see it as suffering because of impermanence and not because of being a cause of suffering — what is the difference between the aspects of impermanence and suffering?

body.text: atrācārya āha. udayavyayadharmitvād iti vistaraḥ. yathā pratikūlatvād duḥkhaṃ. tathā tat pratipādayann āha. anityaṃ tu dṛśyamānaṃ pratikūlaṃ bhavatīty anityākāro duḥkhākāram ākarṣatīti. tad uktaṃ bhavati. yad idam uktaṃ yad anityaṃ. tad duḥkham iti. nākāraikatvād evam uktaṃ. apy tv anityaṃ tat sukhaṃ paśyatāṃ pratikūlaṃ bhavati. pratikūlatvād duḥkhataḥ paśyaṃtīti.
body.translated_text: Here the <s>Ācārya</s> says: 'Because of having the nature of arising and ceasing' — in detail. Just as it is suffering because of being adverse, so, explaining that, he says: 'But the impermanent, when seen, becomes adverse — thus the aspect of impermanence attracts the aspect of suffering.' This has been stated: what was said — 'whatever is impermanent, that is suffering' — it is not said because of the identity of aspects. Rather, that impermanent pleasure, for those who see it, becomes adverse. Because of being adverse, they see it as suffering.

body.text: ekīyā iti bhadaṃtaśrīlātādayaḥ. idam atra duḥkhasyeti. idam atra duḥkhasya lakṣaṇam ity arthaḥ. sukhā vedanā duḥkhato draṣṭavyeti. aparaṃ sūtrapadaṃ. śītoṣṇādaya [Tib. 178a] iti. ādiśabdenāmlamadhurādayo gṛhyaṃte. atyupayuktā atiparibhuktāḥ. akālopayuktāś ceti. tadyathā śītā hemaṃte uṣṇā gṛīṣme. samena veti. sukhahetunā. evam īryāpathavikalpe 'pi vaktavyam iti. ya eva hi śayanādaya iṣyaṃte sukhahetavaḥ. ta eveti sarvaṃ yāvad vyaktim āpadayaṃta iti vaktavyaṃ. duḥkhapratīkāre ca sukhabuddheḥ. kiṃ. nāsti sukhā vedaneti prakṛtaṃ. duḥkhavikalpe ca. kiṃ. sukhabuddheḥ. tathaiva nāsti sukhā vedaneti. duḥkhapratīkāre sukhabuddhiṃ pratipādayann āha. na hi tāvat sukham iti vistaraḥ. duḥkhavikalpeneti pratipādayann āha. duḥkhavikalpe ca bālā iti vistaraḥ. aṃsād aṃsaṃ bhāraṃ saṃcārayaṃto bhāravāhakā duḥkha evāvasthite bhārātikrāmaṇe sukham iti buddhim utpādayaṃti.
body.translated_text: 'Some' — Venerable <s>Śrīlāta</s> and others. 'This is the characteristic of suffering here' — the meaning is: this is the characteristic of suffering here. 'Pleasant feeling should be seen as suffering' — this is another <s>sūtra</s> passage. 'Cold, heat, and the like' — by the word 'and the like,' sour, sweet, and the rest are included. 'Excessively consumed' — excessively enjoyed. 'And consumed at the wrong time' — for example, cold in winter, heat in summer. 'Or by moderation' — by what is a cause of pleasure. 'Similarly, in the case of the variation of deportments too, it should be stated' — for the very lying down and the rest that are desired as causes of pleasure, they too — everything up to 'they become manifest' — should be stated. 'And because of the cognition of pleasure at the counteraction of suffering' — what [follows]? 'There is no pleasant feeling' — this is the topic under discussion. 'And in the case of variation of suffering' — what? 'Because of the cognition of pleasure' — similarly, there is no pleasant feeling. Explaining the cognition of pleasure at the counteraction of suffering, he says: 'For indeed pleasure is not' — in detail. And explaining [the cognition] through variation of suffering, he says: 'And in the variation of suffering, fools' — in detail. Porters shifting a load from shoulder to shoulder, while remaining in suffering itself at the transfer of the burden, generate the cognition of pleasure.

body.text: eṣa eva ca nyāya ity ācāryaḥ. anabhiprītaṃ bhavaty āryāṇām iti kāmasukhaṃ.
body.translated_text: 'This very reasoning' — says the <s>Ācārya</s>. 'That is not desired by the Nobles' — meaning: sensual pleasure (<s>kāmasukha</s>).

body.text: anyathānabhipretatvād iti. pramādapadatvādinākārāṃtareṇa. tadarthaṃ darśayann āha. yā hi vedaneti vistaraḥ. pramādapadam iti. kuśalapracyutikāraṇam ity arthaḥ. mahābhisaṃskārasādhyāṃ ca vipariṇāminīṃ ca. [Tib. 178b] samanaṃtaraduḥkhotpādinīm aduḥkhāsukhotpādinīṃ cety arthaḥ. nyūnarūpatvam āpannām iti vā. anityāṃ ca vināśinīṃ cety arthaḥ. na tu khalu svalakṣaṇākāreṇeti. anugrāhakasvalakṣaṇākāreṇa āryāṇām api hi sukhavedanānugrāhakebhya visaṃvādaḥ. yadi cāsau sukhā vedanā svenātmanānugrāhakātmanānabhipretā bhavet naiva tasyāṃ sukhāyāṃ vedanāyāṃ kasyacid rāgo bhavet. duḥkhavedanāvad ity abhiprāyaḥ. yato vairāgyārtham iti. yataḥ kāraṇāt vairāgyārtham ākārāṃtareṇāpi doṣavatīṃ paśyeyuḥ. anyathānāyāsenaiva rāgābhāvasiddheḥ vairāgyārthaṃ prayatno 'narthakaḥ syāt. uktaṃ cedaṃ bhagavateti sthavirānandavacanam evaitat sūtrapadaṃ. evaṃ hi so 'prakṣyad iti. yatkiṃcid veditam. idam atra duḥkhasyeti etad ayuktarūpaṃ vacanam iti paśyaṃ sthavirānandas tad eva pṛṣṭavān. yatkiṃcid veditam idam atra duḥkhasyeti viruddham eveti kṛtvā. yadi tu tisro vedanā ity etad ayuktarūpam adrakṣyat. tad evāprakṣyat kiṃ nu saṃdhāya bhagavatā bhāṣitaṃ tisro vedanā ity etad viruddham eveti kṛtvā. bhagavān [Tib. 179a] api caivaṃ vyākariṣyad idaṃ mayā saṃdhāya bhāṣitaṃ tisro vedanā iti. na tv evaṃ vyākariṣyat. saṃskārānityatām ānanda saṃdhāya mayā bhāṣitaṃ. saṃskāravipariṇāmatāṃ. yatkiṃcid veditam idam atra duḥkhasyeti. na tv evam āha. punaś ca tisṛṇāṃ vedanānāṃ vacanāt tasmāt saṃty eva svbhāvatas tisro vedanāḥ. idaṃ tu saṃdhāya mayā bhāṣitaṃ yatkiṃcid veditam idam atra duḥkhasyeti vedanād ābhiprāyikam etad vākyaṃ darśayati bhagavān. yatkiṃcid veditam atra duḥkhasyeti saṃskāravipariṇāmatābhiprāyāt. vipariṇāmānityadharmitvād iti. vipariṇāmadharmitvād anityadharmitvāc ca. vipariṇāmaḥ punar anyathātvaṃ. kāmaguṇā iti. iṣṭānāṃ rūpaśabdagandharasaspraṣṭavyānām iyaṃ saṃjñā. upapatter apīṣṭasya janmanaḥ saṃjñā. evam upapattiṃ alpasukhāṃ bahuduḥkhām ekāṃtasukhāṃ paśyato viparyāsaḥ.
body.translated_text: 'Because of not being desired for another reason' — through another aspect, such as being a ground of heedlessness (<s>pramādapada</s>) and the rest. Explaining the purpose of that, he says: 'For that feeling which' — in detail. 'Ground of heedlessness' — meaning: a cause of falling away from the wholesome. 'And that which is to be achieved through great exertion (<s>mahābhisaṃskāra</s>) and is subject to change (<s>vipariṇāmin</s>)' — and that which immediately produces suffering, and that which produces neither-suffering-nor-pleasure — this is the meaning. Or: that which has attained a diminished form — meaning: that which is impermanent and perishable. 'But not through its own-characteristic aspect' — even for the Nobles, there is no discordance from the own-characteristic aspect of pleasant feeling as nurturing. For if that pleasant feeling were not desired through its own nature, through its nurturing nature, then no one at all would have passion for that pleasant feeling — like painful feeling — this is the intent. 'Because for the purpose of dispassion' — because, for the reason that it is for the purpose of dispassion, they would see it as faulty through another aspect too. Otherwise, since the absence of passion would be accomplished effortlessly, effort for the purpose of dispassion would be purposeless. 'And the <s>Bhagavān</s> has said this' — this is the very <s>sūtra</s> passage of Elder <s>Ānanda</s>. 'For he would have asked thus' — 'whatever is felt, this is the characteristic of suffering here' — seeing this as an unfitting statement, Elder <s>Ānanda</s> asked about that very thing — thinking 'whatever is felt, this is the characteristic of suffering here — this is contradictory.' But if he had seen 'there are three feelings' as unfitting, he would have asked that very thing — 'What did the <s>Bhagavān</s> intend when he said "there are three feelings"?' — thinking this is contradictory. And the <s>Bhagavān</s> too would have answered thus: 'I said this with an intention, [namely] there are three feelings.' But he did not answer thus. Rather: 'O <s>Ānanda</s>, I said this with the intention of the impermanence of conditioned things, with the intention of the changeability of conditioned things — whatever is felt, this is the characteristic of suffering here.' He did not say this. Moreover, from the statement of the three feelings, therefore indeed the three feelings exist intrinsically. 'But this was said with an intention, whatever is felt, this is the characteristic of suffering here' — through [the analysis of] feeling, the <s>Bhagavān</s> shows this statement to be intentional — 'whatever is felt is [a characteristic] of suffering here' — from the intention of the changeability of conditioned things. 'Because of having the nature of change and impermanence' — because of having the nature of change and the nature of impermanence. Change (<s>vipariṇāma</s>), moreover, is alteration. '<s>Kāmaguṇa</s>' (strands of sensual pleasure) — this is the designation for desired forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles. For the desired birth (<s>upapatti</s>) too, [it is] the designation. Thus, one who sees a birth that has little pleasure and much suffering as exclusively pleasurable has a distortion (<s>viparyāsa</s>).

body.text: lokānuvṛttyeti. cet. atha mataṃ lokasya vedanāṃ vyavasyato 'nuvṛttyā tisro vedanā iti vacanaṃ. tan na bhavati. sarvaveditaduḥkhatvasya saṃdhāya bhāṣitam iti bhagavato vacanāt. saṃskārānityatām ānanda mayā saṃdhāya bhāṣitaṃ saṃskāravipariṇāmatāṃ. yatkiṃcid veditam idam atra duḥkhasyety [Tib. 179b] ato na lokānuvṛttyā tisro vedanā iti vacanaṃ. kiṃ tarhi. svalakṣaṇato
body.translated_text: 'Following worldly convention' — objection. If it is held that the statement 'there are three feelings' is by following the conventions of the world that determines feelings — that is not the case. Because of the <s>Bhagavān</s>'s statement that the suffering-nature of all that is felt was spoken with an intention: 'O <s>Ānanda</s>, I spoke with the intention of the impermanence of conditioned things, the changeability of conditioned things — whatever is felt, this is the characteristic of suffering here.' Therefore, the statement 'there are three feelings' is not by following worldly convention. Then what? 'Having ascertained from their own-characteristics'

body.text: nidhāryety abhiprāyaḥ. yathābhūtavacanāc ca. na lokānuvṛttyā tisro vedanā iti vacanaṃ. katham ity āha. yac ca sukhendriyaṃ yac ca saumanasyendriyaṃ. sukhaiṣā vedanā draṣṭavyeti. vistareṇoktveti. yac ca duḥkhendriyaṃ yac ca daurmanasyendriyaṃ. duḥkhaiṣā vedanā. yad upakṣendriyam. aduḥkhāsukhaiṣā vedanā ity evaṃādinā vistareṇoktvā yenemāni paṃcendriyāṇy evaṃ yathābhūtaṃ samyakprajñayā dṛṣṭānīti. idam atra vedanātrayasadbhāve jñāpakaṃ. yathābhūtam ity adhyāropāpavādābhāvāt. loko 'pi ca kathaṃ duḥkhāṃ vedanāṃ trividhāṃ sukhāṃ duḥkhām aduḥkhāsukhāṃ vyavasyed duḥkhasvābhāvyena duḥkhavyavasāyasyaiva prāpteḥ. mṛdvadhimātramadhyāsv iti vistaraḥ. atha mataṃ mṛduni duḥkhe sukhabuddhir adhimātre duḥkhabuddhiḥ madhya aduḥkhāsukhabuddhir iti. atra brūmaḥ. sukhasyāpi trividhatvād iti vistaraḥ. [Tib. 180a] mṛdumadhyādhimātrabhedena mṛdvādiṣu duḥkheṣu mṛdumadhyādhimātreṣu. adhimātrādisukhabuddhiḥ syād adhimātramadhyamṛduḥ sukhabuddhiḥ syād ity arthaḥ. kathaṃ. mṛduni duḥkhe adhimātrasukhabuddhiḥ. madhye madhyasukhabuddhiḥ. adhimātre mṛdusukhabuddhir iti. na cādhimātre duḥkhe mṛdusukhabuddhir yuktā. kiṃ kāraṇaṃ. adhimātram eva tad duḥkhaṃ na syād yadi tatra mṛdusukhabuddhiḥ syāt. mṛduni ca duḥkhe yady adhimātrasukhabuddhiḥ kathaṃ tasya duḥkhasya mṛdutvaṃ. na hi tathā vyaktasyānubhavasya mṛdutvaṃ yujyata iti. aduḥkhāsukhānaṃtaraṃ sukhānubhavaṃ paśyann āha. yadā gaṃdharasaspraṣṭavyaviśeṣajam iti. madhyaṃ hi duḥkham aduḥkhāsukhaṃ bhavatāṃ. na mṛduprakāram. ato vaktavyaṃ. tadā katamad duḥkhaṃ mṛdubhūtaṃ yatrāsya sukhabuddhir bhavatīti. viṣayabalād eva hi tat sukham utpadyate. mṛduduḥkhasamanaṃtarapratyayabalād adhimātraduḥkhasamanaṃtarapratyayabalād veti. kiṃ ca yadi mṛduni duḥkhe sukhabuddhir iti manyase. anutpannavinaṣṭe ca tasmin mṛduni duḥkha iti. [Tib. 180b] anutpanne vinaṣṭe ca tasmin mṛduni duḥkhe. sutarāṃ sukhabuddhiḥ syāt aśeṣaduḥkhāpagamāt. yasmād aśeṣaṃ duḥkham apagataṃ. saśeṣāpagate 'pi hi duḥkhe sukhabuddhim icchasi. kim aṃgāśeṣāpagata ity abhiprāyaḥ. evaṃ kāmasukhasaṃmukhībhāve 'pi vaktavyam iti. yathā gandharasaspraṣṭavyaviśeṣajaṃ sukham uktam. evaṃ kāmasukhasaṃmukhībhāve 'pi vaktavyaṃ. katham. mṛduni rāgaduḥkhe kāmasukhabuddhir bhavati. anutpanne vinaṣṭe ca tasmin rāgaduḥkhe sutarāṃ kāmasukhaṃ syāt. na caivaṃ dṛṣṭam iti. kathaṃ ca nāmeti vistaraḥ. kathaṃ ca nāmaitad yokṣyate. yan mṛduni
body.translated_text: — this is the intent. 'And from the statement in accordance with reality' — the statement 'there are three feelings' is not by following worldly convention. How? — he says. 'That which is the pleasure faculty and that which is the mental-pleasure faculty — this feeling should be seen as pleasant' — and having stated in detail: 'that which is the pain faculty and that which is the mental-displeasure faculty — this feeling is painful; that which is the equanimity faculty — this feeling is neither-painful-nor-pleasant' — and so forth — 'by whom these five faculties are thus seen in accordance with reality, with right wisdom.' This is here the indication of the real existence of the three feelings. 'In accordance with reality' — because of the absence of superimposition and denial. 'But how would even the world determine a painful feeling as threefold — pleasant, painful, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant — by the nature of pain, the determination of suffering alone being appropriate?' In mild, middling, and intense [pain] — in detail. If it is held that in mild suffering there is a cognition of pleasure, in intense suffering a cognition of suffering, and in the middling a cognition of neither-suffering-nor-pleasure — to this we say: 'Because of the threefold nature of pleasure too' — in detail. In mild, middling, and intense sufferings, of the mild, middling, and intense divisions, there would be a cognition of intense, middling, and mild pleasure — the meaning is: in mild suffering there would be a cognition of intense pleasure, in middling [suffering] a cognition of middling pleasure, in intense [suffering] a cognition of mild pleasure. How? In mild suffering, a cognition of intense pleasure. In middling, a cognition of middling pleasure. In intense, a cognition of mild pleasure. But a cognition of mild pleasure in intense suffering is not fitting. For what reason? That intense suffering would not be [intense] if there were a cognition of mild pleasure in it. And if in mild suffering there is a cognition of intense pleasure, how is that suffering mild? For the mildness of an experience so manifest is not fitting. 'Seeing the experience of pleasure immediately after neither-painful-nor-pleasant [feeling],' he says: 'When produced from a special [contact with] odor, taste, tangible' — for the middling suffering is, for you, neither-painful-nor-pleasant — not of the mild type. Therefore it should be stated: 'then which suffering is the mild one, in which one has a cognition of pleasure?' For that pleasure arises by the power of the object alone — not by the power of the immediately-preceding condition of mild suffering, nor by the power of the immediately-preceding condition of intense suffering. Moreover, if you think that in mild suffering there is a cognition of pleasure: 'And when that mild suffering has not yet arisen or has perished' — when that mild suffering has not yet arisen or has perished, all the more should there be a cognition of pleasure, because of the departure of all suffering. For even when suffering with a remainder has departed, you accept a cognition of pleasure — how much more so when it has departed without remainder — this is the intent. 'Similarly, in the case of the approach of sensual pleasure too, it should be stated' — just as pleasure produced from a special [contact with] odor, taste, tangible was stated, so in the case of the approach of sensual pleasure too, it should be stated. How? In mild suffering-of-desire, there is a cognition of sensual pleasure. When that suffering-of-desire has not yet arisen or has perished, there should be sensual pleasure all the more. But this is not seen. 'And how indeed' — in detail. And how indeed will this be coherent — that in mild

body.text: vedite yan mṛduni duḥkha ity arthaḥ. tīvrānubhavo gṛhyata iti vaktavyaṃ. sukhaṃ gṛhyate. madhye punar avyakta iti. madhyaduḥkhe aduḥkhāsukhā vedanā gṛhyate ity arthaḥ. mṛduni duḥkhe tenāvyaktena bhavitavyam ity abhiprāyaḥ. triṣu ceti vistaraḥ. triṣu ca dhyāneṣu prathamadvitīyatṛtīyeṣu sukhavacanāt. sukhā vedanā tatreti sūtre vacanāt. mṛduduḥkhaṃ syāt. kiṃ kāraṇaṃ. mṛduni duḥkhe sukhabuddhir iti tavābhiprāyāt. ūrdhvaṃ caturthe dhyāne ārūpyeṣu cāduḥkhāsukhavacanāt [Tib. 181a] sūtre. madhyaṃ duḥkhaṃ syāt. kasmāt. madhye duḥkhe aduḥkhāsukham iti tavaivābhiprāyāt. ity ato na yujyate mṛdvādiṣu duḥkheṣu sukhādivedanāvyavasthānaṃ. kathaṃ hi nāmādhodhyāneṣu mṛdu duḥkham. ūrdhve punar madhyam iti yujyate. rūpaṃ cen mahānāmann iti. rūpaṃ cen mahānāmann ekāṃtaduḥkham abhaviṣyat na sukhaṃ na sukhānugataṃ na saumanasyaṃ na saumanasyānugataṃ na sukhaveditaṃ hetur api na prajñāyate rūpe saṃrāgāya. yasmāt tarhi asti rūpaṃ sukhaṃ sukhānugataṃ pūrvavad ato rūpe hetuḥ prajñāyate yad uta saṃrāgāyeti.
body.translated_text: 'felt' — the meaning is: what is mild suffering. 'Intense experience is apprehended' — it should be said that pleasure is apprehended. 'But the middle is indistinct' — the meaning is: in the case of middling suffering, neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is apprehended. The intent is: when suffering is mild, there must be that indistinctness. 'And in the three' — and so forth in detail. And in the three <s>dhyāna</s>s — the first, second, and third — because of the statement of pleasure. Because in the <s>sūtra</s> it states 'pleasant feeling exists therein.' It would be mild suffering. For what reason? Because of your own intent that 'in mild suffering there is the cognition of pleasure.' Above, in the fourth <s>dhyāna</s> and the formless realms, because of the statement of neither-painful-nor-pleasant in the <s>sūtra</s>, it would be middling suffering. Why? Because of your own intent that 'in middling suffering, [there is] neither-painful-nor-pleasant.' Therefore, the establishment of pleasant and other feelings in mild and other [degrees of] suffering is not tenable. For how can it be said that in the lower <s>dhyāna</s>s suffering is mild, while above it is middling? 'If form, O <s>Mahānāman</s>' — if form, O <s>Mahānāman</s>, were exclusively suffering — not pleasant, not accompanied by pleasure, not [a cause of] mental pleasure, not accompanied by mental pleasure, not pleasantly experienced — a cause would not be discerned for attachment to form. But since indeed form is pleasant, accompanied by pleasure, and so forth as before, therefore a cause is discerned for attachment to form.

body.text: sukhahetvavyavasthānād ity atra brūmaḥ. yadi sukhahetvavyavasthānān na sukham asti vaḥ. duḥkham apy asat syāt duḥkhahetvavyavasthānāt. api ca vyavasthita eva sukhahetuḥ. katham ity āha. āśrayaviśeṣāpekṣo hīti vistaraḥ. yadi hi kevala eva viṣayo hetuḥ syāt syād evāvyavasthito hetuḥ. na tu kevalo viṣayo hetuḥ. yasmād āśrayaviśeṣo 'pi hetur iti. sa evāgnir iti. tadyathā sa evāgniḥ pākyabhūtaviśeṣa [Tib. 181b] īṣatpakvāvasthe taṇḍulasamūhe svādupākahetur bhavati. abhimataudanapākahetutvāt. sa evāsvādupākahetuḥ. taddāhahetutvād ity arthaḥ. na tu yā pākyabhūtāvasthāṃ prāpya svādupākahetur āsīt. tāṃ punaḥ prāpya paścān na hetuḥ svādupākasya tādṛśasyety arthaḥ. eṣa dṛṣṭāṃtaḥ tasya pūrvoktasya dārṣṭāṃtikasyārthasya. dhyāneṣu ca kathaṃ na vyavasthitaḥ sukhahetur iti. na hi tad eva dhyānaṃ prathamaṃ yāvat tṛtīyaṃ cirakālam api samāpannānāṃ duḥkhahetur bhavatīti. dhyānaje ca sukhe kasya pratītkāra iti. na hi dhyāneṣu duḥkham astīti. ādiśabdenedam api vaktavyaṃ. yadi duḥkhapratīkāreṣu sukhabuddhiḥ syāt. rūpaṃ cen mahānāmann ekāṃtaduḥkham abhaviṣyat na sukhaṃ na sukhānugatam ity evamādi noktaṃ syād iti. sukham evotpadyata iti. sukhaiva sā vedanotpadyate. na sā duḥkhā vedanā sukhatvena kalpiteti. yāvad asau tādṛśī kāyāvastheti. sukhotpattyanukūlā. anyathā hi yady avasthāṃtarajaṃ sukham eva notpadyate yāvad asau
body.translated_text: 'Because of the non-establishment of a cause of pleasure' — to this we say: if, because of the non-establishment of a cause of pleasure, there is no pleasure for you, then suffering too would be non-existent, because of the non-establishment of a cause of suffering. Moreover, a cause of pleasure is indeed established. How? — he says: 'Because it depends on a special [condition of] the basis (<s>āśraya</s>)' — and so forth in detail. For if the object alone were the cause, the cause would indeed be unestablished. But it is not the object alone that is the cause, since the special [condition of] the basis too is a cause. 'That very fire' — just as that very fire, when a special material to be cooked is present — at the stage when the mass of rice is partially cooked — becomes the cause of delicious cooking, because of being the cause of cooking desirable rice. That same [fire] is the cause of non-delicious cooking, because of being the cause of burning. But it is not the case that what was the cause of delicious cooking when it reached the state of material to be cooked — that, upon reaching [that state] again later, is not a cause of such delicious cooking — this is the meaning. This is the illustration of the meaning of the aforementioned exemplified subject. And in the <s>dhyāna</s>s, how is the cause of pleasure not established? For that very <s>dhyāna</s>, from the first up to the third, does not become a cause of suffering even for those who have attained it for a long time. And regarding the pleasure born of <s>dhyāna</s>, what is there to counteract? For in the <s>dhyāna</s>s, suffering does not exist. By the word 'and so forth,' this too should be said: if there were the cognition of pleasure in what counteracts suffering, then 'if form, O <s>Mahānāman</s>, were exclusively suffering — not pleasant, not accompanied by pleasure' and so forth — this would not have been said. 'Pleasure itself arises' — that very feeling arises as pleasure. It is not that a painful feeling is imagined as pleasure. 'As long as that condition of the body [persists]' — [the condition] favorable to the arising of pleasure. For otherwise, if pleasure were not produced arising from another condition, as long as that

body.text: tādṛśī kāyāvasthā nāṃtarīyate. anyathā paścād bhūyasī sukhabuddhiḥ syāt. aṃte kuta iti vistaraḥ. atha mataṃ pānabhojanādyaṃte kuto duḥkhabuddhiḥ syāt yadi tasyāditatprāraṃbho nāsīd iti. atra brūmaḥ. kāyapariṇāmaviśeṣāt. [Tib. 182a] kāyasya tādṛśaḥ pariṇāmaviśeṣāḥ paścād utpadyate pānādyāsevanāt yat sukhotpattyavasthāyāṃ duḥkhaṃ notpadyate. aṃte tūtpadyata iti. kim evety āha. madyādīnām aṃte mādhuryaśuktatāvad iti. yathā madyakṣīrādīnāṃ tādṛśaḥ paścātpariṇāmavīśeṣo bhavati. yat pūrvaṃ madhuratāvasthāyāṃ mādhuryasyāvidyamānā śuktatā amlatā aṃte utpadyate. atha vā yathā madyādīnāṃ parīṇāmavīśeṣān mādhuryam eṣām ādau bhavati. āmlaṃ vā. tac cikitsauṣadhakṛtāt pariṇāmaviśeṣān mādhuryaṃ bhavati. pariṇāmaviśeṣād eva ca paścāc chuktatā. mādhuryam iha sukhasyodāharaṇaṃ. śuktatā duḥkhasyeti.
body.translated_text: condition of the body is not interrupted. Otherwise, later there would be an increasingly greater cognition of pleasure. 'Whence at the end?' — and so forth in detail. Now, if it is thought: at the end of drinking, eating, and the like, whence would there be a cognition of suffering if their initial undertaking was not [suffering]? — to this we say: because of a special transformation of the body. A special transformation of the body is subsequently produced from the excessive consumption of drink and the like, such that at the stage when pleasure arises, suffering does not arise. But at the end, it arises. What [is it] like? — he says: 'like the sweetness and sourness of wine and the like at the end.' Just as wine, milk, and the like undergo such a subsequent special transformation that the sourness — acidity — which was non-existent at the stage of sweetness before, arises at the end. Or alternatively, just as wine and the like, due to a special transformation, have sweetness at the beginning, or sourness. And that [sourness], through a special transformation caused by medical treatment, becomes sweetness. And from a special transformation itself, sourness comes about later. Here, sweetness is the illustration for pleasure, and sourness for suffering.

body.text: yat tu samudayasatyaṃ. tad evocyata iti. hetubhūtāḥ śamudayasatyam iti vacamāt. prathame vā kośasthāne
body.translated_text: 'But that which is the truth of origination (<s>samudayasatya</s>) — that very thing is stated.' Because of the statement that 'causes are the truth of origination.' Or, in the first chapter of the treatise:

body.text: iti vacanāt. śūtre hi tṛṣṇaivokteti. samudayasatyaṃ katamat. yāsau tṛṣṇā nandīrāgasahagatā tatratarābhinandinīti. vaibhāṣika āha. prādhānyād iti. anyatrānyasyāpi vacanāt. [Tib. 182b] anyatra sūtre anyasyāpi karmāvidyāder vacanād anye 'pi samudaya iti.
body.translated_text: because of this statement. 'For in the <s>sūtra</s>, only craving (<s>tṛṣṇā</s>) is stated.' 'What is the truth of origination? That craving (<s>tṛṣṇā</s>) which is accompanied by delight and passion, delighting here and there.' The <s>Vaibhāṣika</s> says: 'because of predominance.' Because in other <s>sūtra</s>s, others too — <s>karma</s>, ignorance (<s>avidyā</s>), and so forth — are stated, therefore others too are origination.

body.text: āyatyāṃ paraloka ity arthaḥ. punaś coktam anyatra śūtre. yataś ca bhikṣavaḥ paṃca bījajātāny akhaṇḍāni acchidrāṇī apūtīni avātātapahatāni navāni sārāṇi sukhaśayitāni. pṛthivīdhātuś ca bhavaty abdhātuś ca. evaṃ tāni bījāni vṛddhiṃ virūḍhin vipulatām āpadyaṃte. iti hi bhikṣava upameyaṃ kṛtā yāvad evāsyārthasya vijñaptaya itīmaṃ dṛṣṭāṃtam upanyasyedam uktaṃ. paṃca bījajātānīti bhikṣavaḥ sopādānasya vijñānasyaitad adhivacanaṃ pṛthivīdhātur iti catasṛṇāṃ vijñānasthitīnām etad adhivacanam iti. bījaṃ punar hetuḥ. yaś ca hetuḥ. sa samudayaḥ vijñānasthitayo 'pi pratiṣṭhāhetuḥ. tasmād iti. yataḥ karmādīnām api hetutvavacanāt samudayasatyatvaṃ siddhaṃ. tasmād ābhiprāyikaḥ. abhiprāye bhavaḥ abhiprāyeṇa vā dīvyatīty ābhiprāyikaḥ sūtre nirdeśaḥ tṛṣṇādhikṛtaṃ pudgalam adhikṛtya kṛta ity abhiprāyaḥ. lākṣaṇikas tv abhidharme lakṣaṇe bhavo lākṣaṇiko nirdeśo 'bhidharme. sarvaṃ sāsravaṃ vastu samudaya iti sāsravasya skaṃdhapaṃcakasya samudayasatyatvalakṣaṇayogāt. sa eva vaibhāṣikas tṛṣṇādīnām ābhiprāyikaṃ samudayasatyatvaṃ vivakṣur [Tib. 183a]
body.translated_text: the meaning is: in the next world, the other life. And it is further stated in another <s>sūtra</s>: 'In whatever way, O monks, the five classes of seeds are unbroken, unsplit, unrotted, undamaged by wind and sun, fresh, sound, and well-resting. If there is an earth element and a water element, then those seeds attain growth, sprouting, and abundance.' Thus, O monks, this simile is applied for the understanding of this very meaning. 'Five classes of seeds' — O monks, this is a designation for consciousness with clinging (<s>sopādāna vijñāna</s>). 'Earth element' is a designation for the four stations of consciousness (<s>vijñānasthiti</s>). Now, seed is the cause. And whatever is the cause, that is origination. The stations of consciousness too are causes of establishment. Therefore — since the statement of the causality of <s>karma</s> and the rest [establishes their] being the truth of origination. Therefore [the sūtra statement] is intentional (<s>ābhiprāyika</s>). That which is of the nature of intention, or that which is played [i.e., expressed] by intention — is intentional. The teaching in the <s>sūtra</s> is made with reference to a person dominated by craving — this is the intent. But the definitive (<s>lākṣaṇika</s>) [teaching] is in the <s>Abhidharma</s> — the teaching in the <s>Abhidharma</s> is definitive, being of the nature of definition. All contaminated things (<s>sāsrava vastu</s>) are origination — because the contaminated fivefold aggregates possess the characteristic of being the truth of origination. That same <s>Vaibhāṣika</s>, wishing to express the intentional nature of the truth of origination of craving and the rest

body.text: āha. api tv iti vistareṇa. abhinirvṛttihetuṃ bruvatā samudayasatyaṃ tṛṣṇaivoktā sūtre. upapattyabhinirvṛttihetuṃ sahetukaṃ bruvatā yāvat karma ca tṛṣṇā cāvidyā coktā. upapattihetuḥ karma. abhinirvṛttihetus tṛṣṇā bhaveṣu. tayoḥ punas taddhetvoḥ karmatṛṣṇayor avidyā hetur ity āha. katham etad gamyate. gāthāyām upapattihetuḥ karmābhinirvṛttihetus tṛṣṇeti. karma hetur upapattaye tṛṣṇā hetur abhinirvṛttaya iti sūtrāt. sūtrāṃtare vacanād iti. sahetusapratyaya iti vistaraḥ. atra sūtre krameṇa vā. kāraṇaparaṃparākrameṇa vā. gāthāyām eṣa nirdeśaḥ. karmatṛṣṇāvidyā saṃkārāṇāṃ cakṣurādīnāṃ hetur abhisaṃparāya iti. tad etad uktaṃ bhavati. karma hetur upapattaya iti. ato vā sūtrāt. sahetusapratyayakramasūtrād vā. ayaṃ īdṛśaḥ gāthārtha iti. kathaṃ cakṣur bhikṣavaḥ sahetu sapratyayaṃ sanidānaṃ. kaś ca bhikṣavaś cakṣuṣo hetuḥ kaḥ. pratyayaḥ. kiṃ nidanaṃ. cakṣuṣo bhikṣavaḥ karma hetuḥ. karma pratyayaḥ karma nidānaṃ. karmāpi bhikṣavaḥ sahetu sapratyayaṃ sanidānaṃ. kaś ca bhikṣavaḥ karmaṇo hetuḥ. kaḥ pratyayaḥ. kiṃ nidānaṃ. [Tib. 183b] karmaṇo bhikṣavas tṛṣṇā hetuḥ. tṛṣṇā pratyayaḥ. tṛṣṇā nidānaṃ. tṛṣṇā bhikṣavaḥ sahetukā sapratyayā sanidānā. kaś ca bhikṣavas tṛṣṇāyā hetuḥ. kaḥ pratyayaḥ. kiṃ nidānaṃ. tṛṣṇāyā bhikṣavo 'vidyā hetuḥ. avidyā pratyayḥ. avidyā nidānaṃ. avidyāpi bhikṣavaḥ sahetukā sapratyayā sanidānā. kaś ca bhikṣavo 'vidyāyā hetuḥ. kaḥ pratyayaḥ kiṃ nidanaṃ. avidyāyā bhikṣavaḥ ayoniśomanaskāro hetuḥ. ayoniśomanaskāraḥ pratyayaḥ. ayoniśomanaskāro nidānam iti. bījakṣetrabhāvaṃ pratipādayatā vijñānādayo 'py uktā vijñānaṃ bījaṃ. tasya kṣetraṃ vedanādayaḥ skandhāḥ. te 'py uktaḥ samudayasatyaṃ. na kevalaṃ tṛṣṇādaya ity ābhiprāyikaḥ sūtre nirdeśa iti sādhitaṃ. sarvasya ca duḥkhasya lākṣaṇikaḥ samudayabhāva iti. yonyādiprakārabhedeneti. ādiśabdena jātistrīpuruṣādiprakārabhedeneti gṛhyate. abhedeneti. dhātugatyyonyādīnāṃ. tayor yathākramam iti. upapatteḥ karma hetur abhinirvṛttes tṛṣṇeti. tadyathā bījam iti vistaraḥ. śālibījaṃ śālyaṃkuropapādanasya hetuḥ yavabījaṃ yavāṃkuropapādanasyetyādi. āpaḥ punar abhedena. yathā śālyaṃkuraprarohasya hetuḥ. evaṃ yavāṃkurasyāpītyādi. atas tāḥ sarvāṃkuraprarohamātrasya hetur iti vinā tṛṣṇayā janmābhāvād iti. atra sādhanaṃ. hetur janmanas [Tib. 184a] tṛṣṇā. tadbhāvābhāvabhāvyabhāvitvāt. takyathā bījam aṃkurasya. saṃtatināmanāc cety asyārthaṃ vivṛṇvann āha. yatra ca satṛṣṇeti vistaraḥ. yatra viṣaye rūpādau satṛṣṇā. kā. cittasaṃtatiḥ. tatrābhīkṣṇaṃ cittasaṃtatiṃ namaṃtīṃ paśyāmaḥ. tasnāt punarbhave 'py evam iti. punarbhave 'py evaṃ satṛṣṇā cittasaṃtatiḥ.
body.translated_text: says: 'But moreover' — and so forth in detail. When stating the cause of full production (<s>abhinirvṛtti</s>), only craving was stated in the <s>sūtra</s> as the truth of origination. When stating the cause of birth (<s>upapatti</s>) and full production together with their causes: <s>karma</s>, craving, and ignorance are stated. <s>Karma</s> is the cause of birth. Craving is the cause of full production in [various] existences. And ignorance is the cause of those two causes — <s>karma</s> and craving — he says. How is this understood? In the verse, '<s>karma</s> is the cause of birth, craving is the cause of full production' — from the <s>sūtra</s>: '<s>karma</s> is the cause of birth, craving is the cause of full production.' From the statement in another <s>sūtra</s>: 'with cause, with condition' — and so forth in detail. In this <s>sūtra</s>, either in sequence, or in the sequence of the chain of causes, the teaching is given in the verse: '<s>karma</s>, craving, and ignorance are the cause of the formations (<s>saṃskāra</s>) — the eye and the rest — in the future life.' This has been stated [as follows]: '<s>karma</s> is the cause of birth' — from this <s>sūtra</s>, or from the <s>sūtra</s> on 'with cause, with condition,' this is the meaning of the verse. How [does the sūtra go]? 'How, O monks, is the eye with cause, with condition, with basis? What, O monks, is the cause of the eye? What is the condition? What is the basis? Of the eye, O monks, <s>karma</s> is the cause, <s>karma</s> is the condition, <s>karma</s> is the basis. And <s>karma</s> too, O monks, is with cause, with condition, with basis. What, O monks, is the cause of <s>karma</s>? What is the condition? What is the basis? Of <s>karma</s>, O monks, craving is the cause, craving is the condition, craving is the basis. And craving, O monks, is with cause, with condition, with basis. What, O monks, is the cause of craving? What is the condition? What is the basis? Of craving, O monks, ignorance is the cause, ignorance is the condition, ignorance is the basis. And ignorance too, O monks, is with cause, with condition, with basis. What, O monks, is the cause of ignorance? What is the condition? What is the basis? Of ignorance, O monks, improper mental attention (<s>ayoniśomanaskāra</s>) is the cause, improper mental attention is the condition, improper mental attention is the basis.' By teaching the seed-and-field relationship, consciousness and the rest too are stated — consciousness is the seed, its field is the feeling and other aggregates. They too are stated as the truth of origination — not only craving and the rest — thus the intentional nature of the teaching in the <s>sūtra</s> is established. And all suffering has the definitive character of origination. 'By difference of type such as birth (<s>yoni</s>) and the rest' — by the word 'and the rest,' [we understand:] by difference of type such as birth-type (<s>jāti</s>), sex (<s>strīpuruṣa</s>), and the rest. 'Without differentiation' — of realm (<s>dhātu</s>), destiny (<s>gati</s>), birth-type, and the rest. 'Of these two, respectively' — <s>karma</s> is the cause of birth, craving is the cause of full production. 'Just as a seed' — and so forth in detail. A rice-seed is the cause for producing a rice-sprout; a barley-seed is the cause for producing a barley-sprout — and so forth. But water, without differentiation — just as it is the cause for the sprouting of a rice-sprout, so too for a barley-sprout and so forth. Therefore, that [water] is the cause merely of the sprouting of all sprouts. Because without craving there is no birth — this is the proof here. Craving is the cause of birth. Because its presence or absence determines existence or non-existence [of birth]. Just as a seed [is the cause] of a sprout. 'And from the designation of continuity' — explaining the meaning of this, he says: 'Where there is craving' — and so forth in detail. In whatever object — form and the rest — there is craving. Which [is this]? The mental continuum. Therein, we see the mental continuum repeatedly inclining. Therefore, in rebirth too, likewise — in rebirth too, the mental continuum with craving

body.text:
tasmāt tan namatīti. yatra ca namati. tatra ca pravartata iti vyavasyāmaḥ. sādhanaṃ cātra pravartate. punarbhave cittasaṃtatiḥ. satṛṣṇānamanāt. rūpādiviṣayavat. śuṣkamasūropasnānalepāṃgavad iti. masūra upasnānaṃ. tasya lepaḥ śuṣkaḥ. masūropasnānalepo 'syeti śuṣkamasūropasnānalepam aṃgaṃ. tadvad. yathā śuṣkeṇa masūropasnānalepenāgṛhītam aṃgaṃ. evaṃ tṛṣṇayātmabhāva iti darśitaṃ
bhavati. eṣā yuktir iti. tṛṣṇābhinirvṛttihetur iti.
body.translated_text: therefore, it inclines toward that. And wherever it inclines, there it proceeds — so we ascertain. And the proof here operates [as follows]: the mental continuum [proceeds] to rebirth, because of inclining with craving — like [its inclination toward] objects such as form. 'Like a body with dried lentil-poultice' — a lentil-poultice is a bathing application. Its coating [when] dry — 'one whose body has dry lentil-poultice-coating' — like that. Just as a body not covered by dry lentil-poultice coating — so is the self-existence [of a being] by craving — this has been shown. 'This is the argument' — that craving is the cause of full production.

body.text: (VI.4) atrārthe dve api satya iti satyaprasaṃgenedam ucyate.
body.translated_text: (VI.4) 'In this matter, both truths' — this is said by way of connection with the truths (<s>satya</s>).

body.text: iti. dṛṣṭāṃṭadvayopanyāso bhedadvayopapradarśanārthaḥ. upakramabhedinaś ca ghāṭādayaḥ. buddhibhedinaś ca jalādaya iti. jalādiṣūpakrameṇa rasādyapakarṣaṇānupapatteḥ. atha vā dvividhā saṃvṛtiḥ. [Tib. 184b] saṃvṛtyaṃtaravyapāśrayā dravyāṃtaravyapāśrayā ca. tatra yāsau saṃvṛtyaṃtaravyapāśrayā. tasyāṃ bhedo 'pi saṃbhavati anyāpoho 'pi. yā tv asau dravyāṃtaravyapāśrayā. tasyām anyāpoha eva saṃbhavati na bhedaḥ. na hi paramāṇor aṣṭadravyakasyāvayavaviśleṣaḥ śakyate kartum iti. saṃvṛtisad iti. saṃvyavahāreṇa sat. paramārthasad iti. paramārthena sat. svalakṣaṇa sad ity arthaḥ. evaṃ vedanādyo 'pi draṣṭavyā iti. vedanācetanāsaṃjñādayo 'pi dravyasaṃta eva draṣṭavyāḥ. kathaṃ. vedanādīn dharmān apohya buddhyā vedanāsvabhāve buddhir bhavatīti. dravyasatī vedanā. evaṃ saṃjñācetanādayo 'pi yojyāḥ. ghaṭaś cāṃbu cāstīti bruvaṃtaḥ satyam evāhuḥ. na mṛṣeti. saṃvṛtisatyasya vacane prayojanaṃ darśayati. uktaṃ ca.
body.translated_text: thus. The presentation of two examples is for the purpose of showing two types of dissolution. Pots and the like are dissolved by physical effort. Water and the like [are dissolved] by cognition — because in water and the like, the extraction of taste and the rest through physical effort is not possible. Or alternatively, conventional [reality] (<s>saṃvṛti</s>) is twofold: that dependent on another convention, and that dependent on another substance. Therein, that which is dependent on another convention — in that, both dissolution and exclusion of others are possible. But that which is dependent on another substance — in that, only exclusion of others is possible, not dissolution. For it is not possible to separate the parts of an atom consisting of eight substances. 'Conventionally existent' (<s>saṃvṛtisat</s>) — existing by convention (<s>saṃvyavahāra</s>). 'Ultimately existent' (<s>paramārthasat</s>) — existing ultimately. The meaning is: existing by own-characteristic (<s>svalakṣaṇa</s>). 'Thus feeling and the rest too should be seen' — feeling, volition (<s>cetanā</s>), perception, and the rest too should be seen as existent as substances (<s>dravya</s>). How? When one excludes <s>dharma</s>s such as feeling and the rest through cognition, there is a cognition of the own-nature of feeling — thus feeling is a real substance (<s>dravyasat</s>). Perception, volition, and the rest should be connected similarly. 'Those who say "the pot exists and water exists" speak truly — not falsely' — he shows the purpose of speaking of conventional truth (<s>saṃvṛtisatya</s>). And it has been stated:

children.text:
dve satye samupāśritya buddhānāṃ dharmadeśanā.
lokasaṃvṛtisatyaṃ ca satyaṃ ca paramārthata
children.translated_text:
'Relying on the two truths, the <s>dharma</s>-teaching of the <s>Buddha</s>s:
the truth of worldly convention (<s>lokasaṃvṛtisatya</s>) and the truth in the ultimate sense (<s>paramārthasatya</s>)' —

body.text: iti. tathā paramārthasatyam iti. paramasya jñānasyārthaḥ paranārthaḥ. paramārthaś ca satyaṃ ca tat paranārthasatyaṃ yathānyena jñānena laukikena gṛhyate. tathā saṃvṛtisatyaṃ. saṃvṛtyā saṃvyavahārena jñānena vā kliṣṭenākliṣṭena vā gṛhyata iti saṃvṛtisatyaṃ. trividhaṃ hi yogācārāṇāṃ sat. [Tib. 185a] paramārthasaṃvṛtisat dravyasac ca. dravyataḥ svalakṣaṇataḥ sad dravyasad iti.
body.translated_text: thus. And regarding ultimate truth (<s>paramārthasatya</s>): the object (<s>artha</s>) of the supreme (<s>parama</s>) knowledge — that is the ultimate (<s>paramārtha</s>). It is both ultimate and truth — hence ultimate truth. As it is apprehended by another, worldly knowledge — so too is conventional truth. That which is apprehended by convention (<s>saṃvṛti</s>), by usage (<s>saṃvyavahāra</s>), or by knowledge — whether afflicted or unafflicted — is conventional truth. For the <s>yogācāra</s>s, existence is threefold: ultimately existent (<s>paramārthasat</s>), conventionally existent (<s>saṃvṛtisat</s>), and substantially existent (<s>dravyasat</s>). That which is existent substantially, by own-characteristic, is substantially existent.

body.text: iti vistaraḥ. vṛttaṃ śīlaṃ. tad avyāsaṃgakāraṇam avikṣepakāraṇam ācārakāraṇaṃ ca. satyadarśanasyānulomam iti. yac chrutaṃ satyadarśanādhikārikaṃ
body.translated_text: in detail. Conduct (<s>vṛtta</s>) is morality (<s>śīla</s>). That is the cause of non-obstruction, the cause of non-distraction, and the cause of [proper] behavior. 'Conforming to the seeing of the truths' — whatever has been learned that pertains to the seeing of the truths

body.text: tac chrutam udgṛhṇāti paṭhati. arthaṃ vā śṛṇoti tadarthaṃ śrotradvāreṇa vijānāti. katham. ubhayālaṃbanā cintāmayīti darśayann āha. kadācid vyaṃjanenārgham ākarṣati. vyaṃjananirvṛttena nāmnārtham ākarṣaty ayam asya nāmno 'rtha iti. kadācid arthena vyaṃjanam ākarṣati. idam asyābhidheyasyārthasya vyaṃjanaṃ nāmety arthaḥ. ayaṃ hi vyaṃjanaśabdo nāmni prayuktaḥ. sūtre 'pi coktaṃ. svarthaṃ suvyaṃjanam iti. asyāṃ tu kalpanāyām iti vistareṇācāryaḥ. cintāmayī prajñā na sidhyatīti. śrutabhāvanāmayīlakṣaṇasaṃkīrṇaṃ lakṣaṇam ucyate. nāsaṃkīrṇam iti na sidhyati. yuktinidhyānaja iti. yuktyā nidhyānaṃ nitīraṇaṃ. tato jāta iti. hetau mayaḍvidhānād iti. āptavacanaṃ śrutaṃ sahetu śrutamayyāḥ prajñāyāḥ. atra mayaḍvidhānaṃ. śrutahetukā prajñā śrutamayīti. evaṃ yuktinidhyānaṃ cintā sahetuś cintāmayyāḥ. atra mayaḍvidhānāt. samādhir bhāvanā sahetur bhāvanāmayyāḥ. atra mayaḍvidhānaṃ. tatprakṛtivacane mayaḍ iti lakṣaṇāt. tasya vikāra iti vā lakṣaṇāt. aupacārikas tu vikāraḥ. śrutavikāra iva śrutamayīti lakṣaṇāṃtaraṃ copasaṃkhyātavyaṃ. annamayāḥ prāṇās tṛṇamayyo gāva iti loke prayogadarśanāt.
body.translated_text: that learning one apprehends and recites. Or, one hears the meaning — one comprehends that meaning through the door of hearing. How? Showing that the wisdom born of reflection (<s>cintāmayī</s>) has both [name and meaning] as its object, he says: 'Sometimes through the expression, one draws out the meaning' — through a name produced from the expression, one draws out the meaning: 'this is the meaning of this name.' 'Sometimes through the meaning, one draws out the expression' — 'this is the expression, the name, of this referent (<s>abhidheya</s>)' — this is the meaning. For this word 'expression' (<s>vyañjana</s>) is used in the sense of 'name.' And in the <s>sūtra</s> too it is said: 'well-meaning, well-expressed' (<s>svarthaṃ suvyañjanam</s>). 'But in this supposition' — in detail, [says] the <s>Ācārya</s>: 'the wisdom born of reflection is not established' — a definition mixed with the characteristics of wisdom born of learning and of meditation is stated, not an unmixed one — hence it is not established. 'Born from reasoning and examination (<s>yuktinidhyānaja</s>)' — reasoning (<s>yukti</s>) is examination (<s>nidhyāna</s>), which is investigation (<s>nitīraṇa</s>); born from that. 'Because of the <s>mayaṭ</s> suffix [being used] in the sense of cause' — the testimony of the trustworthy (<s>āptavacana</s>), the learning (<s>śruta</s>), is the cause of the wisdom born of learning. The <s>mayaṭ</s> suffix applies here: wisdom caused by learning is 'born of learning' (<s>śrutamayī</s>). Similarly, reasoning and examination constitute reflection (<s>cintā</s>), which is the cause of the [wisdom] born of reflection; the <s>mayaṭ</s> suffix applies here. Concentration (<s>samādhi</s>) is meditation (<s>bhāvanā</s>), which is the cause of the [wisdom] born of meditation; the <s>mayaṭ</s> suffix applies here. From the grammatical rule: '<s>mayaṭ</s> [is used] in expressing what constitutes that (<s>tatprakṛtivacane</s>).' Or from the rule: 'modification of that (<s>tasya vikāra</s>).' But the modification is figurative. 'A modification of learning, as it were, is born of learning' — and another grammatical rule should be considered. Because in the world, [such] usage is seen: 'living beings are made of food (<s>annamaya</s>),' 'cows are made of grass (<s>tṛṇamaya</s>).'

body.text: (VI.6-8) saṃsargākuśalavitarkadūrīkaraṇād iti. saṃsargadūrīkaraṇaṃ yad advitīyavihāritvaṃ. tasmāt kāyena [Tib. 185b] vyapakṛṣṭo bhavati. akuśalavitarkadūrīkaraṇaṃ yat kliṣṭavitarkavivarjanaṃ. tasmāc cittena vyapakṛṣṭo bhavati. labdhenāpraṇītenāprabhūtena paritāsa iti. paritāso daurmanasyaṃ. tena hi paritasyati. upakṣīyata ity arthaḥ. apraṇītatvād aprabhūtatvād vā. tena labdhena paritāso 'saṃtuṣṭiḥ. alabdhe tu praṇīte 'pi vā prabhūte 'pi vā icchābhilāṣā mahecchatety ācāryamataṃ. kāmāvacaryāv eveti. lobhākuśalasvabhāvatvāt.
body.translated_text: (VI.6-8) 'From the removal of association with the unwholesome and of unwholesome thoughts (<s>vitarka</s>)' — the removal of association is dwelling alone. From that, one is physically withdrawn. The removal of unwholesome thoughts is the avoidance of afflicted thoughts. From that, one is mentally withdrawn. 'Distress (<s>paritāsa</s>) with what has been obtained, which is unrefined and insufficient' — distress is mental displeasure (<s>daurmanasya</s>). For one is distressed by that — the meaning is: one is diminished. Because of its being unrefined or because of its being insufficient — distress with what has been obtained is dissatisfaction (<s>asaṃtuṣṭi</s>). But regarding what has not been obtained, or that which is more refined, or that which is more abundant — [having] desire and longing is great desire (<s>mahecchatā</s>) — this is the <s>Ācārya</s>'s view. 'Belonging to the Desire Realm only' — because [great desire and dissatisfaction] have the own-nature of greed (<s>lobha</s>), which is unwholesome.

body.text: prahāṇabhāvanārāmatā nirodhamārgāramatā. sā na saṃtuṣṭisvabhāveti. kathaṃ caturtho 'py ayam āryavaṃśo bhavaty alobhasvabhāva ity ata āha. bhavakāmarāgavaimukhyād iti. bhavarāgavaimukhyāt. kāmarāgavaimukhyāc ca. vaimukhyaṃ cālobha iti. parityaktasvavṛttikarmāṃtebhya iti. parityaktasvavṛttibhyaḥ parityaktasvakarmāṃtebhyaś ca. tatra vṛttijīvikā yayā jīvyate annapānādinā. karmāṃtaḥ kṛṣiśilpādiḥ. iti bhavavibhavahetor iti. itiśabdo bhavavibhavaprakārābhidyotakaḥ. tatra bhavaprakāre tṛṣṇā aho batāhaṃ indraḥ syāṃ cakravartī syām iti evamādi. [Tib. 186a] vibhavatṛṣṇāpi viṇāśatṛṣṇā. aho batocchidyeyaṃ na bhaveyaṃ paraṃ maraṇād ityādi.
body.translated_text: 'Delight in the cultivation of abandonment, delight in cessation and the path' — that is not of the own-nature of contentment (<s>saṃtuṣṭi</s>). How then is this fourth lineage of the Nobles (<s>āryavaṃśa</s>) also of the own-nature of non-greed (<s>alobha</s>)? — therefore he says: 'Because of turning away from passion for becoming (<s>bhavarāga</s>) and passion for sensual desire (<s>kāmarāga</s>).' From turning away from passion for becoming. And from turning away from passion for sensual desire. And turning away is non-greed. 'From those who have abandoned their own livelihood and occupations' — from those who have abandoned their own livelihood and from those who have abandoned their own occupations. Therein, livelihood (<s>vṛtti</s>) is the means of living — that by which one lives, through food, drink, and the like. Occupation (<s>karmānta</s>) is agriculture, crafts, and the like. 'For the sake of becoming and prosperity' — the word 'thus' (<s>iti</s>) illuminates the modes of becoming and prosperity. Therein, craving in the mode of becoming: 'Oh, may I become <s>Indra</s>! May I become a universal monarch!' — and so forth. Craving for destruction (<s>vibhavatṛṣṇā</s>) too is the craving for annihilation: 'Oh, may I be cut off! May I not exist after death!' — and so forth.

body.text: (VI.9) smṛtir eva smṛtam iti. bhāve ktavidhānam iti darśayati. avatāras tīrthaṃ yenāvatarati. pratyāsannam atyarthaṃ rāgacarita iti. yasyālpena rāgaḥ śīghram upatiṣṭhate. sa pratyāsannaṃ rāgacaritaḥ. yasyādhimātro rāgaḥ. so 'tyarthaṃ rāgacaritaḥ.
body.translated_text: (VI.9) 'Mindfulness itself is what is remembered (<s>smṛtam</s>)' — he shows that the <s>kta</s> suffix is used in the sense of the state [of the action]. A ford (<s>avatāra</s>) is a descent (<s>tīrtha</s>), by which one descends. 'Very close and very intense, one of passionate temperament (<s>rāgacarita</s>)' — one for whom passion quickly arises with little [provocation] — that one is 'very close, of passionate temperament.' One whose passion is intense — that one is 'very intense, of passionate temperament.'

body.text: avicitrālaṃbanatvād iti. vāyau varṇasaṃsthānavaicitryānupalabdheḥ.
body.translated_text: 'Because of having an unvariegated object' — because in wind, no variety of color or shape is perceived.

body.text:
abahirmukhatvād aṃtarmukhatvāt. eṣā vitarkopacchedāya saṃvartata iti prakṛtaṃ. tadviṣayopanidhyānād iti. cakṣurviṣayanirūpaṇād ity arthaḥ.
(VI.10, 11) vinīlakādyākārālabanām ity ādigrahaṇena vipūyakādigrahaṇaṃ. vipaṭumakam iti yad utpannakrimikaṃ. caturvidhaṃ rāgavastu nāstīti. varṇasaṃsthānasparśopacārātmakam. adhimuktiprādeśikamanasikāratvād iti. adhimuktimanasikāratvāt prādeśikamanasikāratvāc cety arthaḥ. adhimuktipradhāno 'yaṃ manasikāraḥ. prādeśikaś cāyam avyāpīty arthaḥ. na hy aśubhā paṃcaskandhālaṃbanā. sakalabhūmyālambanā vā. kiṃ tarhi. rūpaskandhaikadeśālaṃbanā [Tib. 186b] tadbhāvāt. nāśubhayā kleśaprahāṇaṃ viṣkaṃbhaṇāmātraṃ tu bhavatīty arthaḥ. svāṃgāvayave cittam upanibadhnātīti vacanāt na tāvat stryaṃgāvayave prayogakāla eva saṃrāgahetuparihārāt. asthi viśodhayann iti. asthino māṃsam apanayan sakalām asthiśaṃkalāṃ paśyati. yathoktaṃ.
body.translated_text:
'Because of not being outward-directed, because of being inward-directed' — this pertains to the cutting off of thoughts — this is the topic under discussion. 'Because of the examination of that object' — the meaning is: because of the scrutiny of the object of visual consciousness.
(VI.10, 11) 'Having the aspect of bluish discoloration and the rest as its object' — by the word 'and the rest,' the bloated (<s>vipūyaka</s>) and so forth are included. '<s>Vipaṭumaka</s>' — that in which worms have appeared. 'The fourfold object of passion does not exist [therein]' — [the fourfold object] consisting of color, shape, touch, and figurative designation. 'Because of the mental attention being of conviction (<s>adhimukti</s>) and partial (<s>prādeśika</s>)' — the meaning is: because the mental attention is of [the nature of] conviction, and because it is partial. This mental attention is predominantly conviction. And it is partial, meaning non-pervasive. For the contemplation of the impure (<s>aśubhā</s>) does not have the five aggregates as its object, nor all grounds as its object. Rather, it has a portion of the form aggregate as its object — because of being of that nature. 'The abandonment of afflictions by means of the impure [contemplation] is mere suppression (<s>viṣkambhaṇa</s>), not [complete abandonment]' — this is the meaning. 'One fixes the mind on a part of one's own body' — from this statement, it is not on a part of a woman's body, even at the time of initial application — because of the avoidance of the cause of passion. 'Cleaning the bone' — removing the flesh from the bone, one sees the entire skeleton. As stated:

children.text:
yo bhaven navako bhikṣuḥ śaikṣo 'saṃprāptamānasaḥ
gacched asau śivipathikāṃ haṃtuṃ rāgaṃ yadīcchati
tato vinīlakaṃ paśyet tataḥ paśyed vipūyakaṃ.
tato vyādhmātakaṃ paśyed asthiśaṃkalikām apīti.
children.translated_text:
'Whatever monk is a beginner, a learner (<s>śaikṣa</s>) who has not yet attained mastery of mind,
let him go to the charnel ground if he wishes to destroy passion.
Then let him observe the bluish-discolored [corpse], then observe the oozing [corpse],
then observe the bloated [corpse], and the skeleton too' —

body.text: atra samāsato 'śubhāyāṃ vartamāno yogācāras trividhaḥ. ādikarmikaḥ kṛtaparijayaḥ atikrāṃtamanasikāraś ca. tatra saṃkṣepacitta ādikarmiko yogācāra ekasmin pādāṃguṣṭhe mana upanibadhya pādāṃguṣṭhaṃ klidyamānaṃ paśyaty etan māṃsam evaṃ yāvat sarvaṃ śarīram asthiśaṃkalām adhimucyate. kṛtaparijayas tu tathaiva yāvat kapālārdhaṃ. atikrāṃtamanasikāras tathaiva yāvad bhruvor madhye cittaṃ dhārayati. vistaracittas tu āsamudrāsthivistāraḥ saṃkṣepād ādikarmika ity evamāditrividha iti. evaṃ ca kṛtvā catuṣkoṭikaḥ praśno bhavatīti. jitājitamanaskārayor iti vistaraḥ. [Tib. 187a] prathamā koṭir jitamanaskārasya svakāyālaṃbanā aśubhā ālaṃbanaparīttatayā parīttā kāyasyālpatvāt.
body.translated_text: thus. Here, in summary, the <s>yogācāra</s> engaged in the impure [contemplation] is threefold: a beginner (<s>ādikarmika</s>), one with experience (<s>kṛtaparijaya</s>), and one who has transcended the mental attention (<s>atikrāntamanaskāra</s>). Therein, the beginner <s>yogācāra</s>, of contracted mind, fixing the mind on a single big toe, sees the big toe becoming moist — this is the flesh — thus, up to the entire body, one applies conviction to [seeing it as] a skeleton. The one with experience, similarly, up to half the skull. The one who has transcended the mental attention, similarly, maintains the mind up to the middle of the eyebrows. But the one of expansive mind — [extends to] the expanse of bones up to the ocean. The contracted one [starts as] a beginner — and so forth as the threefold [classification]. And having done so, a fourfold investigation arises. 'Of those with mastered and unmastered mental attention' — in detail. The first alternative: for one with mastered mental attention, the impure [contemplation] focused on one's own body — being limited in object due to the smallness of the body

body.text: na vaśitāparīttatayā jitamanaskāratvād atikrāṃtamanasikāratvād ity arthaḥ. dvitīyā koṭir ajitamanaskārasya samudraparyaṃtālaṃbanā aśubhā. vaśitāparīttatatayā parīttā ajitamanaskāratvāt. nālaṃbanaparīttatayā samudraparyaṃtālaṃbanatvāt. tṛtīyā koṭir ajitamanaskārasya svakāyālaṃbanā aśubhā. ālaṃbanaparīttatayāpi parīttā kāyasyālpatvāt. vaśitāparīttatayāpi ajitamanaskāratvāt. caturthī koṭir jitamanaskārasya samudraparyaṃtālaṃbanā aśubhā. nāpy ālaṃbanaparīttatayā parīttā samudraparyaṃtālaṃbanatvāt. nāpi vaśitāparīttatayā jitamanaskāratvāt.
body.translated_text: — not limited in mastery, because of having mastered the mental attention, meaning having transcended the mental attention. The second alternative: for one with unmastered mental attention, the impure [contemplation] extending to the ocean — limited in mastery because of having unmastered mental attention, but not limited in object because of extending to the ocean. The third alternative: for one with unmastered mental attention, the impure [contemplation] focused on one's own body — limited in object too, because of the smallness of the body, and limited in mastery too, because of having unmastered mental attention. The fourth alternative: for one with mastered mental attention, the impure [contemplation] extending to the ocean — neither limited in object, because of extending to the ocean, nor limited in mastery, because of having mastered the mental attention.

body.text: (VI.12) sa sāmāṃtakadhyānāṃtareṣv iti. sāmaṃtakeṣu dhyānāṃtare catuḥṣu dhyāneṣu kāmadhātau ceti daśa bhūmikā. dhyānasāmaṃtakānāṃ catuṣṭvāt. ata evārthālaṃbaneti. varṇasaṃsthānālaṃbanatvād arthālaṃbanā. na tu nāmālaṃbanety abhiprāyaḥ. nāmnaiva siddham aśubhākārety ākārārthaṃ na sūtrayitavyam ity abhiprāyaḥ. yadadhvikā tadadhvikālaṃbaneti. cakṣurvijñānavad atītāyā atītam ālaṃbanam evaṃ yāvat pratyutpannāyāḥ pratyutpannam iti. svālaṃbananiyatatvāt. adhimuktimanasikāratvān na sūtritaṃ. ucitānucitatvād iti. anādim atisaṃsāre ucitatvād vairāgyalābhikī. anucitatvāt prāyogikī.
body.translated_text: (VI.12) 'That [impure contemplation operates] in the preliminary stages of <s>dhyāna</s> and the intermediate [stages]' — in the preliminary stages, in the four intermediate <s>dhyāna</s>s, in the four <s>dhyāna</s>s, and in the Desire Realm — [thus] ten grounds. Because the preliminary stages of the <s>dhyāna</s>s are four. 'For this very reason, it has a real object (<s>arthālambana</s>)' — because of having color and shape as its object, it has a real object — the intent is: not a name-object (<s>nāmālambana</s>). 'The aspect of the impure is established by name alone' — the intent is: one should not formulate [a sūtra] for the purpose of [defining] the aspect. 'Of whatever time-period, it has an object of that time-period' — like visual consciousness, when [the contemplation is] past, the object is past; similarly up to: when present, the object is present. Because of being fixed to its own object. 'It is not formulated because of the mental attention being of conviction' — [this is not stated in sūtra because it involves conviction-based attention rather than direct perception]. 'Because of being practiced and unpracticed' — because of being practiced from beginningless <s>saṃsāra</s>, the [contemplation] that leads to dispassion [is natural]. Because of being unpracticed, the [contemplation] of initial application [requires effort].

body.text: (VI.13) kāyasmṛtyupasthānādīni prajñāsvabhāvāni. [Tib. 187b] tadbalādhānavṛttitvāt. tasyāḥ smṛter balasyādhānena vṛttir eṣām iti smṛtibalādhānavṛttīni kāyasmṛtyupasthānādīni kāyaprajñādravyādīni smṛtyupathānīty ucyaṃte. tadvad ānāpānaprajñā smṛtibalādhānavṛttitvād ānāpānasmṛtir ity ucyate. paṃcasu bhūmiṣv iti. triṣu sāmaṃtakeṣu caturthasāmaṃtakavarjyeṣu. dhyānāṃtare. kāmadhātau ceti paṃcasu bhūmiṣu. kiṃ kāraṇaṃ. upekṣāsaṃprayogitvāt. yasmāt prathamadhyāne sāmaṃtakādiṣūpekṣāvedanā bhavati. caturthadhyāne sāmaṃtake tu yady apy upekṣāsti. sā tv abhūmir āśvāsapraśvāsānāṃ. atha kim artham eṣopekṣā saṃprayogiṇy evāvadhāryata iti. ato bravīti vitarkānuguṇatvād iti. tatpratipakṣasya vitarkapratipakṣasyānāpānasmṛtes tābhyāṃ sukhaduḥkhābhyām asaṃprayogaḥ. sukhasaumanasyayoś cāvadhānaparipaṃthitvāt. ābhogapratyanīkatvāt. tasyāś cānāpānasmṛter avadhānasādhyatvāt tābhyām asaṃprayoga iti. vitarkānuguṇatvāt.
body.translated_text: (VI.13) The foundations of mindfulness (<s>kāyasmṛtyupasthāna</s>) and the rest have the own-nature of wisdom (<s>prajñā</s>). Because they function through the application of the power of that mindfulness (<s>smṛti</s>). The functioning of these through the application of the power of that mindfulness — thus, [the contemplation of] the body and the rest, having the nature of wisdom (<s>prajñā</s>) with regard to the body and so forth, are called 'foundations of mindfulness' because they function through the power of mindfulness. Similarly, the wisdom regarding breathing in and out (<s>ānāpānaprajñā</s>), because it functions through the application of the power of mindfulness, is called 'mindfulness of breathing' (<s>ānāpānasmṛti</s>). 'In five grounds' — in three preliminary stages, excluding the preliminary stage of the fourth [<s>dhyāna</s>], in the intermediate <s>dhyāna</s>, and in the Desire Realm — in these five grounds. For what reason? Because of being associated with equanimity (<s>upekṣā</s>). Since in the preliminary stages of the first <s>dhyāna</s> and the rest, equanimity-feeling exists. But in the preliminary stage of the fourth <s>dhyāna</s>, although equanimity exists, that [stage] is not a ground for breathing in and out. 'Now for what purpose is it determined [to be] associated with equanimity alone?' Therefore he says: 'Because of conformity with thought (<s>vitarka</s>)' — the non-association of mindfulness of breathing, which is the antidote of that thought-antidote, with those two — pleasure and suffering — [is established]. And because pleasure and mental pleasure are obstacles to attentiveness (<s>avadhāna</s>) — because they are opposed to application (<s>ābhoga</s>). And because that mindfulness of breathing is to be accomplished through attentiveness, there is non-association with those two — because of conformity with thought.

body.text: kileti. kilaśabdaḥ paramatadyotakaḥ. tenedaṃ pakṣāṃtaram upanyasyate ye tu mauleṣv iti vistaraḥ. pareṇeti. caturthād dhyānād ārabhya. [Tib. 188a]
body.translated_text: '<s>Kila</s>' — the word <s>kila</s> indicates the other's position. By this, this alternative view is presented — 'those who [hold that] in the fundamental [<s>dhyāna</s>s]' — and so forth in detail. 'By the other' — beginning from the fourth <s>dhyāna</s>.

body.text: kāmadhātvāśrayeti. tatra vitarkabhūyastvāt. prāyogikī anucitatvāt. vairāgyalābhikī ucitatvāt. idaṃdharmāṇām iti. ayaṃ dharmo bauddha eṣām
body.translated_text: 'Having a Desire-Realm basis' — because therein discursive thought (<s>vitarka</s>) predominates. 'Preparatory (<s>prāyogikī</s>)' — because of being unpracticed. 'Obtained through dispassion (<s>vairāgyalābhikī</s>)' — because of being practiced. '<s>Idaṃdharmāṇām</s>' — 'this <s>dharma</s> is the Buddhist [teaching] of these'

body.text: iti idaṃdharmāṇaḥ. teṣām eva bauddhānām ity arthaḥ. upadeśābhāvād iti. bāhyānāṃ hi prāṇāyāmopadeśo 'sti nānāpānasmṛtyupadeśa tit. svayaṃ ca sūkṣmadharmānabhisaṃbodhād iti. upadeśam aṃtareṇa yasmād bāhyānāṃ nāsti svayaṃ sūkṣmadharmābhisaṃbodhaḥ. sūkṣmatvaṃ punar asyāḥ ṣaṭkāraṇayuktatvāt. kāyaṃ cittaṃ vādhyupekṣyety anāsajyety arthaḥ. vitastivyāmāṃtaram iti. balavaddurbalaprāṇiyogāt.
body.translated_text: — hence <s>idaṃdharmāṇaḥ</s>; the meaning is: of those very Buddhists. 'Because of the absence of instruction' — for outsiders have instruction in <s>prāṇāyāma</s> (breath control), not instruction in mindfulness of breathing (<s>ānāpānasmṛti</s>). 'And because they themselves do not awaken to subtle <s>dharma</s>s' — because without instruction, outsiders do not have the awakening to subtle <s>dharma</s>s by themselves. Moreover, its subtlety is because of being connected with six causes. 'Surveying the body or mind' — the meaning is: without attaching. '<s>Vitastivyāma</s> interval' — because of the connection with beings of greater or lesser vital capacity.

body.text: yāvad vāyumaṇḍalam ity adhastād anugacchati. vairaṃbhāś ca vāyava ity upariṣṭhāt. tattvamanasikāratvān na yuktam etat. yāvad vāyumaṇḍalaṃ vairaṃbhāś ca vāyava iti. adhimuktimanaskārasyaiṣā kalpanā yujyeta.
body.translated_text: 'Up to the wind-disk (<s>vāyumaṇḍala</s>)' — it follows [the breath] downward. 'And the <s>vairaṃbha</s> winds' — upward. Because of being a true mental attention (<s>tattvamanasikāra</s>), this is not fitting — 'up to the wind-disk and the <s>vairaṃbha</s> winds.' This imagining would be appropriate for a mental attention of resolve (<s>adhimuktimanaskāra</s>).

body.text: kim anugrāhakā ete yāvad uṣṇā iti. sthāpanaiveyaṃ draṣṭavyā. kāyapradeśa evānugrāhakādiviśeṣasthāpanataḥ. tadāśritāś cittacaitta iti. tatpratibaddhavṛttaya ity arthaḥ. [Tib. 188b] uttarottareṣu kuśalamūleṣv iti. smṛtyupasthānoṣmagatādiṣv iti. darśanamārgādiṣv ity ādiśabdena bhāvanāmārgagrahaṇaṃ.
body.translated_text: 'Are these supportive, up to warm?' — this should be seen as mere designation (<s>sthāpanā</s>). Because of the designation of the distinctions of supportive and the rest in terms of bodily regions only. 'The mind and mental factors that depend on that' — the meaning is: those whose functioning is bound to that. 'In successively higher wholesome roots' — in the foundations of mindfulness, the heat stage (<s>uṣmagata</s>), and the rest. 'In the path of seeing and the rest' — by the word 'and the rest,' the path of cultivation is included.

body.text: kṣayajñānādiviśuddhir iti. ādiśabdena anutpādajñānāśaikṣasamyagdṛṣṭigrahaṇaṃ.
body.translated_text: 'The purity of the knowledge of destruction (<s>kṣayajñāna</s>) and the rest' — by the word 'and the rest,' the knowledge of non-arising (<s>anutpādajñāna</s>) and right view of the learnerless (<s>aśaikṣasamyagdṛṣṭi</s>) are included.

children.translated_text: 'The inhalation and exhalation from which the body' —

body.text: iti. ānāpānasmṛtisaṃbaṃdhena sarvabhūmikāv ānāpānau nirdiśyate. yadbhūmiko hi kāya iti. kāmāvacaraḥ yāvat tṛtīyadhyānabhūmikas tadbhūmikāv etau. nānyabhūmikau. kāyacittaviśeṣasaṃniśritā iti. kāyaviśeṣasaṃniśritāḥ cittaviśeṣasaṃniśritāś cāśvāsapraśvāśāḥ. kasmād ity āha. ārūpoyakalalādigatānām abhāvād iti. kāyābhāvād ārūpyagatānāṃ na bhavaṃti. kalalādigatānāṃ ca. kalalārbudapeśyādigatānāṃ ca na bhavaṃti. kāyaviśeṣābhāvāt suṣirakāyābhāvād ity arthaḥ. acittānāṃ ca na bhavaṃti. cittābhāvāt. caturthadhyānasamāpannānām api na bhavaṃti. āśvāsapraśvāsabhūmicittaviśeṣābhāvāt. ata evāha. yadi kāyaḥ suṣira iti vistaraḥ. indriyavinirbhāgitvād iti. indriyapṛthagvṛttitvād ity arthaḥ. kāyopacayenāpacayān naupacayikau. [Tib. 189a] ucchinnānāṃ cāśvāsapraśvāsānāṃ punaḥpratisaṃdhānān na vipākajau. na hy etad vipākarūpasyāsti vipākātmakasya rūpasya cakṣurāder etat punaḥpratisaṃdhānaṃ nāsti. arūpasya tu cittacaittasya punaḥpratisaṃdhānaṃ na vāryate. nādhareṇairyāpathikanairmāṇikeneti. airyāpathikaṃ nairnāṇikaṃ ca cittam adharabhūmikaṃ saṃmukhībhavati yāvac caturthadhyānopapannasyety
body.translated_text: thus. In connection with mindfulness of breathing (<s>ānāpānasmṛti</s>), the inhalation and exhalation are taught in relation to all grounds. 'For to whichever ground the body belongs' — the Desire Realm up to the third <s>dhyāna</s> ground — these two [inhalation and exhalation] belong to that ground, not to another ground. 'Depending on a special [condition of] the body and mind' — inhalation and exhalation depend on a special [condition of] the body and depend on a special [condition of] the mind. Why? — he says. 'Because of the absence [of breath] in those gone to the Formless [Realm], <s>kalala</s> [embryos], and the rest' — because of the absence of a body, those gone to the Formless Realm do not have [breath]. And those gone to the <s>kalala</s>, <s>arbuda</s>, <s>peśī</s>, and the rest also do not have [breath] — because of the absence of a special body, meaning the absence of a body with apertures. And those without mind also do not have [breath] — because of the absence of mind. Those absorbed in the fourth <s>dhyāna</s> also do not have [breath] — because of the absence of a special mind belonging to the ground of inhalation and exhalation. Therefore he says: 'if the body has apertures' — and so forth in detail. 'Because of the disjunction of faculties (<s>indriyavinirbhāgitva</s>)' — the meaning is: because of the faculties functioning separately. 'Not nutritional (<s>naupacayika</s>), because of growing and decaying with the body.' 'Not fruition-born (<s>vipākaja</s>), because of re-joining of breath that has been cut off' — for this does not exist for fruition-form, for materiality that has the nature of fruition — such as the eye and the rest — this re-joining does not exist. But for formless [things] — mind and mental factors — re-joining is not prevented. 'Not by means of the lower deportmental (<s>airyāpathika</s>) and magical-creation (<s>nairmāṇika</s>) [consciousness]' — the deportmental and magical-creation consciousness of a lower ground becomes present up to [one who has] attained the fourth <s>dhyāna</s>

body.text: ata āśaṃkyocyate. nādhgarabhūmikābhyāṃ tābhyām upalakṣaṇam iti.
body.translated_text: — therefore, anticipating [an objection], it is said: 'not by means of those two belonging to the lower ground' — this is an illustration.

body.text: (VI.15, 16) vipaśyanāyāḥ saṃpādanārtham iti. prajñāyāḥ saṃpādanārtham ity arthaḥ. niṣpannasamādher api hi prajñām aṃtareṇa kleśā na prahīyaṃte. jñānavadhyāḥ kleśā iti vacānāt. kutaḥ prnar etat smṛtyupasthānabhāvanayā vipaśyanā saṃpadyata iti. sūtrāt. ekāyano 'yaṃ bhikṣavo mārgo yad uta smṛtyupasthānāni. kevalo 'yaṃ kuśalarāśiḥ yad uat catvāri smṛtyupasthānānīti vacanāt.
body.translated_text: (VI.15, 16) 'For the purpose of accomplishing insight (<s>vipaśyanā</s>)' — the meaning is: for the purpose of accomplishing wisdom (<s>prajñā</s>). For even one whose concentration is perfected does not abandon the afflictions without wisdom — because of the statement 'afflictions are to be slain by knowledge.' From where then does insight arise through the cultivation of the foundations of mindfulness? From the <s>sūtra</s>: because of the statement 'This, O monks, is a one-way path, namely the foundations of mindfulness. This is the complete wholesome mass, namely the four foundations of mindfulness.'

body.text: iti vedanā vit. svabhāva evaiṣāṃ svalakṣaṇam iti. kaḥ svabhāvaḥ. kāyasya bhūtabhautikatvaṃ. vedanāyā anubhavatvaṃ. cittasyopalabdhitvam. ebhuas tribhyo 'nyeṣāṃ yathāsvaṃ svabhāvaḥ. duḥkhatā sāsravāṇām iti. [Tib. 189b] āryapratikūlalakṣaṇaṃ duḥkham iti vyākhyātam etat. dharmās tribhyo 'nya iti asaṃbhinnavyavasthām abhisaṃdhāyaivam ucyate. sṃbhinnavyavasthāyāṃ tu kāyādayo 'pi nigṛhyaṃte. punaḥ sarve saṃskṛtā asaṃskṛtāś ca dharmā draṣṭavyāḥ.
body.translated_text: thus: feeling-knower. 'Their own-characteristic is their own-nature itself.' What is the own-nature? Of the body, being composed of the great elements and derivative matter (<s>bhūtabhautikatva</s>). Of feeling, the nature of experiencing (<s>anubhavatva</s>). Of the mind, the nature of apprehension (<s>upalabdhitva</s>). Of the others — those other than these three — the own-nature is as applicable. 'Suffering-nature of the contaminated' — the characteristic 'that which is adverse to the Nobles is suffering' — this has been explained. '<s>Dharma</s>s are those other than the three' — this is said with reference to the undivided classification. But in the divided classification, body and the rest too are included. Again, all conditioned and unconditioned <s>dharma</s>s are to be seen [as the objects of the <s>dharma</s>-foundation of mindfulness].

body.text: yasmāt saṃsargālaṃbanam apekṣyeyaṃ prajñopatiṣṭhate. tasmāt smṛtyupasthānam ity ucyate.
body.translated_text: Because this wisdom is established in dependence on the objects of association and objects of apprehension (<s>saṃsargālaṃbana</s>), therefore it is called 'foundation of mindfulness' (<s>smṛtyupasthāna</s>).

body.text: 'ti viśeṣaṇaṃ. yasmāt smṛtyupasthānāni prāyogikāṇi nopapattilabhyāni. kasmāt prajñāsvabhāvam ity ucyate. kim anyathāpi smṛtyupasthānam astīti. ucyate.
body.translated_text: this is a qualifier. Because the foundations of mindfulness are obtained through application (<s>prāyogika</s>), not obtained through birth (<s>upapattilabhya</s>). 'Why is it said to have the nature of wisdom?' — 'Is there a foundation of mindfulness that is otherwise [than wisdom]?' He says:

children.translated_text: 'Others, from the objects of association and apprehension' —

body.text: iti. anye tatsahabhuvo vedanādayaḥ. saṃsargeṇa smṛtyupasthānaṃ saṃsargasmṛtyupasthānam. svabhāvasmṛtyupasthānasaṃsargāt. tadālaṃbanād iti. svabhāvasaṃsargasmṛtyupasthānālaṃbanād ālaṃbanasmṛtyupasthānaṃ. tadālaṃbanā ālaṃbanasmṛtyupasthānam ity apare paṭhaṃti. ālaṃbyaṃta ity ālaṃbanāḥ. ke. kāyavedanācittadharmāḥ. tad evaṃ sati tad ālaṃbanasmṛtyupasthānaṃ sarvadharmasvabhāvaṃ bhavati. uktaṃ ca bhagavatā. [Tib. 190a] sarvadharmā iti bhikṣavaś caturṇāṃ smṛtyupasthānānām etad adhivacanam iti.
body.translated_text: thus. The 'others' are feeling and the rest that co-arise with it. A foundation of mindfulness through association (<s>saṃsarga</s>) is the 'association-foundation of mindfulness' (<s>saṃsargasmṛtyupasthāna</s>) — through association with the essential-nature foundation of mindfulness. 'From apprehending that' — from apprehending the essential-nature and association foundations of mindfulness, there is the 'object-foundation of mindfulness' (<s>ālaṃbanasmṛtyupasthāna</s>).
